Prosperity!
Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Moonlight of Śiva Worship (Śivārcanacandrikā)

Salutations to Śiva, whose neck shines with the luster of a *tamāla* tree, who is the companion of Nārāyaṇī, and whom those learned in the scriptures declare to be this entire phenomenal world residing within even a small fraction of his perfect power.

The worship of Śiva for one’s own sake is a necessary duty for the followers of Śiva (Śaivas). Among their practices—whether purely Vedic, mixed, or Śaiva—the Śaiva method is the most excellent. Even within that, compared to the pure, the mixed, and even the solar (Saura) and other rites, the Śaiva rite performed with the Śakti is praiseworthy; it may be either complete or abbreviated.

It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Therefore, having compiled the worship of Śambhu together with Ambikā for the sake of the Self, I shall demonstrate it as extracted from all the divine Āgamas.
There is no fault in the blending of the meanings of the divine Āgamas, provided they are unified under a single authority; however, this is for the purpose of the Pāśupatas.

And among those [marks], confusion (sāṅkarya) is a defect; yet, even among them, one may be relied upon while another is accepted when required. This applies to human marks, but not to those of self-born (svāyaṃbhuva) origin and the like.
Even when relying upon a single scripture, having set aside what is stated therein,

the Lord taught that one should adopt from elsewhere whatever is commendable, [beginning with the words "That which is praised" and ending with "is required as a limb of worship," though this passage does not exist in other manuscripts].
Although the excellence [of the ritual] is equal for both, that which requires the ancillary rite of worship (*arcanāṅga*) is [preferred];
therein he taught that what is stated in another tantra is also equal [to what is stated here].
Therefore, this *Śrīśivārcanacandrikā* is composed using the necessary portions extracted from all the divine scriptures (*divyāgama*).
Having sipped water (ācamana) and adorned his body with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,

he should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and duly prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya). Having meditated upon the sanctuary of Śiva’s worship as consisting of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), he should perform the sequential worship of the gatekeepers at the unsurpassed door.
Having dispelled the threefold obstacles and entered [the ritual space], and having performed the worship of the weapons (*astra*) and so forth,

one should place all the implements of worship nearby. Seated upon the prepared seat, facing north toward the fire on the right side of the deity— and facing north toward the fire— one should proceed.
One should practice the fivefold purification. When two *muhūrtas* remain before the rising of the sun,
having risen, washed one’s feet and hands, and performed the smearing of ashes (*bhasmāvakuṇṭhana*),
one should contemplate the Supreme Lord in the heart if one is a common initiate (*sāmānyasamayin*), or at the *bindu* on the crown of the head if one is a distinguished initiate (*viśiṣṭasamayin*).
One who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa should contemplate this [disciple] as the teacher and awakener at the *dvādaśānta*; one should also proclaim his heart-pleasing names and deeds.
Having gone to a suitable place, one should perform the voiding of feces and urine.
Facing north during the morning twilights of the day, and facing south during the night;

or else facing east and west during the first and second halves of the day respectively; facing north at midday, and facing south during the night—one should [void] excrement, urine, and direct one's face toward the sky, the cardinal directions, and the moon.
(The phrase "the sight of the sun, Indra’s bow, and the stars") refers to the sight of the sun, the stars, and fire.
One should avoid facing a temple, a Brahmin, an Aśvattha tree, a cow, a sage, a learned man, or a woman.

One should not [cleanse] the anus with grass that is unfit for sacrifice or useless for worship, nor with clods of earth and the like, but certainly not with fine flowers, leaves, wood, fruits, and so forth. One should keep one's gaze downward while attending to the generative organ.

Taking water in his left hand, he should approach a body of water and perform purification with earth and water: one application of earth on the penis, five on the anus, ten on the left hand, six on the back, and seven applications of earth on both hands [the palms and backs]. [One should not use earth] from an anthill, at the root of a tree, or in a house.
On a path, in the midst of water, in saline soil dug up by mice, in a cow-pen, or in a temple.
At the edge of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like; on sandy ground; on a path; in a cremation ground;
on ground defiled by insects, husks, charcoal, and so forth; on dusty ground;
on ground strewn with earth remaining after half of another purification has been performed; on ground turned up by a plough; on mossy ground; and on gravel.

One should not take earth from a pure ground; rather, earth should be taken from a place where a corpse has been, having removed the upper layer of soil, so that it is sufficient for purification and no more remains. First, there should be purification of the anus with a quantity measuring half a *prasṛti*, and then with half that measure.

After that, [the amount] should be half of that; beyond that, it should be the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit for purification with urine. For cleansing the genitals, the clay should be double that amount; for sexual intercourse, it should be triple. This is the purification for a householder for the sake of purity of intention; beyond that, it is even more.

For those such as the *brahmacārī* and others, however, it is respectively double, triple, and quadruple. Whatever the duration of one's daytime impurity may be, half of that is prescribed for the night. Half of that is stated for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey in the forest. [One should wash] the feet up to the ankles with earth.
One should wash the wrists and the bases of the hands;
thereafter, one should wash up to the knees or the elbows with water. One who desires purity through cleansing should not perform the purification by pouring streams of water;
rather, the hands should be purified according to the prescribed rule using handfuls of water alone. For the purpose of applying earth and water during purification, [the hands] must be used.
The two attendants, holding [the vessel] with their left hands, should pour it into the soft [hand] of the right hand.

One should perform twelve mouthfuls of water-rinsing after voiding feces; one should perform four after urinating, and sixteen at the end of a meal. (Regarding "the reciter of mantras facing east"): one should wash the feet, hands, and face while facing east; (or regarding "one should do so facing east"): [alternatively] facing north.
Or, facing eastward, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
The Procedure for Cleansing the Teeth with a Tooth-stick (Dantadhāvana-vidhi)

Then, with the heart-mantra, one should take up a tooth-stick provided with bark, which has no knots, is cut level at the tip, and is frayed at the end. It should be as thick as the little finger or finer according to the fineness of one's teeth; for those committed to lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika), it should be eight finger-breadths long.

For those who enjoy pleasures, it is twelve finger-breadths; for the [four] castes, ten, and also seven or eight finger-breadths; for those who have abandoned [worldly life], six finger-breadths; and for women, four finger-breadths. It should be produced from the *jaṃbū*, *amlaka*, *kakkubha*, *aśoka*, *kapittha*, or *vakula* trees.
The roots of the Plakṣa and Udumbara, Jājī, Campaka, Śaṅkha-ja,
Atimuktaka, Kadamba, and Apāmārga— these are to be taken for the serpents; as well as Śairīṣa, Ciribilva, Karañjaka, Śrīparṇa, Dāru, Nirguṇḍī, Sārasa, Khadira, and Āyata.
[The juice] produced from the Akṣa, Kṣīrī, Dhava, Eraṇḍa, Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Agra, and Śigru; [and that] produced from Akulī, Śelu, Vānīra, Dhātrī, Nimba, Śara, Udumbara, Kharjūra,
Nālikera, Pālāśa, Tāla, and Vaṃśa.

One should avoid [images] made of grass, leaves, or piśāca-materials, as well as those made of bricks, charcoal, or ashes; likewise, one should avoid those made of gold and other such materials. One should also avoid the first, ninth, sixth, twelfth, and fifth lunar days (the five parvan days), the day of fasting, the three birth-asterisms, Saturday, Sunday, and the Vyatīpāta yoga.

On the day of a *grahaṇa-śrāddha*, and after sunrise, the cleaning of the teeth with a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) must be avoided. In the absence of tooth-sticks or on forbidden days, one should cleanse the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water or with [betel] leaves. [One should also perform] the scraping of the tongue.
One should perform purification with means for cleansing the impurities of the tongue.

The impurity produced from the soles of the feet, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, semen, feces, urine, and the limbs, as well as that which resides on the hands and feet—all such impurity must be cleansed. One becomes pure by washing the nose, ears, eyes, and other parts. Having thus purified the impurities, one should perform the ritual bath with water (vāruṇasnāna).
It removes every stain and destroys bad dreams and the like.
Now follows the procedure for bathing.

Having sipped water according to the rules, performed the ritual placement of mantras on the hands (*karanyāsa*), and restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), while holding *darbha* grass, he should address [the deity] thus: "O Lord, while the sun is situated in [the sign of] such-and-such, in this month, on this lunar day, and on this day of the week, by this best of rivers, I shall perform my bath for the sake of worshipping you; be gracious to me. Having thus made his request on pure ground...
Having dug to a depth of eight finger-breadths with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
and having extracted the earth from that spot with that same mantra,
one should take the earth for that object with either the root-mantra ending in *namaḥ* or the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, using first the earth extracted with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Having filled the pit, one should cast it onto the pure bank of a river, lake, pond, or similar body of water with the *namas* mantra at the end of the *śiras* mantra.
For the purpose of bathing, the southern bank of rivers and the like is highly recommended.
Then, having sprinkled the earth with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should [apply] the earth with the *astra* mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Having extracted the root [ingredients] and others, one should divide them into three parts with the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*.

Having washed from the navel down to the feet with one portion, one should visualize the second portion as blazing due to contact with the rays of the weapon-mantra, having been consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra, and then [apply it] to the entire body.

Having smeared himself with that [earth] and entered the water, he should stir the water with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), firmly block his ears with his two thumbs, his eyes with his two index fingers, and his nostrils with his two middle fingers; then,
while reciting the *praṇava* together with the root-mantra, he should visualize a blazing weapon-mantra within his heart and [protect] his body.

Visualizing his own skin as being tawny with a mass of fire, he should remain submerged in water for as long as possible. Alternatively, having divided the clay into two parts, he should bathe after smearing all his limbs with one portion that has been consecrated with the Astra-mantra. This is the bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*). Or else—

The fetching of earth is solely for the purpose of the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) to be described hereafter; however, the bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*) should be performed using pastes of turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth. In this context, [the following types of impurities are considered]:
semen, feces, urine, nasal mucus, saliva, tears, earwax, nails, and the dirt of the feet.

The purification of bodily impurities is achieved through cleansing and by means of rubbing with earth, tooth-sticks, turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth, as well as by sprinkling water— all of which are included within the concluding rites ending with the ritual bath.
(Purification occurs when one has poured water over the head, emerged from the water, and sipped water for ritual purification.)
The "impurity-bath" (*malasnāna*) consists of the recitation of the *praṇava* and other mantras at the time of bathing;

the "impurity-bath" [is further performed] by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) bath and so forth. Then, having risen from the water and gazed upon the sun, one should cast [the water] upon the head with the weapon-mantra. Having emerged from the water and sipped water (*ācamana*), one who is free from attachment—

If a twice-born man has performed the Vedic twilight devotions, he should also perform the Śaiva twilight devotion in brief; however, a detached twice-born man of the fourth stage should perform only the Śaiva twilight devotion.
The Concise Method for the Śaiva Twilight Rite (Sandhyā)

Having sprinkled [the weapon] on the head three times with drops of water held at the tips of the fingers while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should offer the arghya three times to the Weapon residing in the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala) using the Astra-gāyatrī: "We know the auspicious weapon; we meditate upon the fire of time; may that weapon inspire us."

One should recite the Astra-Gāyatrī according to one's ability; or else, in place of the Astra-Sandhyā, one should meditate on the Astra-mantra blazing within the heart. Then, for the sake of the ritual bath (vidhisnāna), [one should invoke] one of the sacred waters (tīrtha) such as the Gaṅgā from among those located at the Bindu-sthāna.

Having drawn [the water] with the *aṅkuśa* mudrā while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having established it before him with the *udbhava* mudrā while reciting the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should visualize that river, pond, or other body of water as being filled by that [water]. Thereafter, taking the portion of earth that was set aside for the purpose of the ritual bath:

Having entered water reaching up to the navel, one should— facing downstream in rivers, or facing east or north elsewhere— prepare a square bathing place (śivatīrtha) one cubit in size in front of oneself, in order to avoid the defects of the water that serve as the habitat for fish, frogs, and other creatures. Regarding this, the following [is said]:
The sequence is as follows: having divided the portion of earth into three parts in the left hand according to the directions of east, south, and north;
one should first consecrate the eastern part with the Astra-mantra repeated seven times, the southern part with the Kavaca-mantra or the other Angas repeated eight times, and the northern part...

Having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra recited ten times by Śiva, one should cast that [earth], over which the Astra-mantra has been recited, into all directions starting from the east using the Nārāca-mudrā and the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. In this manner, [one casts it] upon the portion of earth situated in the direction of Indra, the lord of the obstacles of the quarters.
By casting [the earth] in the various directions, all obstacles situated in those respective directions are pacified. Thereafter,
having cast half of the portion of earth consecrated by the recitation of Śiva’s mantra into the water with the root mantra for the sake of accomplishing the Śiva-tīrtha,
one should cast the other half with the root mantra for the sake of achieving a state equal to that Śiva-tīrtha.

One should cast [the earth] all around by the rotation of the arms. Thus, the portion of earth established in the direction of Soma, being composed solely of nectar, flows forth through the churning with the Śiva-mantra;
therefore, that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) becomes composed of nectar. Having thus prepared the Śiva-tīrtha:

One should bathe according to the prescribed rule. For that purpose, one should first smear all the limbs with a portion of earth consecrated by the recitation of the Brahma-mantra. By touching a portion of earth situated in the direction of Dharmarāja, the destruction of all sins occurs. Therefore, [one should perform this] with the Ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa mudrā.

Having closed the doors of the senses, such as the ears, and having immersed oneself in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha, one should remain within the water for as long as possible while meditating on the Śiva-mantra. Immersing all limbs within the water is the best [method], while immersing half the body is the middling.
The minor [form] consists of immersing only the face. Then, rising from the water, one should contemplate the left and right hands as being of the nature of the Moon and Sun, or as Śakti and Śiva;
and having sprinkled the head with waters consecrated by the *kumbha-mudrā* formed by those two hands, accompanied by the *vauṣaṭ* at the end, one should perform the consecration.
Having sprinkled water in the cardinal and intermediate directions with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for the purpose of pacifying obstacles,
and having poured that [water] into the water of the sacred site (*tīrtha*) for the sake of accomplishing the Śiva-tīrtha,
one should withdraw the remaining half within the boundary of the Śiva-tīrtha by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. In this manner, [one treats] the river and so forth.

If one is unable to go and bathe, one should bathe right there in the house on a pure patch of ground smeared with cow dung, while seated upon a pedestal, using nine, eight, or five jars filled with cold water over which the Śiva-mantras have been recited. This applies to kings, women, children, the sick, and those living abroad.

If one is unable to bathe with cold water, one should perform the bath with warm water. If one is unable to bathe from the head down, one should perform the bath starting from the neck and so forth. If they are kings, for the sake of worshipping Śiva, they should perform the bathing ritual according to the prescribed procedure that includes all the ancillary offerings (*upacāra*) mentioned for the bathing of Śiva, while seated upon a golden throne.
Having stood there,

they should perform the bath with water drawn from golden jars, preceded by the sounding of auspicious musical instruments such as conch shells; thereafter, the body should be wiped dry with a clean, soft cloth.

Having performed all these— putting on two clean garments, sipping water (ācamana), the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), bathing with ashes, and applying the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)— one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana).
The method for the Śaiva twilight ritual (sandhyā).
The manner of that:

Having performed three breath-retentions (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *gāyatrī* mantra according to the *saṃhitā*, and having applied the divine mudrā to the two eyes with the thumbs while reciting "Hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes," one should gaze at the water with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ" and strike it with that same [mantra].

Having sprinkled [the water] with the Armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should draw forth any one of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as Gaṅgā from the location of the *bindu* by means of the Heart mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the Hook gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
Then, having cast that sacred ford into the water with the Udbhava gesture and the Heart mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should consecrate it with the Root mantra.

Having protected [the object] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, having enveloped it with the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should render it nectar-like (*amṛtīkuryāt*) by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) and the power-mantra (*śaktimantra*) ending in *vaiṣaṭ*. Then, one should meditate upon the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). Twilight is threefold: Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī. Regarding these:
Clad in red garlands and garments, reddened and adorned with red ornaments, she sits upon a swan-throne, wearing a sacred thread and matted locks. Four-armed and four-faced, adorned with eight eyes,
she holds a rosary and a sacrificial ladle in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left.

The morning twilight (prātaḥsandhyā) has Brahman as its deity; it is threefold. At the time of dawn, when the stars are few, she is a young girl (subālā), the powerful bestower of liberation. When the stars have vanished at dawn, she is the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation; she is the embodiment of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the intermediate state, having assumed the form of a maiden, and is the bestower of enjoyment.

When half the orb of the sun is visible, she— whose essential nature is the power of action (kriyā-śakti)— having abandoned her maturity, assumes childhood. Seated upon a golden lotus, adorned with white garments and other ornaments,
decorated with a forest garland and a sacred thread, she has two eyes, one face, and four hands.
In the south, she holds a lotus with a mace; in the left, she bears the conch and discus.
This Vaiṣṇavī Sandhyā is indeed the middle [Sandhyā]. She exists in three ways during the fourth part of the second watch (yāma):
in its first portion, she is the bestower of liberation and her youth has just begun to blossom; in its middle portion, she is in the midst of her prime.

Vāgīśī bestows both enjoyment and liberation. Named Jvālā, she resides in the third portion; she grants liberation, possesses full youth, stands amidst a bull and a lotus, has three eyes, and bears the moon upon her crest.
Her body is dark as a rain cloud, she is clothed in a tiger skin, and she holds a trident and a rosary in her right hands.

On the left is the one with the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) spear; she is known as the Evening Twilight (*sāyaṃ sandhyā*) and is Raudrī. She too is threefold, as previously described. At the time when the sun’s rays are reddish, she is slightly past her youth. This Raudrī, called Vāmā, bestows liberation upon those who meditate on her.
At the half-sun [of the day] when it has fallen from the middle of youth, she who is named Jyeṣṭhā bestows both enjoyment and liberation.

When the sun has set, the twilight known as Raudrī is called "bestowing enjoyment" and is past its youth. Thus, these nine kinds of twilights have been declared by Śiva in the Śiva-śāstra; they are witnesses to everything, worthy of worship, and bestowers of desired objects. Brāhmī resides in the heart-lotus, while Vaiṣṇavī...
Situated in the center of the *bindu* and reaching the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), one should contemplate Raudrī during her respective times.

The morning twilight is for the *samayin*, the midday twilight is for the *viśeṣin*, and the triad of twilights is prescribed only for one who has been initiated into *nirvāṇa*. In that regard, the wise man who is intent upon the temple of the seven kalās [should contemplate] those [energies] residing in the three stations of Bindu, Śakti, and Samanā— subtle as a lotus fiber.
One should meditate upon the goddesses named Kriyā, Dṛk, and Icchā, who hold red and white chowries,
preceded by the utterance of the *prāsāda* mantra. However, for one whose mind is fixed on the twelve-syllabled *prāsāda*,
the supreme *sandhyā* should be contemplated, which is perceived at midnight.

From the navel up to the end of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), and then from there down to the navel, the Fourth State (turyā) moves back and forth; it is formless or else it is dark blue. This twilight (saṃdhyā), which is the very nature of the awakening of Śiva, is the most excellent for the wise. [It perceives] Śambhu situated at the end of the twelve-finger space.
Like moonlight resting upon the moon, the twilight (*sandhyā*) is in reality one alone, being the very nature of Śiva and Śakti;

yet, through the distinction of time and presiding deities, she is considered to be threefold. This contemplation of the twilight is what is called the "Sandhyā-vandana" (the twilight worship); everything else, such as the ritual rinsing (*mārjana*) and so forth, is merely an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of this primary rite.
Having thus performed the duties such as the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), the worship of Śiva should be commenced.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: then, having meditated upon Īśāna on the thumb and Amṛtakalā on the ring finger, one should, with the ring finger joined by the thumb, sequentially satisfy the eyes, nostrils, ears, shoulders, heart, navel, and head, saying: "May Āditya be satisfied; may Viṣṇu be satisfied."

While meditating thus, one should touch [the eyes]. When this is done, through contact with the splendor of Śiva, the deities presiding over the eyes and other senses—beginning with Sūrya and ending with Viṣṇu—become filled with the nectar flowing from the agitated *anāmikā* (ring finger) and become subordinate to the presiding presence of the agent. Immediately after that:
For the sake of purifying the thirty-five principles residing within the body, one should perform the sipping of water consisting of pure consciousness alone.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: "I meditate upon Brahmā, who is golden-colored, whose four hands are adorned with a rosary of lotus seeds and a water-pot, who has four faces, and who is the embodiment of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva)."

Preceded by meditation on the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), one should first perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with the mantra: *hāṃ ātmatattvāya svadhā*. By this, one should contemplate the purification of the thirty-one principles (tattvas), beginning with earth and ending with Māyā, within one's own body.
Then, [one visualizes] the [deity] blue in color, holding a discus, an arrow, a lotus, the consciousness-gesture (cinmudrā), a conch, and a bow.

"I meditate upon Viṣṇu, who has one face, whose eight hands are marked with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā), and who is the embodiment of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Having thus meditated according to the principle of knowledge, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra "svadhā to the principle of knowledge. By this, there is the purification of the three principles known as Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

One should meditate: "I meditate upon Rudra, who is the embodiment of the Śiva-tattva, possessing five faces, with four hands holding a crystal-colored rosary of lotus seeds, a trident, and a water-pot; preceded by the knowledge of the Śiva-tattva, [one recites] *huṃ*."
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra "Śivatattvāya svadhā. By this, one should contemplate the purification of the Śakti-tattva.
Then, having wiped the lips twice with the Astra-mantra, one should touch the heart and the other limbs [eyes, etc. with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
As for the rest—such as the meditation on the satisfaction of the respective deities—one should perform it as previously described.
Such is the sequence for sipping water (ācamana).

Then, having consecrated the Lord of Gods and seated him upon the lotus-throne, one should worship the seat, the form, and the body of knowledge (vidyādeha). Having then invoked Mahādeva and worshipped him with the rites of installation and so forth, and having bathed him mentally, one should offer garments and a sacred thread.

Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, and ornaments, and having offered incense and a lamp, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana). One should present the food offering (naivedya), mouth-perfume, and betel leaf. Having offered incense and the waving of lights (ārātrikā), one should present the sacred thread (pavitra).

Having applied white ashes, one should worship with mirrors and other articles. Then, having offered the bali-oblation, one should worship with water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, as well as with perfumes and flowers, preceded by recitation (japa), hymns (stotra), prostrations (namaskāra), and circumambulations (pradakṣiṇa). One should honor [the deity] with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā).

One should worship with the special *arghya*. Having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of Śiva along with his attendants using the *parāṅmukha-arghya*, one should eat what has been offered while meditating on Śiva within the heart at the proper time.

Thus has the sequence of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva been briefly described. We shall now demonstrate it in detail, avoiding excessive brevity or prolixity. First, the rite of sipping water (ācamana) is stated:
*Hīṃ*, obeisance to the head. Having washed the hands up to the wrists and the feet up to the knees—

Facing either east or north and seated in the kukkuṭāsana posture, having placed both hands between the knees, one should assign the mantras to the fingers of both hands, beginning with the little finger: *Hāṃ* to the heart, *Namaḥ*;
*Hoṃ* to the head, *Namaḥ*; *Hūṃ* to the crest-lock, *Namaḥ*; *Haiṃ* to the armor, *Namaḥ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hauṃ, obeisance to the three eyes" and "Haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon," one should form the right hand into the shape of a cow’s ear (*gokarṇa*). Taking water therein sufficient for the immersion of a bean (*māṣa*), one should gaze at it;

then, releasing the thumb and little finger, that water—[visualized] as the moon during the bright fortnight— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the ritual context of the *Tāntrika* purification rites.*

During the dark fortnight, having meditated upon the form of the Sun and contemplated the satisfaction of Sarasvatī residing on the tip of the tongue through the consumption of that [food], as well as the purification of one's own inner body, one should— washing the hands from time to time— offer the *svadhā* with the root mantra using the *brahmatīrtha*.

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times. Then, contemplating the purification of one’s own mouth and the purification of the Praṇava-deity residing within the cavity of the lips, one should wipe both lips twice with the base of the thumb.
Now follows the application of sacred ash (bhasmadhāraṇa).

There are four kinds of ash: *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, *upakalpa*, and *akalpa*. Among these, one should worship a cow together with her calf that is free from disease and other ailments; then, having taken the cow-dung while it has not yet fallen to the ground—collecting it while still suspended in the air—one should form it into balls and dry them thoroughly.

Having burned [the materials] in the Śiva-fire with the five Brahma-mantras and purified them with the root mantra (mūla), both that which has been prepared and that which has arisen from the Agnihotra are fit for the ritual. Having taken dry cow-dung from the forest, having burned it in the Śiva-fire, and having purified it with the root mantra—

The secondary procedure (anukalpa) has been accomplished: having taken the ashes from a house in a forest, a cow-pen, or from brick-furnaces and the like that have been burnt by forest fires and so forth, one should purify them with a cloth,
form them into a ball with cow’s urine, and burn them again in the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
"Prepared" means purified. That which is deficient in mantras and so forth, or prepared by Brāhmaṇas, women, Śūdras, and the like,
even if they have taken pure cow dung, is "unprepared"— that is, it has been burnt by many fires such as those in the kitchen hearths of Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*),
or it has been taken from such sources as the kitchen hearths of Vedic scholars.
If one is unable to visualize it, then having taken up the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), [one should recite]:

*Hoṃ īśānamūrdhne namaḥ* (Homage to the head of Īśāna); *Heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ* (Homage to the face of Tatpuruṣa); *Huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ* (Homage to the heart of Aghora); *Hiṃ vāmadevaguhyāya namaḥ* (Homage to the secret organ of Vāmadeva); *Haṃ...*
Salutation to the form of Sadyojāta. Hāṃ, salutation to the heart. Hīṃ, salutation to the head.
Hūṃ, salutation to the tuft of hair. Haiṃ, salutation to the armor. (p. 11) Hauṃ, salutation to the eyes. Haḥ, salutation to the weapon. Hāṃ, salutation to the Nivṛtti-kalā. Hrīṃ.
*Pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*. *Hrūṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*.
*Hrauṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. *Hauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*.
Thus, one should purify with the mantras of the Kalās, together with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Of such a being...
The wearing of ashes is of two kinds: smearing (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*).
Smearing, too, is of two kinds: in the form of a bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*) and in the form of a ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).
One who has already bathed with water is qualified for both types of ash-bath. In the event of inability to do so—
Having washed [the body] up to the neck, up to the waist, or up to the knees,
and having wiped the washed limbs with a wet cloth, one should put on another garment, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then,
with the Astra-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," [one should burn away impurities] by means of the fire arising from the big toe of the right foot.

Having contemplated that only the external impurities residing in the body have been burnt, one should flood the body with a stream of nectar flowing from the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*) situated in the station of the drop (*bindu*), which has been agitated by contact with fire.
Then, while mentally uttering the root mantra up to the end of the sound (*nādānta*), one should proceed.

One should contemplate one's body as being consecrated by a profuse stream of nectar flowing from the power (śakti) agitated by contact with that [deity]. This mental bath (mānasasnāna) should always be performed in all circumstances whenever there is a doubt regarding impurity. Alternatively, having meditated upon that very power in the form of a cow—

One should bathe the body with the flow of nectar from the rays of its tail; this is the bath of being (bhāva-snāna). Alternatively, one may sprinkle the body with the divine waters of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and so forth, or with the dust of the earth from that sacred field.

One should touch the body with the five Brahma-mantras, the six ancillary mantras (ṣaḍaṅga), and the root mantra. Having performed one of these methods, one should recite the five Brahma-mantras, the six ancillary mantras, and the root mantra either once or three times.
Then, as before, one should perform the two acts of sipping water (ācamana).
One should perform the ash-bath, which eliminates all perceived impurities, both external and internal.
Its sequence is as follows.
Having avoided the presence of cows, Brahmins, deities, fire, teachers, and those engaged in study,

and having settled in a pure place apart from the path— free from the sight and touch of barbarians and outcastes— one should face either east or north, and place [the substance] measuring a single handful, consisting of the primary or secondary ritual forms.

Having taken ashes in the measure of one *niṣka*, one and a half *niṣkas*, or two and a half *niṣkas* according to the sequence starting with the Brahmins, and having cast that portion belonging to the *rākṣasas* in the southwest corner (*nairṛtakoṇa*), one should purify the ashes— provided they are not yet prepared— with the *pañcabrahma* and *ṣaḍaṅga* mantras, preceded by the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).
Having consecrated even the four kinds of ashes seven times with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
one should, if detached, apply it starting from the feet up to the head; if not detached, starting from the head down to the feet,
using a small amount of ash held between the right thumb and forefinger.
One should perform the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) in the form of touching the limbs other than those parts [of the body] that are to be traversed by the hands and feet;
this is the bath of impurity (*malasnāna*). Then, [one should apply] the ashes consecrated with the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) and the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Īśāna.

One should perform the smearing with ashes using the *sadyojāta* mantra on the head, heart, secret place, feet, and the two shoulders; for all other limbs, one should use the right hand, and for those parts that are inaccessible, one should use the left hand. The remainder...

One should sprinkle [the disciple] on the head with the root mantra using the *kumbha-mudrā*. In this manner, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes. Kṣatriyas and others, in their respective order, should apply [the ashes] by making a square, a triangle, and a circle on the forehead, extending from below the throat to above the navel.
They should dust themselves with ashes. A Śūdra, however, having omitted the dusting, should perform the ash-bath consisting solely of the tripuṇḍra to be described hereafter.
This rule applies to Śūdras other than those who are ascetics (tapasvin). For this very reason, it is stated in the Jñānaratnāvalī: "The ascetic..."
By the passage beginning with "If one should duly collect ashes and perform a bath with them," etc.,
the rule for the bath of impurity (*malasnāna*) and the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) has been stated for ascetics according to their specific qualification. Likewise,
even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are not ascetics [should perform] the ash-bath consisting of the *tripuṇḍra* alone.

The two [the husband and wife] should perform it. Or, even the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, if they are unable to perform the *uddhūlana* (smeearing the body with ashes), should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) consisting solely of the three lines (*tripuṇḍra*).
It is precisely with the intention of referring to the ash-bath consisting solely of the three lines that this is stated in certain Āgamas as well.

The quantity of ash is stated to be one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, half of that, and half of that again, according to the sequence starting with the Brahmins. This form of ritual bathing (*vidhisnāna*) must be performed with water by initiated householders during all three daily junctures (*sandhyā*).

Women, ascetics (yatis), those under vows (vratins), forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), maidens, and others who have not received initiation (dīkṣā) should perform [the rite] with water before midday, and after midday it should be performed without water. Thus...

When performing the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), one should put on another garment and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*); or, having covered [the body], one may simply perform the sipping of water alone.
The Ritual for the Triple Mark (Tripuṇḍra)
Now, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

(p. 13) And that [measurement] is, among the various positions taught in the scriptures—such as seven, five, four, three, or two finger-breadths for the letters in sequence; or four finger-breadths on the forehead, the heart, or the arms for all of them; or one finger-breadth on other parts of the body, and so forth—[the following]:

Having adopted a certain practice obtained from the conduct of predecessors, one should apply [the mark] on the forehead and other locations with the three fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers;
or it may be applied on the forehead with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers. The *tripuṇḍra* consists of three thick, continuous lines.
And it should be performed exactly as it becomes manifest: the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the ash-bath;
and [the visualization of] the God of Ashes—three-faced, three-armed, three-legged, three-eyed, smeared with ash, performing the tāṇḍava dance, fierce, adorned with red flowers.

Having meditated, one should perform the rite. In place of the *tripuṇḍra*, one should wear either a square mark, a half-moon, or a lamp-shaped mark as obtained through family tradition, or else a space between the *tripuṇḍras*. And all such marks should be made with pure ashes, or with ashes mixed with sandalwood paste, or sprinkled with water.

Just as there is a mark (*puṇḍra*) on the forehead, so too [should one apply it] at five locations— the forehead, heart, shoulders, and navel— having Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha as their respective deities;
or at eight locations— the head, forehead, throat, shoulders, heart, navel, and back.
Having Brahmā, Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Agni, and Candra as its deities,
[it is placed] upon the sixteen locations: the forehead, neck, shoulders, arms, elbows, navel, heart, chest, belly, navel, and both sides and the back.
[The deities] presided over by the five [beginning with] Śiva and Maheśvara, and the nine [beginning with] Vāmā, along with the two Aśvis,
reside in the head, forehead, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, shoulders, elbows, wrists, heart, sides, navel, the pair of genitals, the two buttocks, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet.
In thirty-two locations— namely, the eight forms (mūrtis), the eight lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), the eight guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and the eight deities of the earth (vasus)—
together with the rows of fingers and toes of the hands and feet, there are thirty-six locations.
Śiva, Śakti, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Vidyā, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṃkāra, Buddhi, Manas,
Śrotra, Tvak, Cakṣus, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Upastha, Śabda, Sparśa, Rūpa, Rasa, and Gandha.

The ritual should be performed according to the available materials, depending on the place, time, and other factors, with the deities of the elements— ether, air, fire, water, and earth— as its essence. In the system of thirty-six principles (*tattvas*),
the principles from Śiva down to ether are circular in shape, [made of] crystal and sun-gem...
Moonstone, cow’s milk, coral, yellow orpiment, collyrium, Indra’s bow (a rainbow),
Indra’s wrath, clouds, ruby, coral, sapphire, saffron, hibiscus flower, Indra’s bow, sun-gem, gold, and durvā grass.
The colors are like turmeric, oleander, dark clouds, sapphire, pearl, ruby, gold, and crystal; black for Vāyu (the wind) in a square shape,
circular for Vāyu, triangular for Agni (fire), white for Jala (water) in the shape of a half-moon, and yellow for the earth in a square shape.

Having meditated upon the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*), one should apply the sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*) at their respective locations with mantras such as "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, whose form is the principle of Śiva" (*śivatatvarūpāya śivāya namaḥ*). In this same manner,
the rule of adaptation (*ūha*) should be applied even in other alternative systems.

Alternatively, one should wear marks (*puṇḍra*) that correspond to various locations, numbers, and other specific deities as prescribed in the various divine Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, which have been established by the traditions of former teachers.
This is the procedure for wearing the sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇakrama*).
The Ritual for Wearing Rudrākṣa Beads.
Now, regarding the wearing of Rudrākṣas: like the application of sacred ash (bhasma), this too is obligatory during the worship of Śiva.
Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, respectively, should take Rudrākṣas that are white, red, yellow, and black. If beads of the specified colors cannot be obtained, Brāhmaṇas may use all four types.
It should be worn. The three colors beginning with red are to be worn by Kṣatriyas; the two beginning with yellow by Vaiśyas;

and by Śūdras, only black should be worn. Alternatively, all [colors] may be worn by all [classes] according to what is available, on the head, the neck, the ears, the arms, the wrists, and the chest.
Or else, it may be endowed with a specific number appropriate to the size of one's own head and so forth:

forty on the head, thirty-two on the neck, six in each of the two ears, sixteen in each of the two arms, twelve in each of the two wrists, and one hundred and eight on the chest; thus [is the distribution].
Or it may be a number two hundred and forty-eight;

or it may be one more than that, namely twenty-fourty-nine, by placing one on the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Alternatively, there are thirty-six on the crest-lock, fifty on the forehead, and one hundred and eight for the sacred thread (*upavīta*) on the neck, ears, arms, and wrists.
"As before" means numbering two hundred and ninety-five;
or, on the head, three garlands numbering one hundred and eight down to the navel; and on the throat, ears, chest, arms, and wrists, "as before" means numbering five hundred and eighty-two.
It should be worn. Wearing rudrākṣa beads together with the five jewels— diamond, ruby, lapis lazuli,
coral, and pearl— is a warder-off of fever, planetary afflictions, spirits, urinary disorders, leprosy, fistula-in-ano, possession by Kumāra-grahas, and epilepsy.
Wearing it on the crown, earrings, ear-ornaments, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, waist-bands, and so forth—

other than when worn as rudrākṣas— destroys untimely death and increases longevity, prosperity, and fame. Wearing it on the crest-lock yields ten million times the fruit, and on the two ears [the same].
The merit of a single-faced rudrākṣa worn on the neck is tenfold, on each successive limb it is ten times greater, and on the hands it is immeasurable.
Concealing and wearing a single-faced rudrākṣa on the crest-lock destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin and removes great fears such as weapons, fire, thieves, and excessive rain.

It increases longevity, prosperity, and fame; it bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants all spiritual perfections (*siddhi*). The two-faced [mantra] removes the sin of killing a cow; the three-faced removes the sin of killing a woman; the four-faced removes the sins of approaching those who should not be approached and eating what should not be eaten; the five-faced—
It removes all sins. The six-faced [mantra] held in the right hand removes the sin of killing an embryo.

The seven-faced [mantra] removes the faults of stealing gold and killing a cow, and it is also a remover of poison. The eight-faced [mantra] removes the fault of violating the teacher’s bed and removes the fault of all fraudulent dealings. The nine-faced [mantra]...

Held in the left hand, it removes the faults of millions and billions of great sins; with ten faces, it removes the fear of planets, piśācas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, serpents, lions, tigers, and so forth;
and with eleven faces, it is worn upon the crest-lock (śikhā).
Wearing it upon the region of the neck bestows the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred vājapeyas, and a hundred thousand gifts of cows; having twelve faces,
it grants the fruit of many sacrificial fees, of gomedha and aśvamedha sacrifices, and causes the increase of sovereign power.

The fourteen-faced [form] removes the fear of fanged beasts, horned animals, and terrible fires; it causes the destruction of all sins, bestows incomparable enjoyments, grants success in alchemy, metallurgy, and the making of medicinal pills, and removes the fault of killing one's father, mother, brother, or wife. The fourteen-faced [form].
It brings about the accomplishment of all undertakings, removes all diseases, and grants success in the yoga of knowledge.

[One should avoid] on parts of the body other than the head, arms, neck, and ears— namely, the limbs— the wasting away or swelling [of the body], contact with a woman during childbirth, the voiding of excrement or urine, and [the consumption of] fish, meat, garlic, and *kataka* [nuts].
One should avoid wearing Rudrākṣas at times such as when eating Śipru or Śleṣmātaka.

According to the procedure prescribed in the *Rudrākṣadānakalpa*, the gift of Rudrākṣas is equivalent to the study of all the Vedas and Purāṇas, the performance of all sacrifices and acts of charity, and the pilgrimage to all sacred fords.

It bestows the fruit [of merit], removes all diseases, grants the fruit of establishing one hundred liṅgas, giving one hundred liṅgas, giving one thousand glorious forms (śrīmūrtis), and giving one thousand trunks (sahasrakandhas);
it grants all sovereign enjoyments together with sons, friends, and others.
It bestows union with Śiva upon the recipient who is a devotee of Śiva, and yields that same fruit for him as well.

On days such as the full moon, the new moon, the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, and birth asterisms, the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads destroys all sins. [This applies] at the time of worship.
The wearing of Rudrākṣas should be performed on the head with the Īśāna mantra,
on the ears with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, on the throat and other parts with the Aghora mantra, and on the chest with the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
The Method of Sakalīkaraṇa (the Process of Imparting Limbs)
Now follows the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the process of making [the self] complete), which consists of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *karas* (hands) and the limbs. That is threefold:

for householders, it takes the form of the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (placement of emanation); for celibate students (*brahmacārins*), it takes the form of the *sthiti-nyāsa* (placement of maintenance); and for ascetics (*yatis*) and forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), it takes the form of the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (placement of reabsorption). Here, the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* is described.

Having smeared both hands with fragrant substances and the like, one should wipe the palm and the back of the left hand twice with the right hand, beginning from the wrist, using the weapon mantra (*haḥ astrāya phaṭ*) for the purification; then, with that same mantra, [one should proceed].
Having wiped the palm and back of the right hand once with the left hand,

and having contemplated that both hands, from the wrists to the tips, are pervaded by the splendor of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should join the palms together with the two thumbs joined in the middle, [visualizing] the power-circle (*śaktimaṇḍala*) in the form of nectar.

Having meditated, one should bathe the two armor-mantras with that nectar using "Hāṃ Śaktaye" and "Oṣaṭ," and having placed them within the single lotus-cup formed by the two joined thumbs as its pericarp,
one should perform the placement with "Oṃ Hāṃ Śivāsanāya Namaḥ," and in the center of that, "Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ."

Having placed the subtle form of Śiva with the mantra "Śivamūrtaye namaḥ"— which is composed of light, resembles steady lightning, and is white in color— one should place [the mantras] on the two thumbs with the two index fingers using "Hoṃ Īśānamūrdhne namaḥ," and then [place them] on the fingers from the index finger to the little finger.

Having performed the placement of the four mantras beginning with "Heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa" using the two thumbs, one should [place] "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" using the two thumbs upon the palms, which consists of thirty-eight kalās.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the gross body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), which is of the nature of Sadāśiva, [one recites] "Salutation to the eyes" (*netrebhyo namaḥ*) and places the eye upon the palms of the hands. Then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should invoke Śiva, who pervades the body of Sadāśiva, [reciting] "Hāṃ Hauṃ, salutation to Śiva" (*śivāya namaḥ*). Thereafter, [one places the seed-syllable] "Hāṃ" on the little fingers and so forth.

Having sequentially deposited the five mantras— beginning with *hṛdayāya namaḥ* and excluding the eye-mantra— one should enclose the left and right hands with the other two hands while reciting *kavacāya namaḥ*.
Then, joining the two hands together, one should perform the consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) by means of the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

The supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) consists of the contemplation that the various parts (*kalā*), such as the heart, head, and crest— which have been deposited with their respective distinct colors— attain their respective original states through the exceedingly white splendor of the invoked Supreme Śiva. Thereafter, one should perform the ritual deposition of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).

p.17) With the right thumb and ring finger, reciting "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva," one should place the white lotus-seat of Śiva, arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, in the center of the body or in the heart; then [recite] "Oṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva."

Thus, having projected the subtle, radiant form of Śiva from the navel-cavity or the heart up to the midpoint of the eyebrows, and having formed a fist and projected the Īśāna-mantra upon the head with the thumb,
one should project [the mantras] upon the face, the heart, and the secret place with the index finger and the other fingers joined with the thumb.
Having sequentially deposited the Tatpuruṣa-mantra and the others upon the two feet,
and having deposited the Vidyā-deha from the middle of the eyebrows up to the Brahma-randhra with "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-deha," one should deposit the Netra-mantra upon the eyes.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] with the three middle fingers, one should invoke Paramaśiva upon that [seat] with the thumb and ring finger, reciting "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Then,
[one should place them] at the locations of the heart, head, and crest.
Having placed [the mantra] with the little finger, ring finger, middle finger,
and thumb joined together as a covering for the neck extending to the middle of the breasts, one should place the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) with the two index fingers;
then, one should place the weapon-mantra (*astra*) three times on the palms of the hands with the ring fingers and thumbs.
All these mantras end with *namaḥ*. However, the weapon mantra (*astramantra*) ends with *huṃ phaṭ*.

Then, having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) preceded by three claps (*tāla*) using the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having encircled [the area] with the armor mantra (*kavaca*), one should display the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
The touching of the body with both hands from the head down to the feet is the *mahāmudrā*.

Thereafter, one should contemplate oneself as having a form identical to that of Śiva. Having thus performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one becomes terrifying, grasping weapons in hand, clad in armor, with a turban bound upon the head and a helmet covering the crown.
Because one becomes invincible to the base like a soldier, it is called *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of complete armor). Then,
having washed the general *arghya* vessel with the *astra-mantra*,
and having filled it with pure water imagined as nectar flowing from the station of the *bindu*, [one offers] *hāṃ* to the heart.

Having filled [the vessel] with "vauṣaṭ," consecrated it seven times with "hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," concealed it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā). This is the water for the general offering (sāmānyārghya); except for Śiva, it is for others.
This is common to the gatekeepers and the others.
Worship of the Gatekeepers (Dvārapālārcana)
Now, the worship of the gatekeepers. Its procedure is as follows:
while contemplating oneself situated within the cage of the *astra* (weapon-mantra), one should mentally transcend the group of thirty-one *tattvas*, beginning with Earth and ending with *Māyā*.

Meditating upon the temple of Śiva-pūjā as circular in shape and consisting of the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) which is red in color, one who desires worldly enjoyment and liberation should worship the gatekeepers at the eastern door; likewise, one who desires fame, victory, and good fortune [should do so].

At the southern gate; one who desires only liberation [should worship] at the western gate; however, worship should not be performed at the northern gate. Having sprinkled the gate with ordinary *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*, one should worship the outer gatekeepers. And they are Gaṇapati and the others. Therein:

At the top of the door, at the opening of the *udumbara* beam, Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī are seated on the right, left, and middle sections respectively. The arrangement of left and right should be understood either with respect to the deity or with respect to the worshipper entering through the door. Of the door—

Outside, on the right side, stands Nandin; on the northern part of that very right side is Gaṅgā; on the left side is Mahākāla; and on the southern part of that very left side is Yamunā. Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.

I worship Gaṇapati, who is dark-complexioned and holds in his trunk a rosary, a noose, a goad, and a citron. Hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. [I worship] Sarasvatī, who is white-complexioned, holds a rosary and a book, and has her two hands occupied with playing the lute.
I worship. Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.

[I worship her] who holds the *śrīphala*, the lotus, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and whose two flanks are supported by golden jars filled with nectar held in the trunks of a pair of elephants standing on either side.
I worship Mahālakṣmī, who is being consecrated by streams [of water]. Hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin.
I worship Nandin, who has a massive body, wears a crown of reddish-brown matted hair, and holds a trident, a rosary, the tarjanī gesture, and a mallet. Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā.

I worship Gaṅgā, who is white in color, whose vehicle is a makara, and who holds a jar of nectar and a chowrie. Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla! [I worship him] who is black in color, with a massive body terrifying due to his fangs and a furrowed brow.
I worship Mahākāla, who holds a trident, a skull-cup, a mallet, and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*).
*Hāṃ*, homage to Yamunā! I worship Yamunā, who is dark-green in color, mounted upon a tortoise, and holding a chowrie and a nectar-filled jar—at their respective places.

One should worship them. All these door-keepers, with the exception of Gaṅgā and Yamunā, are three-eyed; all of them have faces corresponding to their respective doors. Having opened the door-panel with the weapon-mantra preceded by a prayer for the opening of the door using the following verses, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the two eyes with the mantra "Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," [one should proceed].
Having caused the celestial obstructors (*vighna*) to tremble with the sight of divine meditation;
having caused the aerial obstructors to tremble with flowers tossed by the forefinger and thumb;
and having caused the terrestrial obstructors to tremble with three strikes of the right heel—[recite] *astrāya hūṃ phaṭ*.

One should dispel the three kinds of obstacles with the mantra. Then, leaning against the left doorpost while not touching the right threshold with his right foot, he enters the temple of Śiva, [reciting]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Weapon (astra). [I salute] the fire-colored one with four faces."
With four hands endowed with a spear, a trident, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, adorned with a crown of matted hair and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
the dispeller of all obstacles— I worship the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) with affection,
situated in the middle of the threshold facing the temple of Śiva.

Having turned around, he should worship facing him. The King, having turned around, should worship Brahmā facing him. Then: *Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā*. [He is] golden-colored, with a beard, four-faced, and pot-bellied.

"I worship Brahmā, the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati), who holds a staff, a rosary, a water-pot, and a sacrificial ladle. One should worship Brahmā as well in the very middle of the threshold. Then, inside the door on the right side: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Nandikeśvara."
Red in color, with three eyes, his matted hair adorned with a crescent moon;

possessing four hands displaying the gestures of holding a deer, an axe, and making a salutation, while carrying a staff at the base of his arm and a small dagger at his waist; wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads.

One should worship on the inner right side of the door, saying: "I worship Nandikeśvara, who has the face of a monkey. Then: "Hāṃ Suṃ, obeisance to Suyaśā. One should worship Goddess Suyaśā, who is dark-complexioned and whose right hand is adorned with a blue lotus.

One should worship Suyaśādevī inside the door. Then, having circumambulated Śiva, one should worship Brahmā in the southwest (Nirṛti) corner. The worship of these [deities] consists of the offering of a seat, invocation, installation, making present, restraining, and the offerings of water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya.

The worship should be performed for each [deity], ending with the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, or ending with the offering of food (naivedya) and betel (tāmbūla). If one is unable [to do so individually], one should worship all the door-keepers together in the middle [of the rite] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, saying: "Obeisance to all the door-keepers. O door-keepers of the God of gods, protect the gateway!
Having diligently warded off the multitude of obstacles— thus is the command of the Supreme Lord—

one should cause [the disciple] to hear the command of Śiva. Furthermore, this worship of the gatekeepers is subject to option (*vikalpa*) because it is both prescribed and prohibited according to different Āgamas in the context of worship for one's own sake (*ātmārtha-pūjā*).
There is no deficiency [in the rite] regarding this. In not performing it, there is no transgression; in performing it, there is spiritual advancement, according to the principle of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup.

Then, having placed all the implements for worship before Śiva, and standing on the right side or the southeast side of the deity facing north, one should take one's seat upon a beautiful svastika or other familiar seat.
Among the five purifications— of the self, the place, the substance, the mantra, and the liṅga—

one should first perform the purification of the self. This method of worshiping Gaṇapati and the other deities under the *ūrdhvoduṃbara* tree and so forth applies when there exists a temple of Śiva possessing the characteristics as previously described.
This must be performed prior to the purification of the self; for it has been prescribed as follows:
in the north-eastern quarter of the house, one should construct a structure made of stone, baked brick, pure wood, or clay, which is either square, oblong, or circular.

Or, the temple of worship [is measured] by the measure of twenty-four finger-breadths— distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior— based on the space between the third joint and the middle joint of the middle finger of the sacrificer, which has the deities of the joints as its form.

Having constructed a single hall of worship— either two-storied or three-storied— with a measurement of three, five, seven, nine, thirteen, seventeen, twenty, or twenty-one cubits, and having divided it into five parts, one should [place] stone or plaster in its central portion.
Having constructed an altar made of clay or brick, either provided with four-cornered pillars or devoid of pillars,
measuring sixteen or eighteen finger-breadths in height,
and having fashioned upon it, at the western part, a space one *tāla* in width and length;

Having made the area corresponding to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) five finger-breadths in height, and in its eastern part the area corresponding to the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇṭapa*) of the same length, width, and height,
[one should then construct] in its eastern part [an area] five *tāla*s in length.

One should prepare a space for the *veramaṇḍapa* measuring four palm-lengths in width and eight finger-breadths in height; therein, in the place corresponding to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should install a casket (*peṭaka*) made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, which may be square, oblong, or circular.

In a location corresponding to the site of a pavilion, having placed a casket adorned with lotuses— measuring two cubits in length, one cubit in width, or twelve finger-breadths in height— and having spread over it a cloth of the same dimensions, one should place within its center [an image] made of ivory, elephant tusks, or other materials.
Having arranged the pedestal, one should place upon it a lotus-seat made of gold or other materials,
equipped with a halo fashioned at its western side, and facing the east. Furthermore,
the worship pavilion should be strewn with flowers, filled with the fragrance of incense smoke, anointed with sandalwood paste, and provided with a canopy.
One should adorn [the pavilion] with pearl necklaces, banners, flags, mirrors, lamps, and so forth.

In the absence of such a worship-pavilion (pūjā-maṇṭapa), one should mentally visualize the very place of Śiva’s worship as such a worship-pavilion. Seated right there near the Śiva-throne (śivapīṭha)...
One should perform the worship of the gatekeepers either before or after the purification of oneself. Thus ends the worship of the gatekeepers.
The Method for Purifying the Self

(p.21) Now, the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*). It is twofold: that which consists in bringing about the state of Śiva in the living soul of the worshipper, which is the purification of the soul (*jīvaśuddhi*); and that which consists in bringing about the state of a body of Śiva in the body of the worshipper, which is the purification of the body (*dehaśuddhi*). Of these, this [is as follows]:

The method for purifying the *jīva*: Having performed three breath-retentions (*prāṇāyāma*), one should expel the impure air within the body by means of three exhalatory breath-retentions (*recaka-prāṇāyāma*) using the *astra-mantra*. Then, filling the abdomen with external air, one should [visualize] that [air] as split in two, starting from the two big toes up to the *mūlādhāra*.

Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā nāḍī— which extends upward to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), is joined with downward-facing lotus buds, exists within the interior of the body, is exceedingly subtle, radiant like a streak of lightning, and possesses an internal cavity— one should contemplate the syllable "HŪM" in its center.
Having visualized the blazing seed-syllable of the *śikhā*,
one should contemplate the lotus buds situated with their faces turned downward at the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Having meditated upon [the elements] as blossomed, uplifted, and turned face upwards through the practices of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kuṃbhaka), and exhalation (recaka), one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ* blazing like the flame of a lamp in the region of the *mūlādhāra*; by the continuous utterance of "huṃ phaṭ," one should contemplate it ascending upwards, and by that, all five—

Having visualized the knots at Brahmā and the other centers, as well as the knots of the lotus stalks, as pierced, one should turn back from the syllable *huṃ* and exhale the air. Again, meditating on the syllable *hūṃ* at the *mūlādhāra*,
one should, by means of the inhaled breath (*pūraka*), withdraw the all-pervading consciousness from the body and bring it to rest within the heart-lotus.

Having extracted the individual soul (jīva) from the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) consisting of the puryaṣṭaka, which is extremely subtle, solitary, and has the form of a shimmering star; having encased it with the seed-syllable of the heart (the syllable *hāṃ*); and having placed the syllable *hūṃ* upon its head, one should perform the breath-retention (*kuṃbhaka*).
Causing the vital air (vāyu) to move upward, one should take it up by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*,
lead it as far as the *dvādaśānta*, and join it with the Supreme Śiva situated above that. In this way,
the individual soul (*jīva*) is liberated from the adjuncts of the gross and subtle impure bodies.
One becomes pure, endowed with the stainless powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), having attained union with Śiva. Alternatively,

having led the individual soul (*jīva*) as far as the *dvādaśānta* and enclosed it within the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*) right here in the heart-lotus, [one is freed] from the burning of the body which is to be performed at the time of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

One should protect [the self]. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the solar mandala upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus; Hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar mandala; Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire mandala;
Hāṃ, obeisance to the power (*śakti*) mandala," one [recites] "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, to the Self."

Having taken up the individual soul (jīvātman) that pervades the body with the syllable *namaḥ*, and having contemplated it as having its pervasive form withdrawn and appearing in the form of a shimmering star, one should place it above the circle of power (*śakti-maṇḍala*), and above that,
sequentially place the circles of power, fire, moon, and sun.
One should contemplate [the deity] as being flooded by the nectar flowing forth from the two maṇḍalas of power (śakti) situated above and below.

In this way, one should perform the mere protection of the individual soul (jīva). Since that soul is already pure at the very time of initiation (dīkṣā), purity need not be sought for it on a daily basis during the time of worship.
The Method for Purifying the Body

Now, regarding the purification of the body (*dehaśuddhi*): it is twofold, consisting of the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) and the purification of the gross body (*sthūladeha*). Among these, [the subtle body] consists of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which takes the form of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*).

For the sake of purifying the subtle body, I dissolve sound and touch into Brahmā among the causal persons (kāraṇapuruṣa) residing in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); and taste into Viṣṇu.

I dissolve [them]. I dissolve form and smell into Rudra. I dissolve intellect and ego into Īśvara. I dissolve the mind into Sadāśiva—thus one should dissolve the components of the subtle body, such as sound and the rest. Then:

For the purpose of purifying the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*), one should meditate upon the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) residing within one's own body at the twelve locations beginning with the feet and ending with the *dvādaśānta*, endowed with the positions, forms, and characteristics that will be described hereafter; [then recite: "I dissolve earth into water; I dissolve water into fire; I dissolve fire..."

"I dissolve the wind; I dissolve the wind into space; I dissolve space into the Supreme Power (parāśakti); I dissolve the Supreme Power into the Supreme Śiva"—thus one should contemplate. This [dissolution] occurs within its own causes.

The purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) consists of the dissolution of the earth and the other elements; it also consists of the exhaustion of their respective qualities (*guṇa*). This exhaustion of qualities is twofold: that which takes the form of individual purification and that which takes the form of mutual purification. Regarding these, the first is as follows, beginning from the feet:
It extends to the knees, is square, yellow in color,
solid by nature, and marked with vajras; it is joined with the heart-seed syllable *hāṃ* together with the seed-syllable of earth,
presided over by Brahmā, the Lord of Causes, and is the form of the *nivṛtti-kalā*.

Thinking, "I shall contemplate the circle of the earth," one should expel the qualities of earth— smell, taste, form, touch, and sound— with five breath-retentions using the mantra *hāṃ nivṛttikalāyai huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, from the knees up to the navel, there is a white-colored [element] in the shape of a half-moon,
liquid by nature, marked with a lotus, joined with the head-seed syllable *hīṃ* together with the seed-syllable of water (*āpya*),
and presided over by Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Cause.

Having reflected, "I shall meditate upon the water-maṇḍala, which has the form of the *pratiṣṭhā* stage," one should expel the qualities of taste, touch, sound, and form belonging to the waters by means of four exhalations using the mantra: *hrīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai huṃ phaṭ*. Then...
The fire-maṇḍala is triangular, extending from the navel to the throat, red in color, having the nature of digestion (fire),

marked with the svastika, joined with the syllable *hūṃ* and the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*) together with the seed-syllable of fire, presided over by Rudra as Kāruṇeśvara, and consisting of the form of the *vidyā-kalā*.
Thinking "I shall cultivate [this]," one should dispel the qualities of form, touch, and sound residing in the fire by means of three *uddhātas* with the mantra *hūṃ vidyākalāyai hūṃ phaṭ*. Then,
from the throat up to the space between the eyebrows, one should visualize a black hexagon.

Having contemplated: "I meditate upon the wind-maṇḍala, which has the nature of motion, is marked with six dots, is joined with the Haimitika armor-mantra together with the seed-syllable of wind, is presided over by Maheśvara, the Lord of Causes, and has the form of the peaceful kalā," [one recites] *hrauṃ*.
With the mantra "śāntikalāyai huṃ phaṭ," one should expel the qualities of touch and sound from the wind by means of two upward breaths (uddhātas). Then,
[one should visualize] a smoke-colored circle extending from the space between the eyebrows up to the dvādaśānta.

Having contemplated, "I meditate upon the mandala of space, which has the nature of ether, is marked by the power of the *bindu*, is conjoined with the weapon-mantra *haḥ*, and is presided over by Sadāśiva,
the Lord of Causes," one should [recite] the mantra *hauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai huṃ phaṭ* with a single exhalation.

One should dispel the quality of sound from space (*ākāśa*). Having visualized these spheres (*maṇḍala*)—beginning with earth and the others—as being located in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should purify them.
This is the method for individual purification. However, in the case of mutual purification, this is the distinction: all [the spheres]...

At the time of purifying each respective element, one should visualize the spheres of earth and the others as pervading from the feet up to the crown of the head. During the purification of earth, after the five qualities of that element have been expelled, one should contemplate the earth as being overcome by its opposite, air, and as having assumed the form of air during the time of purifying air.

One should meditate upon the wind as being overcome by its own opposite, earth, and as having assumed the form of earth. In the same way, one should also meditate upon water and fire, after the removal of their respective qualities, as being overcome by their own opposites— fire and water— and as having assumed the forms of fire and water.

Immediately after the removal of the qualities of space, space itself— being pure like a flawless crystal— is overwhelmed by the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), which consists of the supreme power (*paraśakti*) and possesses qualities such as eternity, omnipresence, and purity that are contrary to those [qualities of space]; thus it assumes the form of that [supreme space].

"One should meditate" means as follows: by purifying each of the great elements individually or by purifying them mutually, one should contemplate the withering of the body— which consists of a collection of elements— whose power has been exhausted due to the depletion of its qualities.
By means of the Kālāgni (Fire of Time) arising from the big toe and presided over by the power of Śiva,
the body is burnt away without remainder by the mantra *HAḤ ASTRĀYA HUṂPHAṬ*;
or else, only the residual elements such as Nivṛtti and the rest, or merely the defects residing in the body, are burnt.
Having meditated [upon this],
one should drench [the body] with a rain of nectar from the circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala) situated at the dvādaśānta, which is like a hollow space. In this way,
the aforementioned method of power is taught for the purpose of drying up the body.
Alternatively, having cast off the qualities of the elements that constitute the body, [one abandons] the gross body—
which has the five elements such as earth as its seed, is cast into the field of Māyā, has merit and demerit as its root, and possesses the senses as its branches and sub-branches.

The banyan tree, which has its roots above and branches below, whose sprouts are the perceptions of objects such as sound, whose flowers are the manifold of phenomenal existence, whose fruit is pleasure and pain, and which is to be enjoyed by the bird-like Puruṣa.

Having meditated thus, performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should contemplate [the tree] as being devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit, and rigid, by means of the first half of the inhalation (pūraka) joined with five utterances of "hlām" for six measures;
then, by means of the second half of the inhalation joined with four utterances of "hrīm."

Having visualized [the tree] endowed with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruits, one should, in a single exhalation (*uddhāta*) consisting of twelve measures and accompanied by three utterances of "hrūṃ," visualize it as dried up and burnt by the fire of time (*kālāgni*) arising from the big toe of the left foot during the retention (*kumbhaka*).

Having visualized [the body] being reduced to ashes and scattered in all directions by means of the first half of the *recaka* (exhalation) joined with two utterances of "eṃ," one should then contemplate it as pure like crystal, having the nature of the pure void, by means of the second half of the *recaka* joined with a single utterance of "haum," and flood it with nectar. Thus...

Having caused the burning of the body through the aforementioned number of *uddhātas*, or else— without the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the removal of the qualities (*guṇa*) up until the point of the removal of each respective quality— the earth and the other elements cease to function as bondages.

One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) either preceded by the mental recitation "it becomes," or simply up to the point of fixing the wind and mind in their respective locations.
