By the etymology of the word *uddhāta*— "that by which [the elements] are raised up" (*uddhanyate*) or "driven away" (*utsāryate")— it refers to the qualities of the elements.
Then, the means for the removal of that impurity is stated:

having performed inhalation preceded by the utterance of the respective *kalā* mantras, it is the action consisting of the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* as far as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). And that—

Having performed inhalation (*pūraka*), at the time of retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one should impel the vital air upward, then turn it back, and [expel it] through the right channel until the completion of exhalation (*recaka*). In this manner, for each single *uddhāta*, there are three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) beginning with inhalation; thus, on earth—
For the five types of expulsions (*uddhāta*), fifteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) are accomplished.

In [the case of] water and so forth, there are twelve, nine, six, and three [expulsions]. And in each individual form of breath-restraint, such as exhalation (*recaka*) and the rest, the duration is twelve *mātrās*. Therefore, each single...

The *uddhāta* consists of a duration of thirty-six *mātrās*. Alternatively, for the purpose of retention (*dhāraṇā*), the rule regarding the duration of twelve *mātrās* applies specifically to the *kumbhaka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). For the inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), the duration should be taken according to what is possible.

Having circumambulated [the deity] once, neither too quickly nor too slowly, with the knee-circle [touching the ground], the time taken for a finger-snap is the measure of time (*mātrākāla*). However, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other texts that the time taken for a finger-snap is [the measure of time] after having circumambulated three times. And this...

The shortest duration is one *mātrā*; double that is the medium; triple that is the superior. Thus, by reciting mantras for a number of *kalās* equal to the respective qualities, without depending on the *udghāta*—which consists of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) delimited by specific durations of time—[the goal is attained].
Or, it consists of the contemplation of the successive removal of those respective qualities; or, by means of the single recitation of the mantras of those respective kalās,
[it concerns] those things associated with the kalās, tattvas, bhuvanas, varṇas, padas, and mantras.

Or one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), which consists merely of severing the bonds in the form of reflecting upon the cessation of the state of being an obstacle to one’s own self for the sake of the earthly sphere and so forth.

Furthermore, the spheres beginning with the earthly (pārthiva) consist of the kalās of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, Śānti, and Śāntyatīta; these are situated within the body at the feet and so forth, the knees and so forth, the navel and so forth, the throat and so forth, and the space between the eyebrows and so forth.

Alternatively, [the cakras] are located at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); they begin with a dimension of one hundred million yojanas and increase tenfold in each successive stage;
they are square, crescent-shaped, triangular, hexagonal, and circular in form; and they consist of a vajra, two lotuses, and a svastika.
They are marked by six dots and one dot respectively, and are yellow, red, white, black, and smoky in color;
their natures are solidity, fluidity, heat, motion, and space; and they possess five, four, three, two, and one quality, beginning with odor.

One should meditate upon [the elements] as presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva, conjoined with the seed-syllables of earth and the other elements— namely the forms of *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*— which are endowed with the *bindu*. Therein, within the *nivṛtti-kalā*:
The earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*) is one; there are one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*s); the letter *ka* is the single phoneme (*varṇa*);
there are twenty-eight words (*pada*); and there are two mantras named Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya.
Within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, there are twenty-three principles (*tattva*s), beginning with water and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
There are fifty-six worlds; twenty-four phonemes beginning with *kha* and ending with *ma*; two mantras known as Vāmadeva and Śiras;
and within the principle of *vidyā-kalā*, seven principles beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*.

There are twenty-seven worlds ending with Yādīśa, seven phonemes, twenty-one words, and two mantras known as Aghora and Śikhā. Within the Śānti-kalā, there are two principles (tattvas): Śuddhavidyā and Maheśvara, eighteen worlds, and the two phonemes Ha and Kṣa.

There are two mantras called the *puruṣa* and *kavaca*, consisting of twelve syllables each. In the *śāntyatīta-kalā*, there are two principles (*tattva*), namely Sadāśiva and Śakti; fifteen worlds (*bhuvana*); sixteen letters belonging to itself; one word; and three mantras known as Mūla, Īśāna, and Astra.

Thus, the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) consists of eleven mantras; the path of words (*padādhvan*) consists of the ninety-four words contained within the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra; the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of fifty phonemes;
and the path of aspects (*kalādhvan*) consists of the five aspects beginning with *Nivṛtti*. Thus...

The spheres (maṇḍalas) beginning with earth, which contain the entire path within them, are to be meditated upon; or rather, their state of containing the entire path should be meditated upon in brief. For example:
the path of mantra consists of the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
The path of the *pada*s (words) consists of the five states characterized by waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (*turya*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*).

The path of the *bhuvana*s (worlds) consists of the five locations, such as the feet and so forth, or the heart and so forth, corresponding to the five spheres beginning with the earthly sphere (*pārthivamaṇḍala*).
The path of the *varṇa*s (phonemes) consists of the three phonemes beginning with *a*, along with the *bindu* and *nāda*.

Alternatively, the path of letters (varṇādhvan) consists of the five colors of the root mantra, and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) consists of the five kalās. Thus, having visualized [the mandalas] as containing all the paths within them, or having visualized them as endowed merely with their previously described arrangement, color, intrinsic nature, insignia, and seed-syllables.

These are the things to be purified. Thus, [the purification] consists of the dissolution of the earth element and so forth; it takes the form of burning the body by casting out their respective qualities; it takes the form of burning only the internal and external defects residing in the body;
it takes the form of burning the body alone without the exhaustion of the qualities; and [it takes the form of burning] without [external] fire.

Purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) consists of the destruction of each respective quality and the mere severing of the fetters (*pāśa*), which is the contemplation of the cessation of their binding nature. All of this is twofold: with emission (*soddhātā*) and without emission (*niruddhātā*).
The destruction of those respective qualities is twofold: consisting of individual purification and by means of the *paraspara-śodhana* mantra and so forth.
Furthermore, the structural arrangement as containing all the paths (*adhvan*) is also twofold; the contemplation of the elements (*bhūta-cintana*) is likewise [twofold].
It is twofold: by way of being the womb of all time-periods (*sarvādhvagarbhatva*) and by way of mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the contemplation of its being the womb of all time-periods is twofold: elaborately (*prapañcena*) and concisely (*saṃkṣepeṇa*).

In this manner, among the various types of purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) thus described, whichever purification of the elements is appropriate should be performed in accordance with one's previous conduct, place, time, and other factors. Thus has been explained the purification of the body consisting of the purification of the elements. One should contemplate that within the heart-lotus, which faces downward and is situated at the base of the spine, there is a *jvālākula* (flame-filled) fire. Within that fire is the syllable *raṃ*, from which a mass of flames issues forth. By that, one should burn away all the constituent parts of the body, beginning with the feet, so that nothing remains. Then, by means of the syllable *vaṃ*, one should imagine the arising of a lunar disc, and upon that, the syllable *haṃ*. From that, one should contemplate the emergence of a stream of nectar that flows down and completely fills the body. Having thus contemplated the self as being of the nature of the *praṇava*, one should perform the *nyāsa* (ritual placement) of the *praṇava* upon the head, face, heart, throat, arms, and so forth. One should perform the purification of the body as follows: [the elements of] primordial nature (prakṛti), ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas),
ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, sound, touch, form...
The impure *ātmatattva*, which consists of the principles (*tattvas*) of taste, smell, space, air, fire, water, and earth,

is the gross body (*sthūladeha*); the pure-impure *vidyātattva*, which consists of the principles of *māyā*, *kalā*, *avidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *puruṣa*, is the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).

Having meditated upon the pure Śivatattva— which consists of the principles (tattvas) of Śiva, Śakti, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śuddhavidyā— as well as the supreme body, one should dissolve the gross body into the subtle body and that supreme body. Following the performance of any one of the aforementioned methods of purification:
By means of the mantras beginning with "Hauṃ, obeisance to the Kalā beyond Peace," one effects the creation of the pure subtle body consisting of the five subtle Kalās;
and by means of those same five Kalā-mantras, [one effects the creation] of the [body] consisting of the five gross Kalās.
Having visualized the creation of the gross body and its subsequent destruction, one should bathe it with a stream of nectar flowing from the Śakti-maṇḍala, reciting: *Hāṃ Śaktaye Vauṣaṭ*.
Then, in the pericarp of the heart-lotus: *Hāṃ Ādhāra-śaktaye Namaḥ*. Hāṃ.

"Homage to the Seat of Dharma (dharmāsana). Hāṃ, homage to Knowledge (jñāna). Hāṃ, homage to Dispassion (vairāgya). Hāṃ, homage to Sovereignty (aiśvarya). Hāṃ, homage to the Lotus (padma). Having thus deposited the sixfold seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) in the center and in the four corners starting from the southeast, therein—

Again, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Self," which consists of the gross and subtle bodies and possesses an undivided form of hands, feet, and so forth; and having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva, which consists of the thirty-eight *kalās*, with "Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*), [one should then recite] "Obeisance to Śiva."

Having invoked there the individual soul (jīvātman)— which resides at the *dvādaśānta*, possesses the power of stainless knowledge and action, is of the nature of the sacrificer's form, and is in union with Paramaśiva— and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and others in the locations such as the heart, one should consecrate it with the root mantra and then with the power-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with a profuse stream of nectar flowing from the maṇḍala of Power (Śakti) situated at the *dvādaśānta*.
Then, one should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of Daṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Kalā, Śrīkaṇṭha, and the others.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: one should place the Śiva-seat and the unmanifest form of Śiva within the heart. (p. 28) With the words "Heṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the head," one should touch the head with the tip of the thumb while forming a fist. With the words "Heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the face," one should touch the mouth with the thumb and forefinger.

"HUM, salutation to the heart of Aghora"—with the thumb and middle fingers, at the heart; "HIṂ, salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva"—with the thumb and ring fingers, at the secret organ; "HAṂ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta"—with the thumb and little fingers, at the feet.

Thus, one should place [the mantras] upon the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western locations with their respective fingers in the manner previously described. In this way, after the placement of the staff, faces, and sisters, the initiated Brāhmaṇa— whether accompanied by the Śaktis or devoid of the Kalā-Śaktis— [should perform the rite] in the locations to be described hereafter.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). During another age (*yugāntara*), the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas should perform the ritual placement. Others, however, should place only the Śaktis. For example: *heṃ* to Śaśinī, *namaḥ*; *hoṃ* to Aṅgadā, *namaḥ*; *hoṃ* to iṣṭadā, *namaḥ*; *hoṃ* to Marīci, *namaḥ*; *hoṃ* to Jvālinī, *namaḥ*.
Thus, one should place [the mantras] on the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western heads with the fist-mudrā and the thumb-mudrā: "Heṃ, salutation to Śānti; Heṃ, salutation to Vidyā;
Heṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā; Heṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti. Thus.
One should place [the mantras] on the eastern, southern, northern, and western faces with the thumb and forefinger: *huṃ tāmrāyai namaḥ*; *huṃ mohāyai namaḥ*; *huṃ kṣudhāyai namaḥ*;
*huṃ nidrāyai namaḥ*; *huṃ mṛtyave namaḥ*; *huṃ māyāyai namaḥ*; *huṃ*.

*Bhayāyai namaḥ*. *Huṃ tārāyai namaḥ*. With these [mantras], using the thumb and middle finger, one should place [the mudrās] on the heart, throat, both shoulders, navel, abdomen, back, and chest. *Hiṃ rajāyai namaḥ*. *Hiṃ rakṣāyai namaḥ*. *Hiṃ ratyai namaḥ*. *Hiṃ pālyai namaḥ*. *Hiṃ*.
Oṃ *kāmāyai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *saṃyamāyai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *kriyāyai* namaḥ!
Hiṃ *buddhyai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *kāryai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *dhātryai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *brāhmaṇyai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *mohinyai* namaḥ! Hiṃ *manonmanyai* namaḥ!

Thus, with the thumb and ring finger, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the *mūlādhāra*, the private parts, the two testicles, the two thighs, the two shanks, the two buttocks, the waist, and the right side, [reciting]: "Hāṃ, salutation to Siddhi; Haṃ, salutation to Ṛddhi; Haṃ, salutation to Dūtī."
*Namaḥ*. *Haṃ*, salutation to Lakṣmī; *haṃ*, salutation to Medhā; *haṃ*, salutation to Kānti; *haṃ*, salutation to Svadhā; *haṃ*, salutation to Dhṛti.
Thus [one should worship] with the thumb and the little finger.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the two feet, the two hands, the nose, the head, and the two arms, conjoined with the six seed-syllables beginning with *namaḥ* and *svāhā*. Furthermore, one should perform the limb-placement (*aṅganyāsa*).
He who has the opportunity for this and whose mind is not agitated [should do so].

One should also perform the *nyāsa* of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, as well as the *nyāsa* of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and so forth. Thus, having attained the nature of Śiva through a body whose form consists of the mantras deposited after the purification of the individual soul (*jīva-śuddhi*) and the purification of the body (*deha-śuddhi*), one becomes fit for the worship of Śiva. For the scriptures declare: "One who is not Śiva himself should not worship Śiva."

Thus, if one is unable to perform the purification of the living body, one should perform the mere ritual placement (*nyāsa*). If one is unable to perform even the entire *nyāsa*, one should perform at least the *daṇḍanyāsa* or the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*.
By that alone, through the purification of the body and self, one attains the state of Śiva-nature.
One becomes fit for the worship of Śiva. Having thus performed the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
The Sequence of the Inner Sacrifice (Antaryāgakrama)

The sequence for this is as follows: having mentally conceived within the space of the inner heart a pavilion for the worship of Śiva made of divine jewels, and having mentally brought all the materials required for the worship of Śiva there and purified them;

Having performed the consecration by filling the arghya vessel and other offerings with a stream of nectar falling from the lunar disc situated at the *dvādaśānta*, and having performed the worship of the gatekeepers, one should proceed with the salutation of Gaṇeśa and the Guru, and the request for permission, according to the method to be described hereafter.

The previously mentioned blue-colored stalk, which has arisen from the root-tuber (kanda) at the maṇipūrṇa (jewel-colored) navel, is situated in the form of the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, whose eight petals are of an exceedingly white color.

Having meditated upon the liṅga in the form of a flame, which is of the nature of *nāda* and is to be perceived through the union of the ear and the thumb at the seat consisting of the *bindu*, and having worshipped the *śivāsana*— beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti— in the manner to be described upon that seat, [one should worship] the form of Śiva, whose body is the Vidyā, upon the liṅga.
And having worshipped Paramaśiva there by means of the sequence beginning with invocation (āvāhana), having meditated upon Him, having worshipped Him with internal purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
and having bathed Him with a stream of abundant nectar situated at the *dvādaśānta*, [one should worship Him] with garments, ornaments, and so forth.

Having adorned [the deity] with the sandalwood paste of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and offered the flower of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), one should worship with the eight flowers consisting of non-violence, restraint of the senses, forbearance, charity, knowledge, austerity, truth, and purity, in the manner beginning with "Yām" and so forth. Then, in the mind...

Having conceived the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the fire within the vessel and the crest of the incense smoke as the *ahaṅkāra*, one should offer incense. Having conceived the knowledge of Śiva itself as the lamp, one should offer it.

Having placed [the vessel] on his left side and having placed a water-vessel filled with pure water strained through a cloth on his right side, he should set aside the perfumes, flowers, and other materials for worship— distinct from the substances intended for Śiva— using the same base for his own worship, and then fill the vessels for the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya* waters.

There are four types of *arghya*: the general *arghya*, the special *arghya*, the *arghya* for cessation, and the *arghya* for those turned away. The general *arghya* is for the gatekeepers, the deities of the enclosures, and so forth; the special *arghya* is for Śiva alone at the times of offering *arghya* to Śiva.

At the time of the ritual for cessation, there is the *nirodhārghya*; at the time of dismissal, the *parāṅmukhārghya*. For these four types of *arghya*, there are four vessels, each measuring either ten palas or five palas.
[They should be] made from any one of the materials—

gold, silver, or copper— measuring either one and a half *palas* or whatever measurement is appropriate, having five joints raised and five joints opened, and being either circular or square in shape.

The *arghya* vessels should be taken as being marked with external eight-petaled lotuses, measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in length, with a thickness of one-fourth of a finger-breadth; or they may be half that size according to the aforementioned method, or even half of that again. (In the absence of gold and other such materials...)

The vessels for the *arghya* offering may be made of mother-of-pearl, sword-blades, horn, stone, wood, coconut shells, and so forth; or they may take the form of new earthenware vessels; or they may take the form of leaf-cups made from leaves such as those of the *palāśa*, lotus, or plantain tree.

The vessels for water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), as well as the incense, lamps, the bell, and so forth, should also be made according to the same previously mentioned measurements of ten *palas* and so on. Among those, the vessel for water for the feet (*pādyapātra*)...
The *ācamanapātra* (water vessel for sipping) should be made with a width of six *aṅgulas*, a height of four *aṅgulas*, a base (*pāda*) with a width and height of four *aṅgulas*,
a spout (*nāsikā*) of four *aṅgulas*, and lips (*oṣṭha*) of one *aṅgula*; or it may be made with those measurements reduced by half,
or even reduced by half again.
The vessel for the water for the feet (pādya) should be eight aṅgulas in height and sixteen aṅgulas in width;
it should have a base four aṅgulas high and eight aṅgulas wide,
with a lip one aṅgula thick, measuring either half the size of the aforementioned [vessel] or half of that again.

The two sides should be provided with rounded bracelets (*vṛttakaṅkaṇa*). The vessel for sipping water (*ācamanapātra*) should be twelve finger-breadths in height, with a wide belly, and be provided with a base six finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height;
its neck should be two or three finger-breadths in height.
The lip should be one finger-breadth thick and the mouth three fingers wide; it should be joined with a canopy shaped like a bud according to the *aicchika* (optional) measurement,
and the hole at the base and so forth should gradually decrease from a measure of four fingers and three *yava*s for the three faces.

It should be made with a nose of the same measurement as the vessel, or half that measurement; alternatively, the vessels for water for the feet (*pādya*) and for sipping (*ācamanīya*) should also be made in the shape of a circle like the vessel for the respectful offering (*arghya*). (p.
33) The vessel for pouring the sipping water should also be made like the vessel for pouring the water for the feet.
The *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamana* vessels should be made in the form of three-legged stands (*tripadī*),

joined with three faces and feet, eight finger-breadths in height, marked with lion faces on the upper portion above the feet and below the rim; this applies when gold and other precious materials are unavailable.

The vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings should also be accepted as being made of stone, wood, leaves, or folded cloth, just like the vessel for the guest-water (arghya). In that regard, the materials for the general guest-water (sāmānyārghya) are sesame seeds and rice grains. For the special guest-water (viśeṣārghya), the ingredients are cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, jātī-phala, murā, rice, and sesame seeds.

Either water, milk, the tips of *kuśa* grass, rice, *sumana* flowers, sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard; or *darbha*, *dūrvā*, and so forth, along with rice, sesame, *kṣariṇī* water, and white mustard; or excluding white mustard, *darbha* and the others—making six items; or alternatively, *darbha*, white mustard, water, and sesame—making four items.

Alternatively, there are three substances for the *arghya* of cessation: dūrvā grass, saffron, and camphor. For the *arghya* of the five substances, there are five items: *darbha* grass, dūrvā grass, barley, rice grains, and white mustard seeds.
For the *arghya* of the six backward-facing [deities], there are six substances, including sesame seeds.
For the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), there are six substances: *dūrvā* grass, sandalwood, white mustard, vetiver (*uśīra*), *hrīvera*, and saffron;

or those same five excluding saffron; or four substances: *dūrvā*, white mustard, sandalwood, and vetiver; or three substances: *hrīvera*, sandalwood, and vetiver. For the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*)...
Cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, mace, cinnamon, the three myrobalans, sandalwood, and ushira—these are eleven items;
or cardamom, cloves, camphor, cinnamon, murā, and nutmeg—these are six; or cardamom, cloves, camphor, hrīvera, and nutmeg—these are five; or simply cardamom, cloves, and camphor.
There are three types of substances. The substances for the *arghya* offering and so forth,
beginning with *elā*, should be given in quantities of eighty, forty, twenty, ten, or five *vrīhi* grains each, according to whether they are of superior, middling, or inferior quality.
Worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Now, the procedure for the worship beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) is described:

having placed the vessels for the water for the feet, the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the general offering (sāmānyārghya), the special offering (viśeṣārghya), the obstructing offering (nirodhārghya), and the offering for the face-averting [rite] (parāṅmukhārghya), along with their respective three-legged stands (tripadī), in front of the Deity in a sequence starting from the left, one should [proceed] with them.
Having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra on the feet [of the tripod] and Iḍā, Dhara, and Śakti on the rings,
one should wash the vessels for the water for the feet and other offerings with the Astra-mantra, place them upon the three-legged stand,
and fill them with pure water using either the Astra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

One should place the substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth into their respective vessels using the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*). In the absence of these substances, one should simply fill them with pure water. Then, having lifted the vessels for the water for the feet and so forth while reciting the *bindu* [mantra], [one should perform the rite] by means of a stream of nectar flowing from that *bindu*.
Having visualized [the vessels] as being filled with the waters of all the holy fords (tīrtha), such as the Gaṅgā,
one should place them upon the yantras. Alternatively,
one may draw down the divine nectar consisting of the Gaṅgā and other holy fords from the Bindu-sthāna by means of the Aṅkuśa-mudrā.

Having taken that [substance] with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should deposit it into the vessels for the *pādya* and other offerings located within the mandala, using the heart mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* along with the *udbhavamudrā*. Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*), the form (*mūrti*), the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahma*), the body (*vidyādeha*), the eyes (*netra*), and the root-mantra with its limbs (*mūlāṅga*) upon the water of the special *arghya* offering using the root-mantra;
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one should consecrate [the object] with the Brahma-mantra and the root-mantras of the limbs.

Or one may consecrate only the root-mantras of Brahmā’s limbs. One should consecrate the *nirodha-arghya* with the Brahmā-mantras, the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with the limb-mantras, and the *sāmānya-arghya* with the *astra-mantra*.
One should consecrate the water for the feet and the water for sipping with the Brahma-aṅga mantras or with the Astra-mantra. Then,

having performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with the Astra-mantra and the veiling (avakuṇṭhana) with the Kavaca-mantra, one should consecrate [the water] as nectar (amṛtīkuryāt) by displaying the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā) while reciting the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Regarding the rites from the water for the feet (*pādya*) up to the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*),

one may perform each step either according to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* method— beginning with the placement of the three-lamp stand (*tripadī*) and ending with the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*)— or not at all.
Then, the worship of the conch (*śaṅkhapūjā*) should be performed near the water for the guest-offering intended for the deity facing away.
The conch shells, which hold one *prastha*, one *mānika*, or one *kuḍava* of water, are classified as superior, middling, or inferior;

likewise, they are distinguished by having their bases and tips thick or thin, and by being male, female, or neuter in form. For the offering (*arghya*), the Earth resides at the base of the conch, and the Sun is in the rim.
Viṣṇu is in the belly, the Moon is on the side, Aghora is in the stream,

and the seven sacred fords (tīrthas) are in the mouth. Nevertheless, since the conch is as impure as a bone because its root and tip are external, it should be adorned with gold, jewels, and other such materials.

Having thus purified the conch by burning it with *tuṣa* (husks), cleansing it with water consecrated by mantras as before, and having placed it upon a tripod that has been worshipped as previously described, one should worship it with the special *arghya* offering and sprinkle oneself three times on the head with that water. Thus...

If one is unable to procure many vessels or perform their worship, the *nirodha-arghya* and *parāṅmukha-arghya* should be performed using the water from the *nirodha-arghya* vessel alone; or alternatively, all three *arghya* vessels may be prepared using the water from the *viśeṣa-arghya* alone. The same applies to the two sets of *pādya* and *ācamanīya*.

This must be performed with the *viśeṣārghya* (special offering water) alone. In the absence of another vessel for the *viśeṣārghya*, the two offerings of *pādya* and *ācamana*, as well as the three *arghya* offerings, should be performed using only the water from the conch.
For the sake of the deities of the *āvaraṇas* and so forth, only the *sāmānyārghya* (general offering water) should be consecrated in a separate vessel.

(p.35) Thus, in the case where there is a restriction regarding the vessel, if another ritual service is performed with its water, one must perform the purificatory rites using that very same vessel. Alternatively, even purificatory rites belonging to another [vessel] may be performed without contradiction, just as the properties of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are applied to a fire-enclosing stick (*paridhi*). Or else, it is constant.
This should be performed on occasions such as the equinoxes, solstices, and eclipses.
The Ritual for the Five Products of the Cow (Pañcagavyavidhi).
Now, the procedure for the five products of the cow is described: on the eastern side of the deity, or in the northeastern direction, one should prepare a square measuring two cubits or one cubit.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow-dung, and having drawn four lines toward the east and four toward the north,
one should mark out nine squares, each measuring the size of a palm; then, in each square,
[one should place] a measure of rice (*āḍhaka*), or half that measure, or half that again, of either unhusked grain (*vrīhi*), husked rice (*taṇḍula*), or *kuśa* grass.

Having spread [the grass] facing north, and having strewn around the western direction with five-fold numbers of *darbha* blades whose tips point north and east, and having adorned it all around with flowers, [he recites]:
"Obeisance to the Śiva-tattva; obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva; obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva."
Salutation to the principle of Puruṣa (puruṣatattva). Salutation to the principle of Time (kālatattva). Salutation to the principle of Earth (pṛthivītattva).
Salutation to the principle of Water (jalatattva). Salutation to the principle of Air (vāyutattva). Salutation to the principle of Primordial Matter (prakṛtitattva).
Thus [are the offerings] in the central, eastern, southern, northern, western, south-eastern, south-western, north-western, and north-eastern squares.

Having worshipped [the deities] and having washed vessels made of gold, bell-metal, or unbroken black clay, and having placed them in nine compartments, [one should offer salutations]: "Salutation to the well-established vessel! Salutation to the well-pacified vessel! Salutation to the vessel consisting of splendor!"
Salutation to the vessel of jewel-water; salutation to the vessel of nectar; salutation to the unmanifest vessel;

salutation to the vessel of the sun; salutation to the joined vessel; salutation to the unmanifest vessel—having thus worshipped the vessels according to the sequence of the previously mentioned grid, [one offers] the milk of a copper-colored cow.
Three *kuḍavas* of white-colored curd in the central vessel; two *kuḍavas* of tawny-colored [curd] in the eastern vessel;
one *kuḍava* of ghee in the southern vessel for the dark-colored [cow];
one *prastha* of cow urine in the northern vessel; and one *kuḍava* of black-colored cow dung.
The measure [of water] is five *kuḍavas* combined; this, strained through a cloth, is placed in the western vessel.

Then, rice, *āmalaka*, and turmeric ground together—measured at the size of a *kapittha* fruit, or half that size, or half again—that [mixture] is placed in the vessels located in the southeastern, southwestern, and northwestern corners.

With water infused with *kuśa* grass— thirty-six, twenty-five, or twelve times [stirred] by that half-measure— one should perform circumambulation to the right using a bundle of *darbha* grass wound around the northwest direction, measuring one cubit or one palm, with knots two finger-breadths apart and tips four finger-breadths long.

Having poured into the vessel in the northeast corner a mixture of *māḍhika* measure combined with fragrant *dūrvā* grass while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then sequentially add the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)— beginning with milk and ending with cow dung—
with the mantras of Īśāna and the others, using quantities of five, four, three, two, and one [respectively], along with rice flour.
One should consecrate an *āmalaka* fruit with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, turmeric with the *śiras-mantra*, and water infused with *kuśa* grass with the *kavaca-mantra*,
each by reciting the five Brahma-mantras six times. Immediately thereafter, one should place cow dung in cow urine,
both of these in clarified butter, those three in curd, and all four of these in milk.
Having poured [the water] there with the heart-mantra, one should then pour kuśa-water with the root-mantra.

Having consecrated it with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries, protected it with the Astra-mantra, enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, displayed the Dhenu-mudrā, worshipped it with scents and flowers, and presented incense and lamps with the Astra-mantra, one should consecrate it with the Mūla-mantra.
The Ritual of the Five Nectars (Pañcāmṛtavidhi)

Now, the procedure for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) is described: its worship should be performed prior to the worship of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Therein, up until the worship of the vessels, milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar are to be placed individually in the directions starting from the east and ending with the west.
Measuring one *prastha*, or three-quarters of a *prastha*, or half a *prastha*,

fruits such as plantain, jackfruit, and mango should be placed in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) as far as possible; in the northeast (Īśāna) corner, there should be scented water mixed with *kuśa* grass water.

The consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of those [substances] situated in their respective places is as before. [The mixture consists of] sugar, cow-dung, and water; however, there is no joining (*saṃyojana*). Alternatively, one may perform the procedure for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) together with the joining. Its sequence is as follows:
As previously prepared, having drawn five squares on a mound made of rice in the directions starting from the east and in the center,
and an eight-petaled lotus in the northwestern direction,
[one should worship] with the names Śiva, Niyati, Kāla, Vyakta, Avyakta, and Sumaṅgalā.

Having worshipped those [deities] with the six [substances] in the order beginning with the center, one should worship six vessels upon them with the names Amṛta, Soma, Vidyā, Ratna, Udaka, Sudhāprīta, and Suraprīta. Then,

according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should place the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in the vessels starting from the center, and [the remaining substance] in the vessel at the northeast corner.
Having poured coconut water and consecrated those five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with mantras just as one would the *kuśa* water,

one should gradually add sugar and the other ingredients to the milk just as one would the cow dung and so forth, and then add the coconut water just as one would the *kuśa* water. Thereafter, [one should offer] a ripe plantain fruit.
Having sprinkled [the site] while reciting the root mantra, one should rub it with the root mantra.

One should perform the services of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, just as in the case of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). In the absence of the substances prescribed for the *pañcagavya* and other rites, one may use curd and milk in place of each other, and cow dung and cow urine in place of each other.
The substitute for sugar is sugarcane juice.
In the event that the prescribed quantity of vessel-substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) cannot be obtained, the measure for the cow-dung is half the size of a thumb.
One, two, three, five, and one *pala* respectively of cow urine, ghee, curd, milk, and *kuśa* water are to be taken.
In the case of the *pañcāmṛta*, the milk and other ingredients are to be taken as suitable for sprinkling upon the deity’s *liṅga*.
In the absence of cows of the aforementioned colors, [milk from] a faultless cow that has a calf and is free from disease or pregnancy [may be used].

The milk and other products of the cow are to be taken. Milk that has not been touched by the saliva of a calf, curd that has not been churned, cow-dung situated in the open air, ghee, and cow-urine filtered through cloth are to be accepted.
The Ritual for the Bathing Water.

Now, the procedure for the bathing water is described: having obtained permission from Śiva, one should take a pure water-pitcher and go to a riverbank possessing excellent color, fragrance, and taste, or to a pure sacred ford such as a natural lake or a pool dug by the gods; [there] that water—

Having consecrated the water-pot with the Brahmāṅga mantras and washed it with the Astra mantra, one should fill it with that water filtered through a cloth while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra; having brought it and placed it on the right side of the deity, one should perfume it with water scented with cardamom, ushira, cloves, camphor, pāṭala, blue lotus, red lotus, karavīra, and other such flowers.

This preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the water for bathing must be performed prior to the purification of oneself and the worship of the gatekeepers. The water for bathing should be collected at a time when the sun is not visible; the same applies to the gathering of flowers.
The worshiper should perform this himself; however, if he is unable or lacks the necessary materials,
the fetching of flowers and water, the grinding of perfumes, the preparation of food offerings, and so forth may be performed by those who have bathed or are wearing clean garments.
The attendants, with purifiers in hand, must perform [the necessary tasks]. This is because of the logical equivalence of the terms "cut" and "ground.
Thus, having brought together the entire collection of substances required for what is to be described, one should effect their purification.
Purification of Substances (Dravya-śuddhi)

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: while gazing at the root-mantra with eyes touched by the thumb and ring finger, one should sequentially visualize it as dried, burnt, and sprinkled with nectar by means of the eyes of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, which consist of the powers of will, action, and knowledge.
Then, for the sake of purification, having sprinkled [the object] with the *patākā* [mantra] using the *astra-mantra*,

one should strike it with the middle finger using the *astra-mantra* itself in order to manifest the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Thereafter, with the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should sprinkle all of that with the special *arghya* water or with water from a conch shell.
Sprinkling it with *kuśa* grass and flowers, one should meditate on the emergence of sparks of the fire of consciousness from the mass of substances, like sparks of fire from a struck stone. Thus,
by means of the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), the mass of substances [is purified] from its impure form consisting of *māyā*.
That which has been abandoned [by the disciple] becomes fit for union with Śiva, consisting of the power of pure consciousness.
Then, one offers perfume with Sadyojāta, clothing with Vāmadeva, ornaments with Aghora,
the food offering (naivedya) with Tatpuruṣa, flowers with Īśāna, and the other items with the Hṛdaya mantra.

One should consecrate the substances intended for Śiva and the substances for the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā) and so forth. Then, having protected the entire collection of substances with the Astra-mantra, having shielded them with the Kavaca-mantra,
and having rendered them nectarine (amṛtīkṛta) by means of the Dhenu-mudrā and the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should consider them] prepared for the sake of Śiva.

Contemplating that all this is indeed of the nature of Śiva, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps using the Heart and Astra mantras. Then, having sprinkled drops of arghya water from one's own body upon one's seat with the Astra mantra, [one should sit].

Having offered a flower with the mantra *śivāsanāya namaḥ* and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form of Śiva upon one's own body, one should apply a tilaka of sandalwood paste on the forehead. Then, one should offer a flower upon one's own head with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and likewise offer the water of honor (*arghya*) upon one's own head. (Recite the root mantra ten times...)

The phrase "one should recite" (*japet*) appears additionally in another manuscript. Thus, having abandoned the notion of being a bound soul (*paśu*) within oneself, and contemplating, "I am pure, possessing stainless knowledge and action like Śiva," one should worship oneself. This concludes the purification of substances (*dravya-śuddhi*). Although the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*) was previously mentioned, nevertheless—

Since it has entered as an implement of worship by virtue of being the agent of worship, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings just like any other substance; this is the purification of the final substance.
The Method for Purifying Mantras
Now, for the sake of removing the illusory and impure forms produced by the activity of the teeth, palate, and lips of mantras—
which possess sovereignty, the authority of office, and the capacity to bestow fruits that were previously obscured by impurities— of those [mantras]:
And for the purpose of manifesting one's spiritual capacity (*sāmarthya*), purification must be performed. Its procedure is stated as follows:

having formed the *añjali* at the heart, [one should recite] three times in sequence, ending with *namaḥ*, the *praṇava* (Oṃ) in its short, long, and protracted forms, extending respectively to the *bindu*, the *brahmarandhra*, and the *śikhā*.

One should perform the recitation of the root mantra slowly. Then, one should likewise perform the recitation of the Brahma-mantras, the limbs, and so forth. Having thus performed the purification of the mantra, immediately thereafter, if there is the presence of the retinue deities, one should perform their worship. How?
The presence of the retinue deities occurs in the worship of Śiva when performed either with or without his Śakti. Thus, the subtle forms have been described;

those known as pure (*śuddha*), solitary (*kevala*), and mixed (*miśra*)—namely, the worship of Śiva beginning from Saura and ending with Caṇḍa, whether performed without Śakti or with Śakti—are each threefold according to the division into solitary, natural (*sahaja*), and mixed, as stated by Aṃśumat.

*Aṃśumati* refers to the worship of the *liṅga* alone, devoid of any accompanying deities in its retinue. *Sahaja* refers to the worship of the *liṅga* accompanied by a fourfold retinue in the forms of Vṛṣabha, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Pārvatī.
*Miśra* refers to [the worship] of [the *liṅga*] accompanied even by Maheśvara in his dancing form (*nṛttamūrti*), Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and others.

The worship of the *liṅga*. Thus, there are nine kinds of worship: the purely pure (*kevala-śuddha*), the innate pure (*sahaja-śuddha*), the mixed pure (*miśra-śuddha*), the purely solitary (*kevala-kevala*), the innately solitary (*sahaja-kevala*), the mixed solitary (*miśra-kevala*), the solitary mixed (*kevala-miśra*), the innately mixed (*sahaja-miśra*), and the mixed mixed (*miśra-miśra*). Among these:
Prior to the commencement of the Śiva-pūjā, one should perform the Sūrya-pūjā, and immediately thereafter, the Caṇḍa-pūjā; then, having invoked Śiva alone— without Śakti— into the Liṅga,
the worship of Him devoid of his retinue of deities is termed *kevala-śuddha*.
The previously mentioned worship performed together with the fourfold retinue is *sahaja-śuddha* (naturally pure).
The previously mentioned worship performed even together with Maheśvara and the others is *miśra-śuddha* (mixed-pure).
Having omitted the worship of Sūrya and the rest, as well as Caṇḍa, at the beginning and end, [one should perform the worship] of the Liṅga along with the Śakti.

The worship of Śiva alone, performed after invoking him but without the worship of his retinue (*parivāra*), is *kevala-kevala*. The aforementioned worship itself, when accompanied by the worship of the fourfold retinue, is *sahaja-kevala*. When it is further accompanied by the worship of Maheśvara and the others, it is *miśra-kevala*. At the beginning and end, there is the worship of Sūrya and Caṇḍa.

The worship of the *liṅga* alone—whether it be with its power (*saśaktika*), without its power (*aśaktika*), or devoid of attendant deities—is called "purely mixed" (*kevalamiśra*). That which is accompanied by the worship of the fourfold retinue of deities is "naturally mixed" (*sahajamiśra*). And that which is further accompanied by the worship of Maheśvara and others is "mixed-mixed" (*miśramiśra*). Thus, in the case of the purely pure (*kevalakevala*) [worship]:
Even though there is no retinue in the case of the solitary *sahaja* [form], since a retinue does exist in the cases of the solitary *miśra* and the mixed (*miśraka*) forms,
it is indeed appropriate to describe the worship of the retinue in the *kevala* form immediately after the purification of the mantra. Therein,
one should worship the bull facing westward in the eastern quarter of the deity.

One should worship Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Pārvatī facing eastward in the southern, western, and northern directions respectively. When worshipping Pārvatī in her form as Durgā, one should worship her facing southward. However, the followers of the Purāṇas [state otherwise].
They state that the four attendant deities have the forms of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, and Durgā.

Furthermore, when there is a desire for results such as health and so forth regarding the group of four beginning with the Bull, the worship of Sūrya and the others must also be performed among the attendant deities. Regarding the Bull...
On the left side is Sūrya; on the right side of the God is Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
on the west is Skanda; on the left is Viṣṇu; on the northern side is the Goddess;
and on the eastern side is the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti). In this manner, the positions for other deities to be worshipped as prescribed in the Āgamas should also be understood.
The locations are to be seen.
Purification of the Linga.
Now, regarding the purification of the *liṅga*: having opened the chest containing the deity situated within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
one should worship Bhīmarudra, who stands before it, four-armed and three-eyed, holding the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a parasol and a chowrie.

"O God, destroyer of night-stalkers, for the purpose of worshipping the Lord, please be gracious and come to the left of the pure door. Having thus prayed, [he addresses] the Lord situated within the casket:
"Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the lords of gods, the sole leader of all worlds!"

Having prayed, "Arise for the purpose of the ritual bath and for the sake of self-protection," one should grasp the *liṅga* with both hands, discard the cloth, and [place it] upon the bathing altar which has already been honored with the sixfold rite of rising (*ṣaḍutthāsana*).
Having placed [the deity] upon a linga made from any one of gold, silver, bell-metal, tin, lead, or a milky tree,
which is circular in shape, elevated in the center, covered with a spread cloth on top, and provided with a lotus-patterned base, a trembling rim, and a row of lotuses on its pedestal;

Having worshipped the worship performed on the previous day with the *hṛdayamantra*, and having offered the *arghya* with the water of the common *arghya* using the root mantra ending in *svāhā* according to the sequence from the head to the northeast (*īśāna*),
and having presented incense and lamps, [one should worship] the five [faces] beginning with *Īśāna* with the thumbs and so forth up to the little fingers.
Having placed [the fingers] and grasping the flower with the little finger,
ring finger, and middle finger, one should lower the worship from the top of the *liṅga* using the thumb and forefinger while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, having placed that flower upon the crown of the *liṅga*, the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) should be disposed of in the northeast direction.
Having placed [the linga] upon the heart as a pure vessel, one should wash the linga with the Astra mantra and the pedestal (pīṭha) with the Pāśupata-Astra mantra;

then, using the water from the general arghya, one should consecrate it with the Heart mantra ending in "svāhā. When this has been done and the previous worship is concluded, immediately after the withdrawal of the mantras placed upon the linga and the pedestal:
The obstacles that obstruct the worshiper’s attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation, which are attached to the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*), are dispelled.
Furthermore, by bathing the *liṅga* with water from the heart-center, it becomes pure and fit for the ritual placement of mantras (*mantravinyāsa*). Thus concludes the purification of the *liṅga*.

Then, having displayed the *liṅgamudrā* while reciting "Obeisance to Śiva and Śakti," and having worshipped with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) using the mantras of the seat, the image, and the root mantra, and having presented incense and a lamp,
[one should offer] with a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, conch, mother-of-pearl, or cow-horn, whichever is available.
Having sprinkled [the image] with a stream four finger-breadths wide and the size of the tip of a cow's horn,
having anointed it with oil produced from a hand-press or with cow-ghee,
having rubbed it dry with flour-powder and the like, having sprinkled it again with lukewarm water, and having placed a flower upon its head.

Having offered flowers, incense, and lamps to each of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the juices of fruits, and intermittently to the head, the crest-lock, and the eyes, one should [ring] the bell with the *astra-mantra*.

One should sprinkle while striking. In this manner, one should sprinkle with water containing fruits and other substances. In that context, "water with fruits" refers to fragrant water endowed with the following: *vitva*, *panasa*, coconut, *khaṇḍa*, pomegranate with its peel, *bījapūra*, *punnāga*, *likuca*, *nāraṅga*, mango, and plantain fruit.

What? Water containing seeds—namely, *yava*, *nīvāra*, *vrīhi*, *mudga*, *siddhārtha*, *saugandhika*, and golden *śāli* rice—is "seed-water. Having consecrated [the disciple] with that, one should worship him with the root-mantra (*mūlabīja*) using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Water containing crystal, pearl, ruby, coral, hessonite, topaz, emerald, and sapphire is "jewel-water" (ratnodaka). Having consecrated [the image] with that while reciting the Varṇamantra,
one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings, such as sandalwood, agallochum, and musk.
Water mixed with the powder of saffron, camphor, realgar, cardamom, costus, black pepper, cloves, ushira, and campaka buds is "scented water" (gandhodaka). Having consecrated [the image] with that,
one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings while reciting the name-mantra.

Water joined with *campaka*, *mallikā*, *ketakī*, *pāṭala*, *kunda*, *puṇṇāga*, *nandyāvarta*, *jātī*, *mandāraka*, *karavīra*, *padma*, *utpala*, and mountain flowers, mixed with *hrīvera*, *damanaka*, and so forth, is "flower-water" (*puṣpodaka*). Having consecrated it with the Śiva-mantra, [one offers] perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
One should offer it; then, reciting the name-mantra, one should slowly sprinkle pure food around the *liṅga*, having fashioned that food into the shape of a *liṅga*,
and having offered scents, flowers, incense, lamps, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), betel-leaf, and so forth.
Having washed that food and placed the root-syllable (*mūlabīja*) upon the top of the *liṅga*,
and having offered fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp, one should touch it with the Brahma-mantras and form the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*).
This consecration of food wards off untimely death (*apamṛtyu*).

This [rite] bestows longevity, health, and the increase of the king and the kingdom; it is a means of bringing all under control and effects all forms of pacification. Thereafter, one should perform the water-worship (jalārcana). Having filled a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or any one of the sacrificial woods with pure water consecrated by the rites of inspection (nirīkṣaṇa) and so forth, one should proceed.

Having installed the *liṅga* in its center, one should offer *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and worship it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. This is the water-worship (*jalārcana*). Then, having lifted it up and wiped it clean, one should arrange the bath and food offerings as before, using coconut juice, sugarcane juice, and so forth.

One should perform the consecration according to what is possible. By anointing Śiva with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the sin accumulated over thousands of millions of years is destroyed. By consecrating him with clarified butter for one month, the attainment of the state of Śiva occurs for oneself along with twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
Through the consecration with sesame oil produced from a mechanical press, one attains the state of Śiva.
Through the consecration with milk, one obtains the fruit of giving away ten thousand cows adorned with ornaments.
Through bathing with curd, preceded by the destruction of all sins, one attains the world of Śiva.
By bathing with honey, preceded by the destruction of all sins, one attains the world of Vahni (Fire).

By bathing with sugarcane juice, one attains the world of the Vidyādharas. By bathing with camphor and agallochum water, one attains the state of Śiva. By bathing with fragrant sandalwood water, one attains the world of the Gandharvas; and by bathing with flower-water...

It should be understood that the attainment of the world of the Sun occurs through golden water, the world of Kubera through jewel-water, the world of Indra through *kuśa*-grass water, and the world of Brahmā through [other specific waters], and so forth. In the absence of such substances, one should perform the consecration with pure water filtered through a cloth; by that as well, [the goal is attained].
The attainment of the world of Varuṇa, where all desires are fulfilled, has been described.

Then one should perform the consecration by pouring streams [of water]. In the worship for one's own sake, that [mandala] is best when it is twelve finger-breadths in width, one finger-breadth in height, and three barley-corns in thickness;
or it may be seven finger-breadths in width, half a finger-breadth in height, and two barley-corns in thickness.

The medium [size] is five finger-breadths in width, one finger-breadth in height, and the size of a barley grain in thickness. The inferior [size] is the same [in proportions]. It should be made of gold, silver, or copper, either square or circular. If it is square, one should draw nine compartments.

In the center of the middle cell there is one aperture; around the very line of that middle cell, there are four apertures in the cardinal directions starting from the east; and in each of the peripheral cells, there are twelve apertures. Thus, in the superior vessel, there are one hundred and eight apertures.

One should make apertures. (p. 43) In the center of the central compartment, there shall be one central aperture; surrounding it, there are eight [others], and three apertures each in the compartments starting from the east—thus one should make twenty-five apertures for the middle vessel. It is circular.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should fashion nine apertures in the center of the pericarp and around it,

twelve apertures in each petal, and four [more] in the cardinal directions on the circle outside the petals for the superior vessel; for the other two vessels, as with the eight-petalled lotus, they should be square.

The substances are to be viewed. Having thus placed the vessel above the deity with his hands and having filled it with water from a conch shell, while holding it with both hands, he should consecrate [the deity] with streams of water using the root mantra.

Thus, having consecrated with the *astra-mantra* the oils and other substances— distinct from the previously prepared five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth— and having shielded them with the *kavaca-mantra* and protected them with the *astra-mantra*,
one should employ them for the consecration by means of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdayabīja*). In this manner, the consecration is performed through this elaborate procedure.

If unable to perform [this], one should consecrate [the image] with pure water. Then, having offered *mantrapuṣpa* with the root mantra and presented the *mantrānna*, one should gently wipe it with a clean, soft cloth and place it upon the lotus-seat (*padmapīṭha*). Thereafter, rising and circumambulating Śiva,

The presiding deity of the site (Vāstvadhipati) situated in the southwest corner, having gone from the position of Brahmā toward the north in the form of Śiva to the northwest corner of the temple, is there dark-complexioned,
holding in his hands a tooth, a rosary, a noose, and a goad, and in his trunk a citron fruit.

Having worshipped Gaṇapati—who is seated facing south and holding [the tusk]—with all the ritual services beginning with invocation (āvāhana), one should pray: "O Lord Gaṇeśa, may my worship of Śiva be free from obstacles. Then, in the eastern direction...

In the form of the northern direction of Śivakheṭaka, one should likewise worship Mahālakṣmī— who bears the bilva fruit, the lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness, who has three eyes, who is the embodiment of Śiva-Śakti, and who is seated facing south— and then pray: "O Mother, grant me abundance of materials for the worship of Śiva."
Then, in the eastern part of the temple of Śiva, in the form of the northeast corner,
[one should worship] Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Ambikā, Guha, Viṣṇu, and Dhātṛ—
[deities] with serene countenances, wearing yogic girdles, and whose hands are adorned with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*) and rosaries.

Having likewise worshipped with all ritual offerings two white-complexioned men seated facing south— either the seven gurus beginning with Śiva and ending with one's own personal guru, or all the gurus— one should [invoke] the gurus beginning with Śiva.

One should pray thus: "O Great Ones, you ought to grant me permission; I shall perform the worship of Śiva according to the path shown by you. Then, having worshipped the sandals—or rather, the sandals representing the venerable Guru's sandals—saying "Obeisance to the sandals of the venerable Guru" in the place of the Guru.

After performing the worship of Gaṇapati, Mahālakṣmī, and the sandals of the Guru, and having prostrated before all, with knees fixed motionless upon the ground and palms joined in reverence, he said: "O Lord of the Gaṇas, O Ambikā, O Sandals of my Master, O Teacher of the World, grant permission to me as I perform this sacrifice according to my means."

One should pray for them simultaneously. Then, having contemplated obtaining permission from them with the words, "O son, perform the sacrifice to Śiva," and being seated on a beautiful seat in the south-eastern corner or the southern side of the deity's [shrine], one should [perform the recitation] ten times for each [deity].
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) consisting of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kuṃbhaka), and exhalation (recaka),
and having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the worship of Śiva according to my ability, preceded by the intention for my desired fruit," one should begin the worship.
Therein, first is the worship of Śiva’s seat (*śivāsanārcana*), which is the worship of Śiva.
That [seat] has the form of a lotus divided into the pericarp (*karṇikā*), filaments (*kesara*), petals (*dala*), stalk (*nāla*), and root (*granthi*);
it rises to a height encompassing the thirty-two principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
The height [of the body] extends from the form situated above, beginning with the *nivṛtti* kalā and ending with the *śānti* kalā.

Above that is the *vidyā-deha*, which has the measure of the *śāntyatīta* kalā. For the sake of thoroughly understanding its essential nature, the measures of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti* and the essential nature of the *tattvas* contained within them are now analyzed.
It takes the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), measuring one hundred and ten million *yojanas* in extent, beginning with the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
Within that is the single element of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*). Above that is the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, measuring one thousand million *yojanas*.
Therein reside the four elements beginning with water, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) beginning with smell, and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).

The twenty-three principles (*tattva*) consist of the five organs of knowledge, the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Above that is the *avidyā-kalā*, measuring ten million times ten thousand (*ayuta-koṭi*) yojanas.

Therein are the seven principles consisting of the individual soul (*puruṣa*), attachment (*rāga*), necessity (*niyati*), limited agency (*kalā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), time (*kāla*), and illusion (*māyā*). Above that—

The Śāntikalā extends for one hundred billion yojanas; therein reside Śuddhavidyā and Maheśvara, constituting a state of duality. Above that is the Śāntyatītakalā, extending for one trillion yojanas; therein reside Sadāśiva and Śakti, constituting a state of duality. Above that is the immeasurable Śivatattva.
The earth-tattva, consisting of the *nivṛtti* kalā, extends as far as the *kanda*;

the stalk consists of twenty-nine tattvas beginning with water and ending with *kāla*, which are included within the *pratiṣṭhā* and *vidyā* kalās; and within these tattvas from water to *kāla* reside seventy-five worlds (*bhuvanas*).

The thorns are the fifty qualities of the intellect belonging to the living beings within those respective worlds, which are like the fibers within the stalk of the fifty worlds. Within the *vidyā-kalā* alone, the *māyā-tattva*, situated above *kāla*, is the knot of the lotus-stalk. Within the *śānti-kalā*...
There stands a lotus consisting of the petals, filaments, and pericarp of the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva).

Above Pure Knowledge is the principle of Maheśvara, extending as far as the subtle form of Śiva; and situated within the kalā beyond Tranquility (śāntyatīta-kalā) are the two principles of Sadāśiva and Śakti.
This extends up to the body of knowledge (vidyā-deha). The worlds situated within the stalks are as follows:

there are eight worlds each in water, fire, air, ether, ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), and primordial nature (prakṛti), making fifty-six in total; six in the Person (puruṣa); five in attachment (rāga); two in necessity (niyati); and [one] in limited agency (kalā).
Two in knowledge, two in time, and two [in power]—thus, from Puruṣa down to Time, there are nineteen worlds; these fifty-seven worlds are the "thorns.
The five forms of error consist of tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra.

Intellection (*ūha*), verbal instruction (*śabda*), study (*adhyayana*), the destruction of the threefold suffering (*duḥkhatrayavighāta*), acquisition of friends (*suhṛtprāpti*), and charity (*dāna*)—these are the eight perfections (*siddhi*). The internal [perfections] are those called *prakṛti*, *upādāna*, *kāla*, and *bhāga*.
The external objects are threefold, while those produced by the Supreme (God) are fivefold; thus, there are nine groups of four.
The eleven modalities of the senses, such as blindness and muteness;

and the seventeen modalities of the previously mentioned powers and intellects, such as *anūha* (non-deliberation) and so forth—these twenty-eight powers constitute the fifty *bhāvas*, which are the threads of the net. Herein:
Regarding the measurement of the Kanda, Nāla, and so forth, which extends for a *yojana*, another opinion is presented:
the Earth-tattva, consisting of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, is exactly one hundred crore *yojanas* as previously stated;
water is ten times the extent of the Earth-tattva, and fire is ten times the extent of the water-tattva.
Air is ten times greater than fire; space is ten times greater than air;
from that, the ego (ahaṅkāra) is ten times greater; the intellect (buddhi) is ten times greater than the ego;
and the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) is ten times greater than the intellect. Thus, [the progression continues] up to the principle of the qualities.
The increase is by a factor of ten. Beyond this, up to the principle of *māyā*, the increase is by a factor of one hundred. *Prakṛti* is a hundred times greater than the principle of *guṇa*.
Attachment (*rāga*) is a hundred times greater than *prakṛti*. Necessity (*niyati*) is a hundred times greater than attachment. [Necessity] is a hundred times greater than necessity.

Vidyā; then Kalā is a hundred times that; then Kāla is a hundred times that; then Māyā is a hundred times that. For Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, the increase is by a factor of one thousand: Śuddhavidyā is a thousand times Māyā, and [Īśvara] is a thousand times Śuddhavidyā.

Īśvara [is the next]; from Īśvara, Sadāśiva is a thousandfold greater. From that, there is an increase by a factor of one hundred thousand; from the principle of Sadāśiva, Śakti is a hundred-thousandfold greater. Beyond that, the principle of Śiva is immeasurable. And this doctrine [places it] prior to Prakṛti.

This [work] proceeds by accepting the category of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) but not accepting the category of the person (*puruṣatattva*) immediately after the category of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). And so they say: "The earth-category extends for a hundred million *yojanas*, beginning from the waters and ending at the limit of the qualities; its enumeration is thus according to the sequence starting from primordial nature. (Verse 46)

From the hundred-fold [worlds] ending with Māyā, and from the thousand-fold up to Sadāśiva, then up to the end of Śakti, there are ten lakhs; above that is Śiva, whose power is immeasurable, the presiding lord of the Bindu.
If it is asked, "This being so, how many *yojanas* in number does the Nāla become?", the answer is that it is indeed an incalculable (*asaṃkhya*) number of *yojanas*.
Nevertheless, by applying a certain method, its measurement in *yojanas* is demonstrated as follows:
when counting begins from one and increases tenfold at each subsequent step, [the number eventually reaches the required magnitude].

The twentieth place is the number *parārdha*; it is the very last number. And these are the names of the twenty places: one, ten, hundred, thousand, *ayuta*, *lakṣa*, *prayuta*, *koṭi*, *arbuda*, *padma*, *kharva*.

Nikharva, vṛnda, mahāpadma, śaṅkha, mahāśaṅkha, samudra, mahāsamudra, madhya, and parārdha. Thus they have said: one, ten (paṅkti), hundred, thousand, ten-thousand (ayuta), hundred-thousand (lakṣa), million (prapūrvāyuta), ten-million (koṭi), hundred-million (arbudaka), and billion (padmaka).

"Furthermore, the wise know this enumeration as follows: *matha*, *kharva*, *nikharva*, likewise *bṛnda*, *mahāsaroja*, then *śaṅkha*, *samudra*, finally *madhya*, and that which is designated as *parārdha*. And thus:

Having placed the number one hundred million (śatakoṭi) in the position of unity, the calculation of the elements beginning with water is performed. One "padma" is the name for the number one hundred million; consequently, the earth element consists of one *padma* yojanas, the water element consists of one yojana, the fire element consists of ten yojanas, and the air element consists of one hundred yojanas.

The principle of space (*gaganatattva*) extends for a thousand *yojanas*; the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*) for ten thousand *yojanas*; the intellect (*buddhi*) for one hundred thousand *yojanas*; and the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) for one million *yojanas*. Beyond that, the numbers should be understood by increasing them by a factor of one hundred at each step, skipping every other number; as follows:

Nature (*prakṛti*) is ten *yojanas*, passion (*rāga*) is a *nikharva* of *yojanas*, necessity (*niyati*) is a *mahāpadma* of *yojanas*, knowledge (*vidyā*) is a *mahāśaṅkha* of *yojanas*, limited agency (*kalā*) is an *arbudha* of *yojanas*, and time (*kāla*) is a *parārdha* of *yojanas*. Thus, the stalk (*nāla*), which consists of the aggregate of principles beginning with water and ending with time, is ten, a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand [yojanas].
It is measured in *yojanas* by a collection of thirteen numerical units known as *lakṣa*, *prayuta*, *koṭi*, *padma*, *nikharva*, *mahāpadma*, *mahāśaṅkha*, *mahāsamudra*,
and *parārdha*. Within the number *padma*, there is the nature of a single essence.
Even by placing it upon the mind and attributing the existence of a number exceeding a *parārdha*, one is unable to calculate it—
whether as a *kharva*, *nikharva*, *bṛnda*, *mahāpadma*, *śaṅkha*, *mahāśaṅkha*, *samudra*, or a *parārdha* multiplied tenfold, or a *parārdha* multiplied a thousandfold.

The height, measured in *yojanas*, consists of a collection of thirteen numerical units, each being a *parārdha* multiplied by ten million (*koṭi*) and then multiplied by another *parārdha*. This [height] serves as the common support for the worlds situated within the stalk as well.

Since there is no separate enumeration of *yojanas* for the five objects beginning with smell (*gandha*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), the five organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), and the mind (*manas*), the number of *yojanas* is not calculated for those which are considered their supports. Now, even for these [supports], by virtue of being the substratum of the worlds (*bhuvana*)—
Based on the number of separate yojanas, another opinion is presented.

Because they have arisen from the magnitude of a *padma-yojana*, there is a tenfold increase for each subsequent one among the twenty principles beginning with water and ending with the mind (*manas*).
For ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and intellect (*buddhi*), the increase is hundredfold; for primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it is thousandfold; and for the person (*puruṣa*), it is ten-thousandfold.

The power of *niyati* and *kāla* is a hundred thousandfold (*lakṣaguṇā*). The power of *rāga*, *vidyā*, and *kalā* is ten millionfold (*daśalakṣaguṇā*). The power of *māyā* is ten million times ten millionfold (*koṭiguṇā*). The power of *śuddhavidyā* is one hundred million times ten millionfold (*daśakoṭiguṇā*). The power of *īśvara* is one billion times ten millionfold (*śatakoṭiguṇā*). The power of *sadāśiva* is ten billion times ten millionfold (*sahasrakoṭiguṇā*). The power of *śakti* is one hundred billion times ten millionfold (*ayutakoṭiguṇā*).

Regarding the statement that "there is no measurement in *yojanas* for the principle of Śiva": this alternative view has arisen based on a different sequence of the five principles—beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*—situated between [Śiva and the lower levels], in their vertical arrangement.
In this system, the twenty-one principles from *kṣiti* (earth) up to *manas* (mind) [are arranged] one after another.

Increasing tenfold in succession, they are: one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand (*ayuta*), hundred-thousand (*lakṣa*), million (*prayuta*), ten-million (*koṭi*), hundred-million (*arbuda*), billion (*padma*), ten-billion (*kharva*), hundred-billion (*nikharva*), trillion (*bṛnda*), ten-trillion (*mahāpadma*), hundred-trillion (*śaṅkha*), quadrillion (*mahāśaṅkha*), quintillion (*samudra*), and ten-quintillion (*mahāsamudra*). Beyond that is the *madhya*.

Ten *parārdhas* of *yojanas* [is the extent of the earth]. *Ahaṃkāra* and *buddhi* increase by a factor of one hundred respectively, reaching a thousandfold and a hundred-thousandfold *parārdha-yojanas*.
*Prakṛti* increases by a factor of one thousand, reaching a *parārdha* multiplied by a *arbuda* (*100,000,000*) of *yojanas*.

From that point, the Puruṣa extends for ten thousand times increased [in size], measuring a *parārdha* multiplied by a *vṛnda* of *yojanas*. Niyati and Kāla extend respectively by increasing ten million-fold, measuring a thousand *mahāsamudras* and a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* of *yojanas*. Rāga, Vidya, and Kalā, however—
Increasing by ten-fold increments, there are [distances] of one hundred thousand *yojanas* multiplied by a *padma-parārdha*, multiplied by a *mahāśaṅkha-parārdha*,

multiplied by a *śata-parārdha*, and multiplied by a *parārdha-parārdha*. Thus, according to this view, the stalk consists of the aggregate of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with water and ending with *kalā*.

It becomes measurable in *yojanas* by a collection of twenty-nine numbers, beginning with ten and ending with a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* multiplied by ten *parārdhas*. This occurs when proceeding by means of the increase of the principles (*tattva-vṛddhi*).

In both cases, there would be excessive length for the stalk, the knot, and the lotus. To explain: here, in the first case, among the principles (tattvas) situated within the stalk, time (kāla) alone measures one *parārdha-yojana*;
the *kalā* principle is measured at only one-hundredth part of that; and the principles beginning with *vidyā*, *niyati*, and the preceding ones [are progressively smaller].
The stalk measures one hundredth part of that [the root], being slightly more than one *parārdha* yojanas.
But the knot, which is of the nature of *māyā*, is a hundred times a *parārdha* yojanas.
Since *māyā* is a hundred times greater than *kāla*, the lotus is a hundred thousand times a *parārdha* yojanas.
Since Śuddhavidyā, which has the form of a lotus, is a thousand times greater than Māyā,
the length of the connection between the knots and the lotuses would be such even according to this alternative view.
Thus, the length of the knots and the lotuses, starting from the *kanda* and relative to the stalk, is not [as previously stated].
It resembles the shadow of a worldly lotus;

it resembles the shadow of the heart-lotus located within the region of the heart, starting from the nine-navelled *kanda*. Furthermore, adopting the side of the increase of the digits (*kalā*) is indeed conducive to the meditation on the lotus of Śiva’s throne.

And this lotus contains within it five seats: the seat of Ananta, the lion throne, the yoga seat, the lotus seat, and the stainless seat. Among these, the support-power (*ādhāra-śakti*) is the bulb (*kanda*), which is commensurate with the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*). The stalk (*nāla*) itself is commensurate with the principles beginning with water and ending with time (*kāla*).

Together with the lotus bud situated above that, and together with the serpent-form possessing a circle of jewel-crests arisen from the Ocean of Milk which is the nature of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti)— these two, namely Ananta and Rudra who are included among the eight Vidyeśvaras, are called the Anantāsana (the Seat of Ananta).

From the stalk upwards, beginning with the *jala-tattva* and extending as far as the *guṇa-tattva*, there is the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*) situated around the stalk. Above that, reaching up to the knot (*granthi*), is the yoga seat (*yogāsana*).
Above that is the lotus seat (*padmāsana*), consisting of petals and filaments. The pericarp itself is the stainless seat (*vimalāsana*).
Or rather, it consists of the three qualities (guṇas) situated upon the pericarp, representing the three mandalas and the three principles (tattvas).
Although Ananta is described as a serpent adorned with a thousand hoods, his stalk (nāla) is actually his body-staff (bhoga-daṇḍa) standing upright;
it is that very circle of his hoods which is contracted here.

The bud does not exist apart from that [lotus]; nevertheless, that very same [bud] is to be meditated upon in the form of an eight-petaled lotus during the state of meditation on its blossoming—thus it is called *padmāsana*. Alternatively, it is circular in shape and possesses the brilliance of ten million suns.

Beneath the lion throne is the form of the serpent Ananta; there is the form of the infinite lotus, and from its stalk arises another seat for Ananta, circular in shape, upon which are seated, one above the other, the serpents Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kārkoṭaka, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Or else, one may assume the form of the eight great nāgas known as Śaṅkha and Gulika. Alternatively, the infinite seat (anantāsana) should be visualized in this way:
beneath the lion throne, there are the forms of a bull, a lion, a spirit, and an elephant.

Upon a couch consisting of the four feet of Dharma and so forth and the four slabs of the fruits of Adharma and so forth, he stands with five hoods and a tail; in the middle of the hoods, he has the form of a man,
