is clothed in silken garments, adorned with all ornaments, and holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness in his two hands.

The Naga King: surrounding him in the directions starting from the east are the great Naga Kings, beginning with Ananta and ending with Gulika, each possessing a single hood, with palms joined in reverence, gazing [upon the central deity].
Upon the head of the Naga King is the "Ananta-lotus," endowed with eight fully blossomed petals.
Here, relying solely on the first position, the sequence for the worship of Śiva’s throne is demonstrated:
*Hāṃ*, salutation to the Support-Power (*ādhāraśakti*).
[It is] equal in measure to the Earth-principle, which has the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) extending for a hundred million *yojanas*.

I worship Ādhāraśakti, who has the form of a lotus-cavern that is the seat of Śiva, who is white in color, and who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons. Homage to Anantāsana! [I worship] that which has the form of a stalk, measuring the extent of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Water and ending with Kalā.

Together with the knot of illusion (*māyāgranthi*), its height is eleven thousand *koṭi* yojanas; or it is ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million (*prayuta*), ten million (*lakṣa*),

a hundred million (*arbuda*), a billion (*padma*), ten billion (*kharva*), a hundred billion (*nikharva*), a trillion (*bṛnda*), ten trillion (*mahāpadma*), a quadrillion (*śaṅkha*), ten quadrillion (*mahāśaṅkha*), a quintillion (*samudra*), or ten quintillion (*mahāsamudra*).
The middle half; a parārdha multiplied by ten hundred; a parārdha multiplied by a thousand parārdhas; a parārdha multiplied by a hundred thousand parārdhas;
a parārdha multiplied by a billion (arbuda) parārdhas; a parārdha multiplied by a vṛnda; a parārdha multiplied by a great ocean (mahāsamudra); and a thousand parārdhas.
Multiplied by a *parārdha* of lotuses, multiplied by a *parārdha* of *guṇitas*,
multiplied by a *parārdha* of great conchs (*mahāśaṅkha*),
multiplied by a *parārdha* struck by a hundred *parārdhas*, multiplied by a *parārdha*.

Its height is measured in *yojanas* equal to a multitude of lotuses multiplied by thirty times a *parārdha* squared, further multiplied by a *parārdha* multiplied by a *parārdha* of a lotus; and above that wind is a single-faced, four-armed [being] adorned with a lotus bud in the form of a circle of a thousand hoods.
In my heart, I worship the form of Ananta-Rudra, together with the Namaskāra-mudrā, seated upon the Ananta-throne.

Hāṃ, obeisance to the thorns of the lotus-stalk of the Śiva-throne. Obeisance to the constituent parts of the lotus-stalk of the Śiva-throne, which has emerged from the bulbous root (kanda) of the Earth.
O Lord of the Immortals, you who reside in the principles beginning with Water and ending with Kalā;
O Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Āṣāḍhi, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhūtala, Śuddhīśvara, Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Japyeśvara, Āmrātakeśvara, and Madhyameśvara!
Mahākāla, Kedāra, Bharava, Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhala, Kanakakhala, Vimaleśvara, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, Bhīmeśvara, Avimukta, Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi,
Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, Sthāṇu, and Chagalaṇḍa.
Dviraṇḍa, Mahākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālāñjana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, Sthaleśvara, Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yakṣa, Gandharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājāpatya,
Brāhma, Akṛtakṛta, Bhairava, Brahmavaiṣṇavakaumāra, Nāla, and Śrīkaṇṭha.

I worship the thorns that take the form of the seventy worlds, whose names are Vāmadeva, Bhīmogra, Bhava, Īśāna, Ekavīra, Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, Ekaśiva, Krodhacaṇḍa, Dyuti, Saṃvarta, Śūra, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikheda, and Hāṃ— to the threads.

Homage! I worship the lotus-stalk threads of the seat of Śiva, which consist of fifty meditations (bhāvanās) in the form of the five errors, the eight perfections, the nine contentments, and the twenty-eight powers.

Thus, immediately after the worship of the stalk consisting of infinite seats, one should worship the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) and the yoga-throne (yogāsana) situated around the stalk. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma.
In the southeast corner of the auspicious throne (śivāsana), there is the form of a foot in the shape of a lion.

I worship Dharma, who rises up through the qualities and principles beginning with water, faces the southeast, has his mouth wide open, has his neck turned, gazes like a lion toward the northwest corner, is surrounded by ten million lions, and is the color of camphor. Hāṃ, homage to Knowledge.
The form of the leg at the southwest corner of Śiva’s throne is lion-shaped;
it rises up to the level of the qualities beginning with water (rasa), faces the southwest, has its mouth wide open,
its neck turned back, and gazes toward the northeast like a lion, surrounded by ten million lions.
I worship the saffron-colored knowledge. Hāṃ, salutation to dispassion (vairāgya).

It has the form of a lion-leg at the northwestern corner of Śiva’s lion-throne; it is shaped like a lion, elevated as far as the qualities and principles beginning with water, facing the northwest, and with its mouth wide open.

I worship Vairāgya (Dispassion), who has turned his neck to gaze like a lion toward the southeast corner, who is surrounded by ten million lions, and who is golden-hued. Homage to Hāma for the sake of sovereignty.
[He is] the form of the foot located in the northeast corner of the Śiva-siṃhāsana.

I worship the Lion-form, facing the northeast, rising from the elements beginning with water up to the principles (tattvas), with mouth wide open, neck turned toward the east, gazing like a lion toward the southwest corner,
surrounded by ten million lions, cloud-colored, the embodiment of sovereignty; for the sake of the Dharma of joy.

Homage! I worship Adharma, who is the form of the eastern seat of Śiva’s lion-throne, white and black in color, human in shape, with his head to the south and his feet to the north, facing downward; homage to Avidyā. (p. 51) Of the lion-throne of Śiva...

I worship Ignorance (Ajñāna), who has the form of the right palm, is white and red in color, has the shape of a man, with his head toward the east and his feet toward the west, and is face-down; *Hāṃ*, obeisance to Avairāgyā (Non-detachment). [She] has the form of the western palm of Śiva’s lion-throne.

I worship the one who is red and yellow in color, in human form, with the head to the north and the right foot downward, representing non-detachment (*avairāgya*). Homage to Hāman for the sake of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). [I worship] that which has the form of the northern arm of Śiva’s lion-throne, being yellow and black in color.

I worship [the deity] in human form, with the head toward the west, the feet toward the east, facing downward, and devoid of sovereignty. Immediately thereafter, having worshipped the entire lion-throne with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-lion-throne," one should worship the yoga-seat (yogāsana).
His elemental forms— white, red, yellow, and black—
are the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas, which, as the feet beginning with the southeast (Āgneya), represent the Unmanifest (Avyakta), Necessity (Niyati), Portion (Kalā), and Time (Kāla);
and [his] crystal, black, emerald, and pomegranate-flower-colored [forms], which as the faces beginning with the east, represent the Unmanifest, Necessity, Portion, and Time.

And having worshipped [him] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, whose form is the fruit in the midst of the yoga of Śiva," one should worship Viṣṇu in the center— blue in color, three-eyed, and holding a conch, a discus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Then, [one worships him] as reddened by the quality of rajas...
"Homage to the lower cover, which has the form of Māyā and appears as if filled with the cotton of the quality of Tamas.
Having thus worshipped the lower cover, which has the form of a bed spread beneath the upper girdle of the yoga-seat, in the southwest corner; Hāṃ.

"Salutation to the one white with the wounds of living beings, whose upper covering is the form of pure illusion. Having thus worshipped the upper covering—which serves as the bedsheet above the girdle—in the southwest corner, [one should worship] the entire yogic seat with: "Hāṃ, salutation to the yogic seat of Śiva."

One should worship. According to the view that the Śivāsana consists of three seats—namely the Yogāsana and the Vimalāsana, without [the other two]—one should contemplate the Śivāsana itself as elevated up to the knot of Māyā;
then, after worshipping its foot-plinth, one should [worship] the two plinths situated in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya).

Having worshipped the four ages, beginning with Kṛtayuga, as the joining-pins (sandhānakīla), and having worshipped Śrī Mahāviṣṇu within them as the two side-panels (phalaka), one should worship the lower cover and the upper cover.

Then, having meditated upon the lotus bud in the form of the circle of the jewels on the hoods of Ananta as fully blossomed, one should worship its petals and filaments with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the petals of the lotus of Śiva’s throne.
The petals of the lotus of Śiva’s throne have the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras and are white in color.

I worship. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the filaments (*kesara*). At the base they are golden-colored, in the middle they are coral-colored, and their tips are adorned with pearl-like forms; I worship these filaments, which embody the four and six arts (*kalā*), or which take the form of the eight Rudras accompanied by the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā.

In the view that the filaments (*kesara*) represent the nature of the eight Rudras, each of the eight filaments is to be meditated upon as one individual Rudra. Alternatively, since the infinite lotus (*anantapaṅkaja*) possesses a thousand petals in the form of hoods, it likewise has a thousand filaments; all of these [are to be so visualized].

Having divided the number one hundred and twenty-five into eight parts, they are to be worshipped in the form of the eight Rudras beginning with Vāma. Alternatively, the eight filaments together with the pericarp are likewise to be worshipped. This method is [also applied] by way of the form of the eight Vidyeśvaras.

It should also be applied to the petals that are to be worshipped: *Hāṃ, obeisance to the pericarp*. I worship the pericarp of the lotus-seat of Śiva, which is Vimalā, whose form is power (*śakti*), and who is golden-colored. *Hāṃ, obeisance to the seed-syllables*. Or [one may worship] those whose forms are the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, or those whose forms are the fifty letters.

Or, I worship the seed-syllables of the lotus at the center of the seat of Śiva. Then, having visualized the lotus complete with all its parts, one should worship it with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Seat (Padmāsana)" and display the lotus-gesture (padmamudrā) with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Gesture. Thereafter—

One should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, one by one, on the eight filaments in the eight directions starting from the east in a clockwise direction: *Vāmāyai namaḥ*, *Jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*,
*Raudryai namaḥ*, *Kālyai namaḥ*, *Kalavikariṇyai namaḥ*, *Balavikariṇyai namaḥ*.

Salutation to Balapramathinī; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. I worship the powers beginning with Vāmā, who stand upon the filaments facing Śiva, their reddish faces holding chowries, one hand placed upon the seat of Śiva, and [the rest] directed toward Śiva. Salutation to Manonmanī.

I worship Manonmanī, who is crystal-colored, holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, seated upon the lotus pericarp of Śiva’s throne in the northeast direction— or situated in the center of the northeast direction. Then, [I worship] those [deities] together with their presiding lords.

One should worship the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire one above the other. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the solar maṇḍala. I worship the solar maṇḍala, which resembles ten million suns and pervades the tips of the petals of Śiva’s lotus seat. *Hāṃ*.

Homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Five-faced, four-armed, with three eyes in each face, possessing the luster of molten gold, and endowed with the *namas* mudrā; he is the cause of emanation (*sṛṣṭikāraṇa*), [the cause of emanation being the *ātmatattva*].
I worship Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc, who is the cause and whose form is the essence of the Self. Hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc.
It pervades the tips of the filaments of the lotus seat of Śiva and is as cool as ten million moons.
I worship the lunar maṇḍala. Hāṃ! Homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala.

[I worship] the lord of the lunar maṇḍala, who is dark as a cloud, whose four hands are endowed with the gestures of salutation to the conch and discus, and who is the cause of sustenance (*sthiti-kāraṇa*).
I worship Viṣṇu. Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala.
I worship the fire-maṇḍala pervading the tip of the pericarp of the Śiva-throne lotus.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala. [He is] ruby-colored.

I worship Rudra, the Lord of the Vahni-maṇḍala, who possesses four hands joined with the trident, fire, *namaḥ*, and *mudrā* gestures; who is the cause of dissolution (O Śiva, the cause of dissolution), the embodiment of the Śiva-tattva.
According to the view that the pure seat (*vimalāsana*) is distinct from the pericarp, [one worships] from the southeast to the northeast.

Having worshipped the three qualities (guṇatraya) from the south to the north, the three mandalas, and the three principles (tattvatraya) from the southwest to the northwest, one should worship this entire pure seat (vimalāsana) with the mantra: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the pure seat."

Immediately after that, in the center: *Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śakti-maṇḍala*. I worship the Śakti-maṇḍala, which is white in color, pervading the three maṇḍalas, and whose form is the power of the will (*icchā-śakti*). *Hāṃ, obeisance to Maheśvara, the lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala*, who is crystal-colored and has eight hands.

I worship Maheśvara, the lord of the circle of powers (śakti-maṇḍala), who holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus in his hands, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness. Then, having visualized the entire Śiva-throne, [one should offer salutation] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-throne."
One should worship the Śivāsana, which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

Within this succession of seats (*āsanaparaṃparā*), having first worshipped Ādhāraśakti upon the lotus-throne (*padmapīṭha*)— which stands in the place of the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*)— in the self-oriented worship (*ātmārthapūjā*), one then [worships] starting with Ananta.

One should worship [the deity] from the end of the *śakti*-maṇḍala up to the navel of the *liṅga*, layer upon layer upon the pedestal (*vedikā*) of the *liṅga*. Thus, if one is unable to perform the worship of each individual limb of the *śivāsana*, one should contemplate the *śivāsana* together with its limbs and sub-limbs, and [worship it] simply by saying: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the *śivāsana*."

One should worship. This is the method for worshipping the Śiva-seat (śivāsana) which contains multiple seats. Alternatively, one should visualize a lotus during the invocation (āvāhana), Ananta during the bathing (snāna), Vimala during the worship (arcana), Yogāsana during the food offering (naivedya), and a lion-throne (siṃhāsana) during other services such as the offering of garments and so forth. Or else, [one may simply use] the lion-throne.

One should assign *ananta* during the bath, *padma* for the garment, and *vimala* for the ornaments, scents, and flowers; one should assign *yoga* for the food offering (*naivedya*) and for other services. Having thus worshipped the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*), one should worship the form of Śiva from the navel of the *liṅga* with the mantra: "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva," which consists of the principle of Maheśvara.

Having worshipped the form— which resembles steady lightning, is staff-shaped, and has undivided limbs— one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with mantras such as "Obeisance to Īśāna on the head" and others,
arranging [the deities] from the head to the feet in the manner of a staff, beginning with Īśāna and so forth, whether with or without their Śaktis.
One should place the thirty-eight *kalās* in their respective locations. A *śūdra*, however, should place only the powers beginning with Śaśinī.

Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others. Having thus performed the placements for the sake of accomplishing the body of Sadāśiva, [one recites]: *Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the Body of Knowledge*.
Having thus worshipped Sadāśiva, whose body consists of knowledge (vidyādeha) and whose limbs are clearly distinguished, one should meditate upon His essential nature in detail.

From the element earth up to Śuddhavidyā, [the seat] is endowed with the bulb (kanda), stalk, and petals; it is joined with the pericarp and filaments, adorned with the solar disc and other features. With a form reaching as far as Īśvara, possessing the brilliance of a steady lightning flash, its parts undivided, it shines brilliantly upon the upper surface—from the element earth up to the principle of Īśvara.
Together with Mūrti, who had been previously mentioned, [he stayed] in that place which was distinguished by millions of various cloth tents rising to a height of many yojanas.
One should always worship Sadāśiva, who is seated upon a great lotus measuring ten million *yojanas* and is sitting in the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*).

Or rather, [it is adorned] with millions of peaks and corners, with rows of dancers and actors, with new dances, foods, and drinks, and with meditations (or sciences); it is measured by the golden [peaks], and by hundreds of millions of yojanas elevated by the multitude of aerial chariots of the sciences.

Seated upon the excellent lotus-throne in the Yogavīṭha, [the Lord] is surrounded by those beginning with Antakaṇḍa Tejormūrti, who are divided tenfold and sevenfold, and whose number is beyond calculation.

I take refuge in Sadāśiva, who is seated upon a lotus throne, whose height has reached ten times a *prayuta* plus a *parārdha* of *yojanas*, and whose expanded body occupies a space of a *parārdha* of *yojanas*.

The lotus increases tenfold successively from the bulb (kanda) to the stalk (nāla); its increase is by one, two, and three [units] up to twenty, and then it increases by way of a sequence ending at one hundred mouths and ten lakhs.
Then, at the node (granthi), it is ten million (koṭi), and from the lotus onwards, the count is by multiples of ten million. Thus is the external measurement.
Or he may be situated upon a great seat of yoga (mahāyogapīṭha), which possesses vastness through a multitude of yojanas that can be calculated.
Above that, it is celebrated as having the measure of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) in a form consisting of a flood of one hundred crore yojanas;
it shines above that with ten thousand crores, and increases further by a direction of one million crores.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with three eyes in each face;
in his right hands, he holds a trident, a vajra, a sword, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness.
And in the left hands, he holds a serpent-noose, a bell, fire, and a goad;
or alternatively, an excellent khaṭvāṅga, a trident, a spear, and a five-pronged dart.
He wears a necklace, armlets, and all ornaments, with eyes like blue lotuses and a rosary;
the upper face of this god is enchanting in its childhood state.
The eastern face of Maheśa is serene, facing upwards, stainless, and with the luster of crystal; it possesses the brilliance of molten gold.
The southern face of Śambhu was entirely still and serene, having attained fresh youth,
and possessed the luster of a mass of blue collyrium.
His three eyes were red and round, his brow was furrowed with a terrible frown,
his fangs were formidable, he was invincible, and his sprout-like lower lip was quivering.
The northern face of the Lord has hair blazing like the moon, possesses the splendor of mature youth,
and shines with the luster of fresh coral.
Adorned with a tilaka on his forehead, embellished by dark locks of hair,
alluring, three-eyed, and radiant with the ornament of the moon.
The western face, resembling Caṇḍa, was endowed with the playful creeper-like eyebrows of Pārvatī’s countenance and marked by the characteristics of royalty.
Having thus meditated upon the one adorned with a beautiful moon-crest, his eyes tranquil through meditation,
one should again meditate upon the Lord Sadāśiva.
His three eyes shine forth as the forms of will, knowledge, and action;
his crest is adorned with the digit of the moon of wisdom, and his circle of arms extends through the ten directions.
It has faces consisting of the five Brahmās, faces known as the five Sādākhya-sounds,
and is graced by thighs shaped like the venerable five-syllabled mantra.
And it has the form of the entire Tantra, consisting of the phonemes, Brahman, and the Kalās;
from the Nivṛtti-kalā it extends as far as the knees, and from the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā as far as the navel.
The forehead is perfected by the Vidyā-kalā up to the neck;
above that, it is fashioned by the kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
Thus, this body of Sadāśiva consists of the form of the five kalās.
Nivṛtti has four faces, the color of lightning, and holds a vajra;
Pratiṣṭhā has one face, the luster of the moon, and holds a lotus.
Vidyā is fire-colored with three faces, her hands radiant with power;
Śānti is black-colored with four faces, bearing a banner.
The noose-bearer has five faces, transcends tranquility, and possesses the luster of the moon;
all of them are resplendent with a lotus, a rosary, and the gesture of fearlessness.
They have four arms and three eyes, with full and elevated breasts;
because they contain the five paths within them, Sadāśiva is the essence of the six paths.
The path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme, the path of world, the path of principle, and the path of energy—
these are considered the six paths.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), consisting of two hundred and twenty-four worlds, should be contemplated as being of the nature of the multitude of hairs belonging to the All-pervasive Lord.
The conceptualization of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is performed by means of the fifty phonetic colors (varṇas), which possess the forms of the fifty Rudras;
this [path] should be contemplated as the skin-essence of the trident-bearing God of gods.
The path of mantra of the Lord of Pārvatī should be contemplated as being of the nature of blood;
the path of the feet of the Lord should be contemplated as consisting of veins and flesh.
The thirty-six principles beginning with earth have been taught by those who know the Āgamas;
by these, the path of principles (tattvādhvan) is constituted, bearing the forms of semen, marrow, and bone.
In his body there is no bone, no blood, and no flesh; nothing exists at all, like a reflection in a mirror or a rainbow in the sky.
This body of Sadāśiva is established as consisting of light;
nevertheless, even through its constituent parts (kalās), this [universe] is merely a mental construction of the paths (adhvans).
One should worship the head with the *Brahmasvīśa* mantra and the four-faced [face] with the *Puruṣa* mantra;
the heart and other [limbs] with the *Aghora*, and the private parts and others with the *Vāmadeva*.
One should meditate upon the feet and other limbs of the Lord of the Universe by means of the Sadyojāta [mantra];
all [these forms] are remembered as having five faces and being adorned with ten mighty arms.
They hold swords, scimitars, bows, arrows, water-pots, and rosaries;
their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they carry tridents and lotuses.
Among these, Aghora and Ghora are fierce, while the others have gentle forms;
having thus meditated upon the five-fold Brahman nature of the pervasive Lord together with His seat.
One should contemplate and fashion the limbs from the divisions of those portions of Brahman belonging to you;
the five portions of Īśāna have become the nature of the five heads.
O Lord of the World, those four [energies] of Puruṣa are to be meditated upon as his four faces;
all eight energies belong to Aghora.
The heart, throat, arms, navel, belly, back,
and chest are declared to be the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva, as proclaimed by Śiva.
The secret parts, thighs, knees, shanks, hips, waist, and sides are likewise considered [the locations];
these are proclaimed as the eight digits (kalās) of Sadyojāta.
The feet, hands, two nostrils, head, and arms are considered those [limbs];
the thirty-eight kalās are deities with three eyes and four faces.
Their lotus-like hands shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, along with axes and spears;
or else, they may bear the specific forms, colors, and weapons appropriate to each respective deity.
To the left of these [deities] are the Śaktis beginning with Śaśinī;
they should be meditated upon as having smiling faces and holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
One should meditate upon the Rudras, headed by Śrīkaṇṭha, who possess the forms of the phonemes and are accompanied by their Śaktis,
as the limbs of the Lord according to the method of ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should remember the Rudras together with their Śaktis, in the form of Ardhanārīśvara,
with their left and right sides resembling vermilion and gold respectively.
Adorned with the noose, goad, rosary, and the boon-granting mudrā,
their lotus-like faces are serene, and they bestow all that is desired by the world.

One should contemplate the lotus of the feet as the source of all desires, the pair of ankles as born of yoga, the form of the toes as the object of meditation, and the two extended hands as the causal principle.
The pair of knees of the Lord is invincible; his two thighs are radiant;
his subtle secret seed-syllable is the essence; and the region of his brow is a thousandfold.
The back is said to be Bhārgava, the sun; the navel is Śrīsuprabhedaka;
the belly is called Vijaya; and the heart is Niśvāsa.
The Svāyambhuva [Tantra] is the pair of breasts; the Anala [Tantra] is the three eyes;
the Vīrāgama is the region of the throat; and the Raurava [Tantra] is the two ears.
The *Makuṭa* and *Makuṭa-tantra* are his arms; the *Vimalāgama* is the chest of Śambhu;
the *Candrajñāna* is his lotus-face.
The tongue is the *prodgīta* of the Lord; the two cheeks are the *lalita*;
the forehead-plate is the *siddha*; and the two earrings are the *santāna*.
The sacred thread is declared by Śarva; the necklace and garland belong to Pārameśvara;
the *kiraṇa* is his jewel ornament; and the *vātula* constitutes his garment.
In this way, one should contemplate the form of the Lord as consisting of the Tantras,
which bestows the knowledge of Śiva upon men and promotes the dharma of Śiva.
One should know that the upper face of the All-pervasive Lord is the pure light called Śivasādākhya, which flashes forth in all directions like a mass of lightning in the sky.
Then one should meditate on the formless [state] known as Sādākhya, heard of as the "Root Pillar," which is the Liṅga consisting of a pillar of light; this is its northern face.
One should meditate upon the western [form], known as Mūrtisnāda, which arises from a single portion of the Jyotirliṅga, has one face, and three eyes.
He holds a trident, an axe, a thunderbolt, and the gesture of fearlessness with his right hands,
and a noose, fire, a bell, and the gesture of granting boons with his left hands.
One should meditate upon the southern face, which is radiant with four lotus-like mouths, situated within the center of the *liṅga*, and which maintains what is called the "agent of bestowal."
The five-faced, ten-armed pedestal, which has emerged from the *liṅga*, is well known as Kartṛsāda; it is the eastern face of Purāri.
One should meditate upon the five Brahmās— the faces of the Lord— as being located above, in the east, south, north, and west, beginning with Īśāna in due order.
The heart-mantra is white in the heart; the head-mantra is tawny in the head;
the tuft-mantra is red in the position of the tuft; and the armor-mantra is situated on both sides.
One should meditate on the eye as dark blue and the weapon in the hand as black;
they have four arms and three eyes, and are adorned with crowns of matted hair.
Holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a skull-cup and a trident.
The Aṅgadevas are remembered as having gentle eyes, yet possessing fierce forms;
they declare that the trident represents the three qualities (guṇas), while the axe is established in truth.
The sword is the prowess of Vajra, and the spear is the invincibility of Śambhu; the power of Agni is the capacity for destruction, and the power of the serpent is invulnerability.
Impurity, illusion, and the bond of karma are the nature of the sound of the bell;
they know the power that protects from fear to be the goad of self-restraint.
The trident is considered to consist of the powers (śakti) whose forms are will, knowledge, and action;
these very powers are said to be the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), which sets the pure principles (tattva) in motion.
She is called Bījapūrā because she sets in motion the seed of the universe;
she brings forth the principle of Māyā, which is endowed with the agitation of the hand-drum (ḍamaru).
The serpent Kākodara is the primary digit (kalā) that sets in motion the multitude of effects;
he is considered to be the power that impels the mind, appearing in the form of a blue lotus.
She is to be known as Akṣamālā, the activator of the senses;
she is Śakti, whose nature is the weapon Śakti, the destroyer of the wicked.
The *vara* [mudrā] bestows enjoyments, the *śakti* [mudrā] grants fearlessness, and the *abhaya* [mudrā] bestows liberation;
thus [the Lord] bears ten weapons and is as cool as ten million moons.
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, adorned with all ornaments,
and graced by a crown of matted hair six finger-breadths in length.
Upon its right extremity rests the crescent moon with its three-fingered digit as a crest;
upon its left extremity dwells the celestial river in the form of a serpent.
He wore the *tripuṇḍra*, the half-moon, the *bhūya* (the letter *bhū*), the yantra, the lamp, and the crescent moon in sequence;
he bore the sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*) on his face with the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Aja.
One should meditate on Unmanī, who possesses a divine form, on his left side—
resembling a hibiscus flower and adorned with white garments.
Adorned with all ornaments, possessing full and fleshy thighs, hips, and breasts, she holds a thousand lotuses, blue water-lilies, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Thus, meditating upon Sadāśiva, the manifest God, as united with Manonmanī even within the liṅga,
one should abandon the notion that it is a mere liṅga.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the three eyes with the mantra "Hauṃ,
to the eyes," one should then invoke Paraśiva eternally within the lotus of the heart.
Now, the sequence of invocation: "O immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and stainless one;
subtle, omnipresent, eternal, firm, immutable Lord—I, commanded by you, bow down to you with this mantra. Having thus made this request, with the body held straight and upright...

Having first restrained the mind and the eyes, filling the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] and performing *kuṃbhaka*, one should place a handful of flowers in the heart, firmly form the *āvāhana-mudrā*,
and [visualize] Paramaśiva, who consists of mantra and resides in the *mūlādhāra* within one's own body.

Having drawn up the light starting from the *mūlādhāra*, having passed beyond the letter *ha* situated there, and having led it as far as the heart, [one should contemplate] the twelve vowels beginning with *a*, together with the earth and other elements, the net of bonds, and the causal lords such as Brahmā, which reside in the locations of the heart, throat, palate, and so forth.

And having sequentially transcended those [levels] preceded by the contemplation of each respective one, while indeed pronouncing [the mantra] as far as the *dvādaśānta*, he should also lead the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) as far as the *dvādaśānta*, making it consist of the mantra.

Having united [the disciple] with the Supreme Śiva residing at the end of the twelve [fingers] (*dvādaśānta*), one should bring [the consciousness] from there— uninterruptedly in the form of a drop dripping with supreme nectar—
and contemplate it as resting within the pavilion of Śiva located between the eyebrows.
Visualizing [the deity] like a thousand autumn moons, holding one's joined palms at the center of the heart,

and having drawn up even the vital breath through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], one should contemplate the supreme Śiva-light brought into the midst of the handful of flowers, reciting: *Hāṃ Hauṃ Śivāya Namaḥ*.
One should join [it] to the *brahmarandhra* of Sadāśiva. To clarify the meaning already stated, the root mantra, its letter *ha*, and the twelve locations of its *kalās* are now demonstrated.

That which is the location in the middle of the body, the *mūlādhāra*, from there up to the *brahmarandhra*—extending for the measure of four *tāla*s—is situated within the body. Above that, for the measure of one *tāla*, is the location of the crest (*śikhā*). Therein:
The emergence of the Prāsāda mantra occurs within the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus situated at the *mūlādhāra*.
From there, extending as far as the navel, is the letter *ha*, subtle as a lotus fiber and brilliant like lightning.
Above the navel, extending for twelve finger-breadths, it is endowed with the letter *a* and possesses the luster of lightning.

The letter *ha*. From that, the heart-lotus is five or four finger-breadths in measure. Beginning from there up to the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), there are the locations for the twelve *kalās*. Among these, the vowel *au* has an extent of four finger-breadths, consists of three morae (*mātrā*s), and possesses the luster of a mass of extinguished embers. And it—

It is presided over by Brahmā, together with the twenty-four principles beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti), through the power of withdrawal (nivṛtti-kalā). Above that is the pervasion of a sixteen-petaled lotus, measuring eight finger-breadths, situated at the location of the throat.
The letter *nū* consists of two morae (*mātrās*) and possesses the luster of the sun and moon arising simultaneously;
it is presided over by Viṣṇu together with the six principles (*tattvas*), beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Kāla, along with the *Pratiṣṭhā-kalā*. Above that—

The letter *ma* is located at the root of the palate; it has the extent of a four-petaled lotus measuring four finger-breadths, consists of one *mātrā*, and is the color of lightning. It is presided over by Rudra, together with the *vidyā-kalā* and the principle of *māyā*. Above that—

Situated between the eyebrows, it has the measure of two finger-breadths, pervades a two-petaled lotus, is circular in shape like a dot (bindu), consists of half a mora, and is the color of lightning; it is presided over by Maheśvara, together with the Śānti-kalā and the two principles (tattvas) of Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara.

Above that, in the middle of the forehead, is the *ardhamātrā*, with its tip pointing upward, shaped like a half-moon, measuring one-quarter of a *mātrā*, and moon-white in color. Above that, on the forehead, is the *nirodhin*, with its tip pointing upward, triangular in shape, measuring one-eighth of a *mātrā*, and smoke-colored. Above that...

In the head is the *nāda*. It is shaped like a staff (*daṇḍa*), joined at both ends by two *bindus*, measuring sixteen parts, and the color of a ruby (*māṇikya*). Beyond that, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), is the *nādānta*;
it has the shape of a plow facing south and is joined with a *bindu* on its right side.

It is thirty-two finger-breadths in size and the color of lightning. Thus, from the location of the *bindu* up to the *brahmarandhra* situated eleven finger-breadths above the space between the eyebrows,
there are four [states]— the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructer (*nirodhinī*), the sound (*nāda*), and the end of sound (*nādānta*)— which abide in those respective locations.
Accompanied by the Śāntyatīta-kalā and the Sadāśiva-tattva, Sadāśiva himself is the presiding deity.
Above the Brahma-randhra, situated at a distance of one finger-breadth,
is Śakti, shaped like a plough with its head facing all directions and accompanied by a bindu on her left side.

The [Nirodhinī] measures exactly sixty-four parts. Above that, situated in the space of three finger-breadths, is the Vyāpinī, which has the form of a trident, is accompanied by a dot (bindu) on its right side, and measures one hundred and twenty-eight parts. Above that—

The space between the pair of curved lines situated within two equal dots four *aṅgulas* apart is equal to a beautiful line measuring exactly two hundred and fifty-sixth part [of that distance]. Above that,
it extends upward from the station of the *unmanī*-dot situated four *aṅgulas* high.
Consisting of lines in the form of staffs, it is composed of mind alone; here,

above the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), at the location of the crest extending upward in a sequence of one, three, and four finger-breadths up to twelve finger-breadths, [the lines are] placed one above the other.

The Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā are situated there, possessing the radiance of a hundred million suns and presided over by Anāhata-Śiva. When these four are combined, they are called the Supreme Space (Paramākāśa). Thus, the letter A is four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in extent, and the letter U is eight finger-breadths.

The letter *ma* measures four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The point (*bindu*) is two finger-breadths; the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructer (*nirodhin*), sound (*nāda*), and the end of sound (*nādānta*) together measure eleven finger-breadths. The power (*śakti*), the pervasive one (*vyāpinī*), the equalized one (*samana*), and the beyond-the-mind (*unmanā*) each extend for twelve finger-breadths. Thus, for all twelve [levels], the total is forty-one finger-breadths.

It is the locus of the pervasion of the *kalās*. Consequently, from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *dvādaśānta*, as the measures are released at their respective locations, there is the letter *ha* joined with *ma*, the letter *ha* joined with *au*, the letter *ma* joined with *ū*, the circular form (*vṛttākāra*), the *bindu* whose upper tip is half-circular in form, and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The *mūrdhva* is triangular in shape; the *nirodhinī* has the form of a staff situated between two dots;
and the *nādānta* has the form of a plow with its tip pointing upward and facing south, accompanied by a dot located on its right side.
The Śakti, shaped like a plow with its tip pointing upward and its left face accompanied by a dot situated on the left side;
the Vyāpinī, shaped like a trident with its tip pointing upward and accompanied by a dot situated on the right side;
and the Samanā, whose form is a straight line situated between two curved lines located in the space between the two dots.

Having instantly contemplated with the mind— above the *bindu* of the *samāna* [vital air]— the straight-lined form of the *unmanā*, which has its tip directed upward, together with the Lords of the Causes (*kāraṇeśvaras*) who are the essence of the *kalās* situated in the locations beginning with the heart, by means of the successive abandonment of each preceding stage; and above that...
Arising from the river of the supreme ether, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, cool as ten million moons, consisting of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*), resplendent with filaments,
enriched with the seed-syllables of the five letters at the pericarp of the *praṇava*, and filled with the honey of supreme bliss.

One should mentally plunge into the partless Supreme Śiva— the ocean of supreme bliss, whose form is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), who resides in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus frequented by liberated bees, and whose radiance is like that of many tens of millions of autumnal moons rising all at once. Thus...

Preceded by meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), having brought the Supreme Śiva [to the heart] with the root mantra, having caused him to reach the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva with the invocation mudrā (āvāhana-mudrā), and having established him therein with the stabilizing mudrā (sthāpana-mudrā).

Having turned the Lord toward oneself with the *sannidhāna-mudrā*, and having announced, "Welcome to you, O Mahādeva," one should mentally contemplate the Lord’s words, "Child, a very warm welcome," and after offering the guest-offering (*arghya*),
one should bind [Him] with the *sannirodhana-mudrā*, saying: "O Lord, Master of the Entire World!"
"Until the conclusion of the worship, remain present within this *liṅga* with a state of affection"— having thus prayed heartily with hands joined in *añjali*, and having contemplated Śiva’s consent,
one should offer the *nirodhārghya* (the water of confinement) with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [specifically] that of Kālakaṇṭhī.

Having dispelled the obstacles and protected Śiva with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should assign the heart, head, crest, and armor mantras to the deity’s heart and other locations using their respective mantras;
then, following the ritual of "making complete" (sakalīkaraṇa)— which consists of the assignment of the limbs such as the heart and the hands— one should offer a flower.

Having rendered [the deity] supreme by means of the root mantra, one should consecrate it as nectar using the *dhenumudrā*. Here, "invocation" (*āvāhana*) is the bringing forth of Śiva into the body of Sadāśiva; "establishment" (*sthāpana*) is the placing of Sadāśiva within the lotus of the heart;
"proximity" (*sannidhāpana*) is making [the deity] face toward oneself; and "immobilization" (*sannirodhana*) lasts until the completion of the worship.

Sannidhānaprārthanam (the prayer for presence) is the invocation for the deity to remain present. Avakuṇṭhanam (concealment) is the covering with the Kavaca-mantra for the sake of manifesting [the deity] among the devotees and to prevent the arrival of obstacles. Sakalīkaraṇam (the act of making complete) is the application of the five limbs, beginning with the heart. Paramīkaraṇam (the act of supreme transformation).

One should contemplate the identity of Śiva within the heart and other limbs, which possess white, yellow, red, black, and reddish colors. The "rendering nectar-like" (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is the realization of the body as non-different from Śiva. Now, [one might ask] regarding Śiva, who pervades the entire universe...
How is it that invocation (*āvāhana*), which consists in bringing [the deity] to the desired location, is spoken of?

Because Śiva possesses inconceivable, wondrous, and infinite powers, he has both pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) and non-pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*); thus, his bringing [himself] to another location is logically established. Or else—
Just as the all-pervading *jīva* possesses the limitation of being delimited by the body (*śarīrāvacchedopādhikatva*), so too for Śiva,
the attainment of another desired location is not contradictory, just as there is delimitation by mantras and *taijasa* [forms]. Or alternatively:

Just as fire pervading wood is manifested in a particular place through the act of friction, so too, invocation (*āvāhana*) is simply the manifestation of Śiva in the locus identified as the Śivaliṅga by means of an action consisting of the mental cultivation of bringing [Him] to that desired location. But is this not the case everywhere?

What is this that is called the manifestation of Paramaśiva, whose nature is the light of eternally arisen consciousness-bliss? It is like a mass of glowing embers, which, though self-luminous, remains covered by ashes.
Just as [the fire] is manifested by the act of blowing away the ashes,
so too, although Paramaśiva is self-luminous, he is [manifested] toward him through the mental activity of the worshiper's mind being directed toward him rather than toward other objects.

For one who is concealed, "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) is precisely the departure from the continuous flow of mental attention (*anusandhāna-santāna*)— which must be maintained until the dismissal (*visarjana*) at the desired location, such as the *liṅga*, preceded by the act of invocation (*āvāhana*) performed with undistracted mind— for the purpose of offering those various ritual services (*upacāra*). Alternatively:

According to the method described in the Śiva Purāṇa, *āvāhana* (invocation) is simply the contemplation of the manifestation of the divine form of Paraśiva— consisting of consciousness and bliss and accompanied by Umā— within the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva. That procedure is now demonstrated.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva in the *liṅga* with an unwavering inner self,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās* within one's own body, just as [one does for the deity].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having abandoned the notion that [the image] is merely a symbol (liṅga),
I shall meditate with compassion upon Śiva, the Supreme Cause, who possesses form within that form, as the abode of the vital breaths and the essence of all existence.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise other gods and asuras,
even today long for a vision of him through their fierce austerities.
Because all this— beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra,
together with the elements and the senses— is first brought forth by Him alone.
And he who is the creator of causes, the meditator, the supreme cause—
he is never produced from anything else at any time.
Complete with all sovereignty, he himself is by name Sarveśvara;
Śambhu, dwelling in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all those seeking liberation.
Dwelling above all, yet dwelling in all,
he is the eternal Lord of this entire world consisting of the sixfold path.
He is the highest among all successive beings, and he is unsurpassed;
he is an ocean of infinite majesty, whose sovereign power is unlimited.
He is the manifestation of pure intellect that is unfailing regarding all objects without exception;
he is intensely longing for the abundance of joy from tasting the nectar of his own power.
A bee for the nectar of the mass of infinite bliss,
he is skilled in condensing the entire multitude of cosmic eggs.
He is the abode of the makara-emblem of magnificence, vigor, profundity, and sweetness;
the incomparable king of kings and great lord of all beings.
I bow to You, whose body is non-material, who possess a form that intoxicates the mind,
and whose physical manifestation is the condensed essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss, formed through the observance of sacred discipline.
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautiful in every limb,
with red face, hands, and feet, and a countenance with a gentle smile like a kunda flower.
Resembling pure crystal, with three eyes like blooming lotuses,
four-armed, of noble form, and bearing the beautiful crescent moon.
One should meditate upon Hara, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who holds a deer and an axe,
and who is far removed from the entire range of comparisons.
Then he should meditate upon Maheśvarī on his left side,
her wide and long eyes resembling the petals of a full-blown blue lotus.
Her face has the luster of the full moon, her hair is dark blue and curled,
she resembles the petals of a blue lotus, and she wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She possessed breasts that were exceedingly round, firm, lofty, smooth, and full;
she had a slender waist and broad hips, and her very fine garment was displaced.
She was endowed with all ornaments, radiant with a tilaka of rubies,
and captivating with her mass of hair strewn with various flowers.
Her form was entirely graceful,
her face slightly downcast with modesty, and she held a blooming golden lotus in her right hand.
Placing her other hand like a staff, she sat upon the throne—
the Goddess who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
To Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Hara, Śrīśa, and Dhruhiṇa; to the Mother, the sovereign of the entire circle of powers (śakticakra) such as Gaurī and Lakṣmī.
Having thus meditated upon the god and the goddess as being sixteen years of age,
one should worship them in due order with a collection of offerings made with devotion.

Thus, in the view that the form of Sāmbaśiva manifests within the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva, his establishment within the lotus-heart of Sadāśiva constitutes the act of turning him toward oneself; in this way, everything is perfectly consistent.

However, the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) consisting of the realization of the non-difference between the body and the embodied soul is only possible in the context of the manifestation of the form of Sāmbaśiva; for it is only when the form of Sadāśiva has been invoked into one's own preferred *liṅga* or other support that its manifestation occurs for the sake of worship.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon the worshipper who makes this request, that very reality which is non-different from Śiva— being existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda)—
appears in the form of a conch, a pearl, and so forth, through the power and majesty of His inconceivable and wondrous creative energy (māyā-śakti), just as a drop of water appears in various forms.
The established tradition of the Śiva Purāṇa and other texts is that [the deity] is manifested in the form of the body of Sāmbaśiva, complete with all its limbs. Likewise, it is from this very form—
which is whitened by the radiance of the body of Paramaśiva, whose nature is consciousness and bliss— that [it proceeds].

Even though the body of Sadāśiva consists of thirty-eight kalās of various colors, the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of it as being crystal-colored is appropriate. However, the faces of Sadāśiva— namely Tatpuruṣa and the others— are yellow, blue, white, and red in color.
This is employed to imitate those respective colors in order to stabilize the yellow, blue, white, and red complexions of the lords of the directions— Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera—
which correspond to their respective functions. Such is the invocation of Paramaśiva in this form.
While this is being performed, one should contemplate that for the face of Sadāśiva which faces upward— that is, the Īśāna face—
the ritual dismissal (*avisarjana*) is like that of the Tatpuruṣa face, and its orientation should be conceived as facing east.
[One should perform] the consecrations beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
In the view that the form of Sadāśiva with Ambā (Sāṃbasadāśiva) is being manifested, the [ritual] should be performed precisely within the central form of Sadāśiva.

Therein alone, the offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth should be performed for both Paramaśiva and Ambikā individually, according to the sequence of the ritual procedure for each object.

In the case of the Sadāśiva-mūrti, when the procedure involves the invocation of the pure consciousness of Paramaśiva alone, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) and other services after that invocation. In the case of the Manonmanī-mūrti, having consecrated Ambikā through the invocation and other rites, one should worship her with the offerings of water for the feet and other services.
The manner of offering water for the feet and so forth.

Lifting with the left hand the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*)— each containing three blades of grass— one should contemplate the *pādya* as extending up to the principle of Īśvara, the *ācamana* up to the principle of Sadāśiva,
and the *arghya* up to the principle of Śiva; then [one offers] the *pādya* and so forth.

Having meditated upon the worshipper as one who attains the principles (tattvas) of Īśvara and Sadāśiva, one should visualize the mantra beginning with *Prāsāda* arising from the *mūlādhāra*, pronouncing it in the sequence of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, extending up to the space between the eyebrows, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the twelve-finger limit (*dvādaśānta*).
Uttering the mantra sequence "Hāṃ Hauṃ Śivāya" ending with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, or *svadhā*,
[he should touch] with his right hand— palm upturned, holding flowers— with the tips of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, following the order beginning with Sadyojāta.
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two feet in the order from left to right;
water for sipping (*ācamana*) at the faces in the order beginning with Tatpuruṣa; and the respectful offering (*arghya*) on the heads in the order beginning with Īśāna.
Then, having meditated upon the fragrant flower as consisting of knowledge and being the cause of union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*), [one should offer it].

Having visualized the mantra being uttered as far as Śiva, who resides above the *dvādaśānta*, one should offer it upon the head [of the deity] with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, following the sequence beginning with Īśāna. One should also give the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings to Ambikā at those very same moments, according to the method of offering each item individually (*padārthānusamaya*). Thus...

The same should be understood regarding the perfumes and other offerings. In this regard, the specific difference is that the mantras are "namaḥ śivāyai" and "svadhā śivāyai," and so forth. Then, having offered incense and a lamp ending with "svāhā" using the root mantra, as well as water for sipping (ācamana) and the arghya offering to Śiva and Śivā according to the previously mentioned method, one should also [use] the Astra-mantra.
Touching the lower part of the pedestal with his left hand while holding a flower with his right hand, he should remove the previously offered [flower], dismiss Tatpuruṣa,
and mentally visualize all [the rites] such as the anointing (abhyaṅga) and so forth in the manner previously described, [uttering] "Hāṃ."

Having bathed [the deity] with a drop of water for the *arghya* offering while reciting "Obeisance to the Śiva-tattva," and having offered the *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya* as before, one should offer two garments, two sacred threads (*upavīta*), and *ācamana* with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, [reciting]: "Hāṃ! To the Lord of the Ātma-tattva."
"Obeisance to Śiva. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva).

"Hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva). Having thus offered three handfuls of flowers to Śiva and one handful of flowers to the Goddess with the mantra "Obeisance to Śivā," [one should worship] with those [offerings] mentally conceived and visualized.

Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments such as golden garments, bracelets, crowns, earrings, armlets, and bracelets, using the root mantra ending with *namaḥ*, one should offer fragrances and flowers. Therein, the fragrance consists of camphor,
water, ghee, equal parts of *gorocanā*, saffron, sandalwood, cardamom, camphor, and black agallochum.
Or a powder of *dāru*, *kuṣṭha*, and musk; or a powder of sandalwood, *agaru*, camphor, saffron, *patraja*, and *uśīra* in equal parts;
or [the same] in equal parts, half that amount, or half of that again.
Or a powder of sandalwood, agallochum, kuṣṭha, and saffron mixed with camphor;
or a powder of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron in equal proportions;
or a powder of sandalwood, camphor, musk, and saffron in equal proportions. Of the fruit—
Or, according to the available measure of one *niṣka*,

there may be either powdered sandalwood mixed with camphor and other substances, or pure powdered sandalwood, or pure powdered pieces of *bilva* wood, or pure powdered pieces of *kṛtamāla* wood— all of these being suitable.

Fragrances are exceedingly dear to Śiva. Even the scent of pure devadāru wood rubbed with water alone brings about the attainment of the world of Śiva for as long as a kalpa. Even a single piece of bilva grants great sovereignty in this world and leads to the attainment of Śiva in the hereafter.

Even the scent of *kṛtamāla* alone, by bestowing long life, brings about the attainment of the status of the Lord of the Ganas in the hereafter. The scents of sandalwood (*candana*) of this kind are twice as effective in their results.
White agallochum (*śuklāguru*) is six times more potent than sandalwood; black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*) is twice as potent as that.

Therefore, saffron should be four times that amount. In this regard, there is a great distinction through the addition of camphor and other ingredients according to the previously described method. Having placed the well-prepared fragrance among such scents into a vessel possessing the characteristics mentioned for the *arghya* bowl, [one prepares] those fit for the anointing of the Deity.

While meditating on the limbs beginning with the forehead, one should offer perfume— whether sufficient for the pedestal and the *liṅga*, or sufficient for the *liṅga* alone, or as much as is available— with the heart-mantra. Then, [upon a surface] twenty finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in height...

In a vessel made of gold or other materials, or fashioned from leaves and such, measuring eight finger-breadths in height and width at its base, with two stalks extending from both sides each eight finger-breadths long, and provided with a lid that lacks stalks and base and is of half that dimension.

One should worship with excellent flowers that have been properly cleaned, freed from their stalks, and are free from defects such as being placed on the ground, fallen while still buds, crushed, smelled, touched by living beings, entwined by spiderwebs, or gathered in stale cloth; and these excellent flowers [should be worshipped] with the root mantra and the deer-gesture (*mṛgamudrā*). And the excellent [flowers are]:
Flowers such as the *droṇa*, *punnāga*, *mandāra*, *nandyāvarta*,
*śriyāvarta*, *karavīra*, *arka*, *vakula*, *kuravaka*, *lodhra*, *śatapatra*, *dhuttūra*, *palāśa*, *pāṭala*, *campaka*, *kṛtamāla*, and *karṇikāra*.
Munī, mātuluṅga, arjuna, priyaṅgu, devadāru, tamāla, agnigandha, maruvaka, aśoka, bhadrā, aparājitā,
kataka, kalhāra, red lotus, blue lotus, safflower, and saffron.
Giripuṣpa, kuśa, apāmārga, bhṛṅgarāja, pūga, sarala, kovidāra, kadamba, āmra, madhūka, jambū, hemā, akuli, guñjā, musalī, vejikā, jājī,
mallikā, paṭṭikā, and mālatī.

Lakṣmī, nirguṇḍī, viṣṇukrānti, kadalī, śāribā, devatālī, dvikaṇṭhī, granthiparṇī, and so forth—among these, white flowers are sāttvika and bestow liberation; reddish flowers are rājasa and bestow enjoyment; yellow flowers...

Those that are mixed [in color] bestow both [results], accomplish all undertakings, and increase sons and grandsons. Those that are black in color—excluding the blue lotus—are of the nature of *tamas* and should be avoided;
however, even those such as *atasī*, *kūraṇḍa*, and *viṣṇukrāntā*, when specifically prescribed, bestow nourishment (*puṣṭi*).

In that regard, collecting flowers of all colors constitutes the highest form of worship. Worship with black-colored flowers, excluding others, is middling. Worship with flowers of white, red, and other colors, or with flowers of a single color, is progressively lower. As for garlands:
Those fashioned from flowers of a single color for each [deity] are the best;
those fashioned from flowers of many colors are middling; and those fashioned from leaves and flowers are the lowest. [Examples include:
the *arka*, *karavīra* flower, *bilva* leaf, *gandhapatrikā*, *puṇḍarīka*, *śatapatra*, and *sahasrapatra*.
Baka, dhuttūra, droṇa, apāmārga, kuśa, śamī, kṛtamāla, śaṅkhapuṣpī, vyāghrī, sadābhadrā, kṛṣṇanirguṇḍī, bṛhatī, śvetārka, bṛhaddroṇa,
and nīlotpala yield fruits that are ten thousand times more efficacious in each successive order. Among these, the arka flower [is preeminent].
The gift of ten gold pieces is equal [in merit]. A blue lotus is equal to the worship of a thousand golden flowers.
Tulasī, Kṛṣṇatulasī, Indravallī, Viṣṇukrāntī, Śyāmā, Priyaṅgu, Nṛpapuṇḍra, and other such flowers are equal to the Arka flower.

The flowers of the *nandyāvarta*, *vijaya*, *śatapatra*, *mandāra*, *cūta*, *madhuka*, white *girikarṇī*, *mālatī*, *kadalī*, and *śāribā* are equal to the *karavīra*. The *lakṣmī*, *sahadevī*, *nāgadantī*, *campaka*, and others are equal to the *bilva* leaf. The *pāṭala*, *vakula*, and others are equal to the *padma*.

The flowers of the *jātimallikā*, *madhūra*, *śaṅkhanāga*, *sūryāvarta*, *siṃhakesara*, *mahābhadra*, and so forth, are equal to *apāmārga*. The flowers of the *japā*, *kadamba*, *punnāga*, and others are equal to a *droṇa*. The flowers of the *aśoka* and white *mandāra*, as well as barley and wheat, [are likewise measured].
Wild rice, śāli rice, bamboo shoots, *tilaka*, mung beans, *niṣpāva* beans, fragrant grass, and sprouts of *māṣa* beans,
grown for seven days and resembling the flowers of the *kṛtamāla*;
as well as diamonds, rubies, emeralds, pearls, sapphires, and great sapphires.

The sun-stone (sūryakānta), the moon-stone (indukānta), flowers, and flowers of a thousand gold pieces are equal to the karavīra and the blue lotus (nīlotpala). That the blue lotus is the most excellent of all is established in all the scriptures (āgama).
In one scripture the karavīra is [stated to be] the most excellent, in another the vaka flower, and in yet another the mountain-flower (giripuṣpa).

Thus it has been said. Some maintain that the lotus (*padma*) is the most excellent of all. The excellence of specific flowers depends on specific times; for example, *kadamba*, *campaka*, *kalhāra*, *punnāga*, *kuśa*, and *bṛhatī* flowers, when offered in worship to Śiva during the spring season, bestow the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

In summer, *pāṭalī*, jasmine, and *śatapatra* flowers are equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. In the rainy season, lotuses and jasmine flowers are similar to the Aśvamedha. In autumn, *dhuttūra*, white water-lilies, *sujāta*, and blue lotuses bestow the fruit of the Sattra sacrifice. In winter, the *karavīra*.

Well-grown blue lotuses are equal to the hundred sacrifices (*śatakratu*). In the winter, the *karṇikāra* flower bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. Likewise, during the twelve months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, [one should offer] *arka*, *bilva*, *apāmārga*, *droṇa*, blue lotus, lotus, *kṛtamāla*, *bṛhatī*, *vyāghra*, and *śamī*.
The flowers of the *campaka* and *pāṭalī* are most highly praised. Likewise [are those of] the *nandyāvarta*,
*śriyāvarta*, white *arka*, white lotus, *palāśa*, *punnāga*, *mālatī*, *paṭṭikā*, red *agastya*, *vakula*, *lakṣmī*, *dvikaṇṭhī*, *vejikā*, *pāṭala*, and *aśoka*.
Kadali, śaṅkhinī, and flowers are most highly recommended for worship during the morning time. (p.
72) Flowers of the droṇa, karavīra, kṛtamāla, dhuttūra, vyāghrī, bṛhatī, pāṭala, kamala, utpala, campaka, and kuraṇḍa are for worship at midday.

Campaka, dhuttūra, mālatī, mallikā, vejikā, balakarṇi, sahabhadra, bhadrāmasa, atasī, śamī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and fragrant leaves are for the evening worship. Jātī, nīlotpala, kanaka, kadamba, and sthalakamala—

For worship at midnight, one should offer *ketaka*, *pūga*, *punnāga*, *danti*, *hrībera*, and *bilva* leaves. *Kadamba*, *kanaka*, and *jātī* flowers are to be offered only at night. Likewise, *mādhavī*, *ānanda*, *yūthikā*, *madayantikā*, *śirīṣa*, *sarja*, and *bandhūka*.

The flowers of the *kumuda*, *ḍāḍima*, *lāṅgalī*, *śrīparṇī*, *kārpāsa*, *nimba*, *kūśmāṇḍa*, *śalmalī*, *śinditavoṭa*, *girivaṭa*, *matsyākṣi*, *kapittha*, and *tiṃtṛṇī* are to be avoided. The prohibition regarding *ketakī* refers to times other than midnight. The prohibition regarding *kadamba*—
The prohibition regarding the day refers to the *girikarṇikā* flower; the prohibition regarding the *nīlagirikarṇikā* refers to the *girikarṇikā*;

and the prohibition regarding the *kiṃśuka* refers to the thorny *kiṃśuka*. In this same manner, for flowers such as the *japā* and *vakula*, which are prescribed in some places but prohibited in other scriptures, [the distinction] follows the difference in results.

The arrangement should be understood either according to the different types of worship, or according to the specific varieties of worship obtained through the respective traditions (*āgama*) of various cities, or according to the different forms (*mūrti*) to be worshipped. Even flowers that are otherwise prohibited may be accepted for the decoration of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) and similar purposes. Among leaves, those of the *bilva* and *tulasī* are [recommended].
Black *tulasī*, *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, *apāmārga*, *karavīra*, *nandyāvarta*, *śamī*, *sahā*,

*dhātakī*, *viṣṇukrānti*, *bhadrā*, *mahābhadrā*, jasmine (*jātī*), *jambū*, *badara*, *udumbara*, mango (*cūta*), the two types of *palāśa*, the two types of *munidvaya*, *ṭaṅkola*, *koraṇḍa*, the two types of *girikarṇī*, and *rudravarṇī*.
The leaves of bhūpatra, hrīvera, madana, maruvaka, droṇa, sinduvāra, śaṅkhinī, gokṣura, vakula, kṛtamāla, and others are recommended. Among flowers, the blue lotus is excellent;
among leaves, the bilva leaf is most excellent; and the two types of tulasī are even more excellent. As for those [plants] whose flowers...
Their leaves are also highly praised; namely, the lotus, blue water-lily,
*kuṭaja*, *campaka*, jasmine, oleander, *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *bilva*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
*pāṭalī* flowers, the five *bilva* fruits, the two types of *tulasī*, *dūrvā*, *agastya*, and leaves having the shape of fragrant foliage.
On leaves of the *śiva* flower, whatever form of leaf or flower is desired may be fashioned;
however, a golden flower and leaf are highly recommended.
With one hundred and eight golden flowers filling the hollowed palms (*añjali*), the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Śiva of the Vidyā-body is performed.
Worship performed daily with eighty-one, fifty, or twenty-five golden flowers yields incalculable fruit;
if one is unable to procure golden flowers, it may be done with pieces of gold.

Or it should be worshipped with silver flowers. There is no fault of being "worn" (nirmālya) regarding a golden flower. After one year, that becomes worn; even after a year, having purified it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), it may be worshipped again. The same applies to blue lotuses, palāśa, vakula, and karavīra.

There is no such thing as "worn-out" (nirmālya) status for mountain flowers, bilva leaves, or tulasī. Flowers and leaves originating from one's own garden are the most excellent. Those grown in the wild, those produced in another's garden, and those requested at the time of worship are progressively inferior.

However, those flowers originating from a temple garden must certainly be avoided. In the absence of flowers, one should worship with the leaves of whatever flowers are suitable for Śiva. In the absence of leaves as well, one should worship with their fruits. Among fruits, [the preferred ones are] citron, lime, and plantain.

Pomegranates and other such fruits are highly recommended for worship. Even in the absence of fruits, one should perform worship with sesame seeds, rice, and white mustard. Worship of Śiva with black sesame seeds destroys all sins.
Having thus worshipped with flowers and other offerings using the root mantra, [one should recite]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva; Hāṃ..."

Haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva. Hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva. Hoṃ, salutation to the head of Īśāna. Heṃ, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Huṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora. Hiṃ, salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva. Haṃ.

"Salutation to the form of Sadyojāta. Having thus worshipped the form of the seat with the five root-mantras of the Brahmas and the eight-fold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should worship with the limbs (*aṅga*) beginning with "Hāṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth. Thereafter, one should worship by means of the thousand names or the hundred names.
In the absence of that opportunity, [one should offer salutations]: "Obeisance to Śarva, whose form is earth; obeisance to Bhava, whose form is water;
obeisance to Rudra, whose form is fire; obeisance to Ugra, whose form is air;
obeisance to Bhīma, whose form is space; obeisance to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer."
Salutation to Īśāna, whose form is the Sun; salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is the Moon; salutation to Śiva; salutation to Maheśvara; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Viṣṇu;
salutation to Pitāmaha; salutation to the Physician of Saṃsāra; salutation to the Omniscient One.

"Salutation to the Supreme Self"—thus one may worship with these eight names. Or one may worship with these three names: "Salutation to Prabhava," "Salutation to Śambhava," and "Salutation to Umāpati.
Or, having worshipped with the single name "Salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha," [one should proceed] as far as possible.

One should adorn [the deity] with flower garlands. These garlands, fashioned from gold flowers numbering in the hundreds and so forth, or from blue lotuses numbering in the thousands and so forth, as well as those made of *karavīra*, white lotus, *vijayā*, white *pāṭala*, *punnāga*, white *mandāra*, *nāgakesara*, and *campaka* flowers, are highly praised. And these...

Garlands composed of various flowers should be richly fashioned and tied on both sides of the support of Umā. Upon the crown of the Liṅga, one should offer a hanging garland known as an *iṇḍa*, made of gems, gold, or flowers, consisting of one, two, three, or four tiers. Thus...
Following the offering of flowers, comes the offering of incense and lamps.
Its form is as follows: it is fashioned from any one of gold, silver, copper, or brass;
it is four finger-breadths in length and half that measure in height; it has a rim eight finger-breadths wide;
on its rear side, it is marked with a lotus petal and has a neck two finger-breadths in circumference and two finger-breadths high.

The incense burner (dhūpapātra) has feet shaped like well-formed hooves, measuring two finger-breadths in circumference and endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics; it is provided with a mouth-tube and fitted with a lid shaped like a lotus bud, which may have either many perforations or a single perforation.

Having filled [the vessel] with stainless charcoal fire, having placed incense materials therein, having covered the incense vessel, having consecrated it with the rites of inspection and so forth, having worshipped it with scents and flowers,
and having displayed the incense mudrā, one should take the incense vessel with the right hand while holding [the other hand] in the left.
One made of pure bell-metal, with a height of four, five, or six *aṅgulas*, a length of the same measure,
a tongue of that same measure, a circumference three times that [height], and provided with a rim of half an *aṅgula* and a lip of one or two *aṅgulas*.

While ringing a bell— whose top is two and a half finger-breadths high, its neck half a finger-breadth, its circumference three finger-breadths, its handle four, five, six, or seven finger-breadths long, and which is marked above with any one of the symbols such as a trident, lotus, bull, conch, or wheel— he should hold it near the nose of the deity.

Having presented incense with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya dhūpaṃ svāhā*, and having lifted the incense vessel above that, while whirling it, one should visualize the resonance (*nāda*)— shaped like a staff with two dots on its sides— within the crown, and the dot within the orb of the face.
One should visualize the syllable *ha* on the two arms, the syllable *rau* on the two feet, and the syllable *ū* by means of the circling of the incense burner.
Incense substances— camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, *takkola*, nutmeg, cloves, *śilhaka*,

and the powder of *māṃsī* and *mustā* leaves, known as *yakṣakardama*. Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon bark, leaves, flowers, *śilhaka*, and the powder of *jaṭāmāṃsī* is named *prājāpatya*.
The powder known as *vijayā* consists of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, clove, cinnamon,
*śilhaka*, sugar, and *mustā*. The powder [known as *sarvasaugandhika*] consists of camphor,
black agallochum, *hrībera*, saffron, *kunduru*, *turuṣka*, *visa*, and sandalwood.

Mixed with honey in successive proportions of one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven parts, it is named *Śītāṃśu*. The powder of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *silhaka*, resin of the *sarja* tree, costus, and musta-grass is named *Kalyāṇa*. [The mixture of] sandalwood, agallochum, and musk...

Mustāsilhaka powder is known as Amṛta; the powder of takkola, pūga, karpūra, jātīphala, and lavaṅga is known as Sugandha. Such are the incense substances well-known by their individual names. Likewise, sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and kuṣṭha...
Guggulu powder mixed with ghee and honey; sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and kuṣṭha powder mixed with sugar, ghee, and honey; camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood resin powder;
and saffron with one, two, four, six, or seven parts of agallochum resin and sandalwood powder.

In successive order, [one should take] powder of agaru, candana, and uśīra mixed with a little camphor and honey; powder of kuṣṭha and candana mixed with honey; and powder of gulma and bilva leaves mixed with ghee—each increasing by one, two, three, and four times [the previous amount] respectively.
Guggulu powder mixed with clarified butter, or Guggulu alone,
as well as the powder of any one of the following— gum-resin (niryāsa), sandalwood, agallochum, or saugandhika—
is a substance for incense. Among these, incense made of pure Guggulu removes the sins committed during seven lifetimes.
Sandalwood incense removes all sins;
fragrant incense accomplishes all purposes and goals;
black agalloch incense removes all sins; white agalloch incense bestows liberation.

Incense made of lac and musk bestows birth as a virtuous Brahmin who studies the four Vedas. Guggulu incense mixed with ghee, when offered for half a month, secures the status of a sovereign and the enjoyment of the city of Śiva for a duration of ten million times a thousand kalpas.

Incense made from mahiṣākṣa and guggulu, combined with the powder of the palmyra tree, yields a two-thousandfold fruit and bestows union with Śiva. For the five faces beginning with Īśāna, incense of śītāri, black agallochum, white agallochum, saugandhika, and guggulu are recommended in their respective order.
Thus, following the offering of incense, comes the offering of the lamp:

its vessel is three finger-breadths in measure, shaped like an elephant's trunk, and provided with a stand as described for the incense vessel. The wick may be made of camphor, a piece of cloth, or strands of thread.
It should be made of cotton, four finger-breadths in length,

with a circumference corresponding to its flame of four, three, two, or one finger-breadth; if it is made of cloth fragments and the like, it should be done according to the sequence of "excellent" and so forth, provided that the materials are available.

It should be prepared containing the powders of camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, and so forth; and among these, the ghee of a tawny cow is the best. The ghee of other cows is middling. Goat’s ghee and sesame oil are inferior.
Ghee from camels, buffaloes, and the like, as well as that derived from tree seeds and such, must be avoided. Or else:

Cow-ghee alone is the best; goat-ghee and buffalo-ghee are middling; oils with a foul odor, such as those from *nimbaka*, *raja*, *eraṇḍa*, and so forth, are to be avoided; and any oil at all is inferior. Thus, one should offer a lamp lit upon a wick prepared in a vessel according to the aforementioned characteristics.
Having consecrated [the deity] with gazing and other rites, having worshipped with flowers, having displayed the lamp-mudrā,

and having raised the lamp while ringing the bell, one should display it before the eyes with the mantra "Hāṃ Hauṃ, Svāhā to Śiva, the lamp," and then, as with the incense vessel, [proceed] from the crown down to the feet.
One should rotate the lamp alone through the meditation on the arrangement of its colors.
Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the respectful offering (arghya) to Śiva, and having meditated upon the God as being satisfied, one should request:
"O Blessed One, grant me permission; I shall worship the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅgas)."
One should perform the worship of the enclosure. Now follows the worship of the enclosure.
The first enclosure consists of the five Brahmās and the six limbs; the second, of the Vidyeśvaras;

the third, of the Gaṇeśvaras; the fourth, of the Lokapālas; and the fifth, of their weapons. Having worshipped Śiva in the pericarp of the lotus that serves as the seat of Śiva, these five enclosures [are to be worshipped].

One should worship at the bases of its petals, in the middle of the petals, in the spaces between the middle and tips of the petals, at the tips of the petals, and in the portions below them. Alternatively, one may worship at the base of the *liṅga*— which corresponds to the bases of the petals of the lotus seat of Śiva— and at the upper front portion of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), which corresponds to the tips of those petals.
One should worship on the neck of the pedestal, on the feet of the pedestal, on the lotus-pedestal situated at the place of the *brahmaśilā*, and [on the head] of Īśāna:

"Oṃ Homa Īśānamūrdhne namaḥ. I worship Īśāna, who is crystal-colored, whose hands hold a trident and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and who is accompanied by Umā. "Heṃ Tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ."

I worship Tatpuruṣa, who is golden-colored, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread, holding a citron and a rosary, and accompanied by Gaurī. *Huṃ*, obeisance to Aghora, whose heart is [the source].
[I worship] him who is cloud-colored, with tawny beard and hair, and a face formidable with fangs.
Adorned with ornaments of snakes, scorpions, and garlands of skulls, his four left hands hold a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose,
while his four right hands hold a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff.
I worship Aghora together with Gaṅgā. Hiṃ! Homage to the secret Vāmadeva.
I worship Vāmadeva, who is ruddy, wearing ruddy garments, garlands, and a sacred thread, holding a sword and a shield, and accompanied by Gaṇa and Ambikā. Haṃ.
