Homage to the form of Sadyojāta! I worship Sadyojāta, who is white in color, wearing white garlands, perfumes, ornaments, a turban, and garments, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, accompanied by Ambikā. Thus.

In due order, in the directions starting from Īśāna, Indra, Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, and so forth, at the time of their respective worship, one should draw [the deities] from their respective locations— consisting of the upper face, heart, secret place, and feet— by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.

Having meditated upon them as non-different from one another, following the manner of lamps ignited from an original lamp, one should worship them. Alternatively, all five [faces], beginning with Īśāna, should be visualized as having four hands holding a trident, an axe, the gesture of fearlessness, and a beautiful object. In this way, their meditations as established in other scriptures should also be observed. Hāṃ.

Hṛdayāya namaḥ | Hiṃ śirase namaḥ | Huṃ śikhāyai namaḥ | Haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ | Hauṃ netratrayāya namaḥ | Haḥ astrāya namaḥ | Thus, [one should visualize them] seated upon lotus postures, with colors like the moon, gold, vermilion, a bumblebee, lightning, and fire.

[He visualizes] the deities of the heart, head, crest, and armor, who wear crowns of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon and the Nandī elephant; who have four faces, each with three eyes; who hold a skull-bowl, a trident, and grant boons and fearlessness with their hands; and who are accompanied by Vāminī, Nīlinī, Cakriṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Khaḍginī, Gaṅginī, and Śakti.

Thinking "I worship," one should draw [the deities] from their respective locations— the heart, head, crest, and so forth— using the *akuśa-mudrā*, and place them upon the petals situated in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners, as well as the four petals starting from the east, and the *astra* (weapon) at the tips.

One should perform worship. On the petal of Īśāna, one should worship Brahmā, Sva (Vāyu), and Īśāna on the limbs, the eyes, and the head respectively, situated in progressively northern directions. Alternatively, one should worship Īśāna and the Eye in front of the deity upon the pericarp. Or, one may worship the Eye like the Weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions.

Now, the second enclosure: Homage to Ananta together with Bhūmi; homage to Sūkṣma together with Svāhā; homage to Śivottama together with Svadhā; homage to Ekanetra together with Kṣānti; homage to Ekarudra together with Puṣṭi; [homage] to Trimūrti...

Salutations to Śrīsahita; salutations to Śrīkaṇṭha accompanied by Kīrti; salutations to Śikhaṇḍin accompanied by Medhā. Thus, [one should meditate on] those who possess the colors of gold, fire, cloud, and bee, as well as snow, coral, and crystal; who bear the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the *jñāna-mudrā*, rudrākṣa beads, and rosaries; and who are three-eyed.

One should worship the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), who have descended with the knowledge of Śiva and are accompanied by their respective powers, in the various directions starting from the east and ending in the northeast, or in the sequence beginning from the east and ending in the northeast corner, thinking: "I worship [them]. (p.
78) Homage to Nandikeśvara, who is accompanied by Kuṇḍalī and is of a ruddy color.
I worship Nandin, who holds a trident, a rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is accompanied by Kuṇḍalī.
Homage to Mahākāla together with Padminī. [I worship him] who is yellowish-black in color, with tawny beard and hair, and who bears a trident, a skull-cup, a sword, and a shield.

I worship Mahākāla together with Padminī. Homage to Bhṛṅgin together with Hrādinī. I worship Bhṛṅgin together with Hrādinī—he who is white in color, whose body is fleshless, who bears a staff and a rosary, who has a topknot, and who is intent upon gazing at Śiva. [I worship] Bhṛṅginī.

Salutation to Gaṇapati accompanied by Bhadrā. I worship Gaṇapati, who holds a jewel, a noose, a goad, a tusk, and a ripe mango fruit, and is accompanied by Bhṛṅgiṇī. Salutation to Vṛṣabha accompanied by Bhadrā. [I worship him] who is crystal-colored and whose nature is Dharma.
I worship the bull, who is intent on meditating upon Śiva and accompanied by Bhadrā.

Homage to Skanda, together with Devayānī. I worship Skanda, who is golden-hued, dressed as a youth, holding a spear, a cock, an elephant-goad, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, and accompanied by Devayānī.

Salutation to Ambikā. I worship Umā, who is dark-complexioned, mounted upon a lion, and holds a trident and a mirror in her two hands. Salutation to Caṇḍeśvara together with Rūpiṇī. [I worship him] who is of a yellowish-white complexion and possesses four faces.

"I worship Caṇḍeśvara, who holds a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), a trident (*śūla*), and an axe (*paraśu*), who wears a serpent as a bracelet and a sacred thread (*upavīta*), and who is accompanied by Rupiṇī. Thus one should worship [the deities] starting from the east and ending at the northeast corner. Alternatively: Vṛṣa, Nandin, Gaṇeśa...

One should worship Mahākāla, Skanda, Bhṛṅgin, Gaurī, Caṇḍa, Nandin, Gaṇapati, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vṛṣa, Skanda, Gaurī, and Caṇḍa in order starting from the east; or alternatively, Gaurī, Caṇḍeśvara, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣa, Bhṛṅgin, and Skanda.

Gaurī, Caṇḍeśvara, Mahākāla, Vṛṣabha, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Vāyu are to be worshipped in order starting from the north. Umā, Vṛṣabha, Gaṇapati, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Caṇḍa, Skanda, Kubera, Śakra, Yama, Varuṇa, Nir-ri... [the remaining deities].

Alternatively, they may be worshipped in the directions starting from the northeast, the northwest, the north, and the east; the specific variations in their meditative visualizations (dhyāna) should be understood as those well-known from their respective Āgamas.
Having thus worshipped the third enclosure with the lords of the Gaṇas,
one should worship the fourth enclosure with the world-protectors (lokapālas). [One should offer] salutation to Indra together with Śacī—
[him who is] golden-colored, mounted upon Airāvata, and whose hands hold the thunderbolt, the goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I worship Indra together with Śacī. Homage to Agni together with Svāhā.

I worship Agni, who is red in color, mounted upon a ram, and endowed with the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), the spear (*śakti*), and the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*), together with Svāhā. To Yama...

Salutations to him who is accompanied by Kālakaṇṭhī. I worship Yama, who is black in color, holding a staff, a noose, and granting boons and fearlessness, mounted upon a buffalo, and accompanied by Kālakaṇṭhī. Salutations to Nairṛta, who is accompanied by Dāhinī; he is red in color.

I worship Nairṛta, who holds a sword, a shield, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, mounted upon a spirit (bhūta), together with his consort Dāhinī. Homage to Varuṇa, together with Bhoginī. [I worship] Varuṇa, moon-colored, holding a noose, a lotus, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, mounted upon a crocodile, together with Bhoginī.

I worship. To Vāyu, together with Ghorā, obeisance! I worship Vāyu, smoke-colored, holding a banner, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, mounted upon a deer, together with Ghorā. To Kubera, together with Gaṃbhīriṇī, obeisance! [I worship him] gold-colored...

I worship Kubera, who has a dwarf-like body, is mounted upon a human, is accompanied by Gaṃbhīrīṇī, and holds a mace, a treasure-vessel, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Homage to Īśāna, who is accompanied by Harṣiṇī; he is moon-colored, three-eyed, and holds a trident, a noose, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship with the thought, "I worship Īśāna, mounted upon a bull and accompanied by Harṣiṇī," following the sequence starting from the east.

[Then one worships] Brahmā, together with Sāvitrī, with the mantra: *namaḥ* to Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī. [He is] golden-colored, four-faced, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), a sacrificial ladle (*sruc*), and a staff (*daṇḍa*), mounted upon a swan (*haṃsa*), and accompanied by Sāvitrī.

I worship Brahmā. Homage to Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī. I worship Viṣṇu, who is lightning-colored, adorned with a thousand hoods, possessing infinite forms, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, mounted upon the tortoise, and accompanied by Lakṣmī.
One should worship Vidhātṛ and Vaikuṇṭha between Indra and Īśāna, and between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
or alternatively, one may worship them on the northern side of Yama and the southern side of Kubera.

Now, the fifth enclosure with the weapons of the World-Protectors: *Namaḥ* to the Vajra together with the Blissful Self-Power (*prasannātmaśakti*). I worship the Vajra, which possesses various colors, has a firm and hard form, a vajra-head, and is blazing, together with the Blissful Self-Power.

Salutation to Śakti. I worship Śakti, who is of a ruddy complexion, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who bears a spear upon her head, and who has the form of a woman. Salutation to Daṇḍa, who is accompanied by the Power of Wrath (Kopātmaśakti), who is black in color, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose eyes are red.
I worship the staff-headed [deity], who is accompanied by the power of anger.

Homage to the sword, which is accompanied by the power of the qualities (*guṇa*). [He is] dark-colored, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possessing half an eye, and having his head adorned with a sword.

I worship the sword accompanied by the power of the Guṇātman. Homage to the noose accompanied by the power of the Komalātman. It has the color of a Kiṃśuka flower; it is shaped like a serpent from the navel downwards, and from there upwards it has the form of a man with a head endowed with seven hoods.

I worship the noose (pāśa) together with its gentle power (ātma-śakti). Homage to the banner (dhvaja) together with its poisonous power (viṣātma-śakti). I worship the banner, which is yellow in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with mouth wide open, adorned with a banner upon its head, and accompanied by its poisonous power.

Salutation to the Mace (Gadā). I worship the Mace, which is yellow in color, in the form of a woman, with a mace upon its head. Salutation to the Trident (Śūla) accompanied by the power Vikṛtātman. [I worship] the Trident, which is dark in color, marked on its top with a trident, joined with palms in *añjali*, and accompanied by the power Vikṛtātman.

I worship. Homage to the lotus accompanied by the power of the Great Self (mahātma-śakti). I worship the lotus, which is white in color and has its top marked with a lotus bud, accompanied by the power of the Great Self.
Homage to the discus accompanied by the power of the Auspicious Self (maṅgala-ātma-śakti). [It is] dark blue in color.
I worship the Discus (Cakra), whose head is marked with a hundred spokes and which is accompanied by its own power, Maṅgalātmā-Śakti.
These deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇadevas) should be meditated upon as seated on their respective thrones, facing Śiva and gazing at Ambikā with devotion.

These [deities], whether two-armed or four-armed, should be meditated upon with their hands joined in the añjali gesture. Thus, when one is unable to perform the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), one should worship a single enclosure consisting of the forms of the Five Brahmās and the Six Limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). And of these:

One should perform the eight purificatory rites for the deities of the six limbs of Brahman, known as invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), and the offering of flowers (*puṣpa*). Alternatively, one may simply recollect the eight purificatory rites beginning with invocation as a collective whole.

Having offered a mere *arghya* to each [deity] individually, and as a concluding act up to Brahmā, at the end of each respective *arghya*, one should sequentially display the mudrās known as the fragrant (*surabhi*), the lotus (*padma*), the trident (*triśūla*), and the makara-garland (*makarasraj*); then, one should display the *namaskāra* (salutation) mudrā for the limbs (*aṅga*).
If one is unable to perform the worship of the five Brahmans and the six limbs, one should worship either only the enclosure of the Brahmans or only the enclosure of the limbs. Alternatively,
having worshipped the powers such as Vāmā and others in their respective places in the directions beginning with the east, [one should worship] on the lap of Sadāśiva.
One should worship Manonmanī situated on the left side.
Thus, after the worship of the enclosures,
one should worship Śiva with the "eight-flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā), and having offered water for sipping (ācamana) and the arghya libation, [one should proceed] with the root mantra.

One should offer a flower. This is for the sake of achieving the splendor produced by the state of being an attendant (*āvaraṇabhāva*) of Śiva, and to avoid the fault of the worship becoming *tāmasa* (dull or inert), which might arise from worshipping the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and so forth as if they were separate from Śiva. (p. 81)

One should contemplate all the deities of the enclosures as being of a single color with Paramaśiva and non-different from Paramaśiva, due to their immersion in the mass of rays consisting of Paramaśiva which flows with the supreme nectar and resembles ten million autumnal moons. Then, [one should contemplate them] within Śiva.

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā*, and having worshipped the bell with scents and flowers using the *astra-mantra*, one should present incense and lamps to the deity together with his retinue (*sāvaraṇa*). Thus, it is optional whether the worship of the retinue should be performed or not.
Because in some Āgamas, the worship of objects of enjoyment as limbs of the ritual is prohibited within the context of worship for one's own sake.
Now follows the procedure for the food offering (naivedya).

Among those, rice (*vrīhi*), *śāli*, *priyaṅgu*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), wheat (*godhūma*), bamboo grain (*vaiṇava*), and barley (*yava*) are recommended. Among these, rice is the lowest, *śāli* is middling, and the others are superior.
Even among those, *priyaṅgu*, wild rice, wheat, and bamboo grain are the best.

The fruits increase a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, and infinitely, becoming more and more excellent. Alternatively, there is a distinction: *śāli* rice is the best, barley, bamboo-seed rice (*vaiṇava*), and so forth are middling, and *vrīhi* rice is the lowest. Furthermore, white-grained rice is *śāli*, while other varieties are *vrīhi*. This applies to worship performed for one's own sake.
From one *kuḍava* up to four *droṇas*, each subsequent measure is considered superior.
One *śukti* is said to consist of two hundred and twenty-five grains of rice;
two *śuktis* make one *tala*; two *talas* make one *prakuñca*; and two *prakuñcas* make one *prasṛti*.
Two *prasṛti*s make one *kuḍava*; two *kuḍava*s make one *añjali*; two *añjali*s make one *prastha*;
two *prastha*s make one *pātra*; two *pātra*s make one *āḍhaka*; two *āḍhaka*s make one *śiva*; two *śiva*s make one *droṇa*. Alternatively, two *guñjā*s make one *māṣa*.
Twenty *māṣas* make one *niṣka*; eight *niṣkas* make one *pala*; four *palas* make one *pāda*;
four *pādas* make one *prastha*; four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*; and four of those make one *droṇa*.
[One should remove] hair, insects, and other such things from more than four *droṇas* intended for the *naivedya* offering.
Having separated and freed the grains from the husks, and having repeatedly rinsed the rice— which is free of broken pieces and possesses extreme whiteness—
with water that has been strained through cloth and is endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste; and having squeezed it out [of the water] time and again.
Having thoroughly washed the sand and other materials six times with the six-limbed mantras, and having purified them well,
one should place them in a cooking vessel and pour water over them until they are more than half-submerged.

Then, in a place smeared with cow dung, sprinkled with water, secluded from the sight of birds and others, enclosed on all sides, and out of the range of those who should not enter, [one should proceed].

In the kitchen, having placed the cooking vessel— which was lifted from the hearth that had been worshipped with the *hṛdaya-mantra*— upon it using the *vāmadeva-mantra*, and having applied fire with the *aghora-mantra* and kindled it with the *mukha-mantra*,
[he should cook] in such a way that the food is neither undercooked nor overcooked.

One should cook it with care. Thus is the preparation of pure rice (*śuddhānna*). Alternatively, it may be prepared with twice the amount of milk and half the amount of mung beans relative to the rice;
or with three times the amount of milk and a quarter the amount of mung beans relative to the rice; or with the appropriate addition of jaggery and plantains.

The preparation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is as follows: the preparation of *kṛsara* rice is made with rice, one-fourth part sesame seeds by weight, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) measuring either half of the sesame, or a quarter of the sesame, or [the same amount as] the rice;
or alternatively, it may be prepared with rice mixed with half its measure of mung-bean flour and a small amount of salt powder.

The preparation of *kṛsarānna*: *gulānna* is prepared with milk and jaggery each measuring half the amount of rice, and ghee measuring half of that; or else, with twice the amount of milk as rice, together with jaggery equal to half the rice, and ghee equal to half the jaggery.
Preparation of Gulānna-pāka: Take three parts rice and one part mung beans;
mix them with milk three times the quantity of the rice, add sugar equal to one-fourth the quantity of the rice, and include plantain fruit—this is the preparation of Gulānna-pāka.

The cooking of mung-bean rice may be prepared with mung beans that are one-fourth, one-third, or equal in measure to the rice, either combined with pieces of coconut or without them. Pure rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), kṛsara rice, gulānna, and mung-bean rice follow in order of increasing merit.
The fruits are a thousandfold. Likewise, food mixed with curd and mixed with honey is recommended. Among these, one or another should be prepared according to one's means.
With an eighth or sixteenth part of the *naivedya* (food offering), [one should prepare] mung beans, *āḍhakī*, and mungo beans.

It should be prepared with black gram (*rājamāṣa*), lentils (*viṣpāva*), horse gram (*kulattha*), or any one of these; likewise, if available, mung beans (*mudga*) and others should be taken in their peeled, split form. Regarding the vegetables, they should be measured at two *palas* for the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of one *prastha* of cooked rice, or at one *pala*. As for plantains (*kadalī*)...

Fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*), pumpkin (*kuśmāṇḍa*), cucumber (*urvāruka*), *kāravallī*, *vyāghrī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *kośātakī*, mango, coconut, and others; as well as other roots such as the *śiśukanda*, *vallīkanda*, and *sūraṇakanda*,
provided they possess excellent flavor and aroma— whether fresh or dried— as appropriate, along with salt and black pepper.
Cumin, cardamom, and powder [of other spices], along with sugar and all other necessary seasonings, should be fried in clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (p.

83) A cooling drink (*coṣya*) should be prepared consisting of sour *ghana-takra* mixed with the powders of salt, black pepper, cumin, *kulattha*, and white mustard, together with sugar. [Likewise, preparations of] *māṣa*, *mudga*, and wheat...

Various preparations made from rice flour and other grains, enriched with sugar and scented with powders of camphor, cardamom, and so forth, as well as many types of *apūpa* cakes and *pānaka* drinks, should be prepared. For the food offering (*naivedya*), the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be one-sixteenth, one-thirty-second, or one-sixty-fourth part [of the total]; and thick curd (*ghanadadhi*).
One-eighth [of the measure]. In all cases, milk, curd, and clarified butter must be taken from cows alone. The vessels should be made of gold, silver, copper, or pure bell-metal;
they should be forty-eight finger-breadths in length and one finger-breadth in height.
Those possessing lips as thick as a finger are the best; according to the sequence from the highest-of-the-best downwards,
they range from thirty-six fingers in length down to twelve fingers,
and their lips range from nine *yava*s in measure down to one *yava*.

They should be made with a length equal to the size of a lip, or excluding that [lip], nine finger-breadths in length; those of half that measure are the minimum. All of them should be made without feet and perfectly circular in shape. These are the three-legged stands for supporting the cooking pots (*sthālikā*).

The [pillars] should be made as high as the height of the pedestal (pīṭhikā) of the worshipable liṅga. And one should have all the food offerings (naivedya) prepared by attendants who have been consecrated by Śiva-initiation (dīkṣā), who wear clean garments, who are adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, and who bear sacred threads; or likewise by women similarly adorned.

Having had [the offerings] prepared, at the time of purifying the substances, the worshipper should recite the mantras for washing the rice and so forth. If the food offering (naivedya) already prepared should be uncooked, overcooked, too cold due to the lapse of time, or stepped upon by people, then another cooked offering must be presented.
Now, the offering of the food oblation (naivedya): having offered water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful offering (arghya) to the deity,
one should prepare a square mandala with cow dung in front of the deity,
decorate it with flour-powder and other substances, and fill it with pure rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), and other foods.
With fruits such as plantain, coconut, mango, jackfruit, grape, and date; with sweets such as *laḍḍuka*, musk-powdered cakes, and *modaka*; with cakes;
with vegetables such as plantain and jackfruit; with offerings of fresh *urvāruka* (cucumber) and other greens; and with side-dishes such as mango and orange.
Adorned with soups made of split peas, mung beans, and other ingredients, arranged in the form of a circular staircase, and decorated in the center with milk, curd, and thickened cream,
they were freshly sprinkled with ghee and [mixed with] sugar, curd, and milk.

(p. 84) With various kinds of drinks, sips, and linctuses prepared from fruit juices and other transformations; with jars for bathing filled with very cool water scented with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, cardamom, campaka buds, camphor, musk, lāmajja, and pāṭalī flowers—[measuring] one āḍhaka or half thereof.
Having arranged the offering plates for Śiva and Śivā, filled with water measuring half that [of the previous vessels], and having set out the offering plates for Sadāśiva and Manonmanī,
as well as for the attendant deities and the deities of the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās).

Having placed a leaf over the vessels, sprinkled them with water while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, performed the three *tāla*-claps, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the *dhenu-mudrā*, and having displayed the food-gesture (*anna-mudrā*) and the mountain-gesture (*parvata-mudrā*), one should lift the leaf previously placed [therein], sprinkle it all around with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

Having offered the *āpośana* water with the heart mantra for each [deity], first offer the food offering (*naivedya*) to Gaṇapati with the *mṛga-mudrā* and flowers; then, releasing those flowers and washing the hands, offer the food offering to Śiva five times or three times with the mantra: *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svadhā*.
Alternatively, having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) once with devotion, accompanied by flowers and using the *mṛgamudrā* gesture,
one should offer the food offering separately to each of all [the deities] in the sequence beginning with Sadāśiva. In the absence of separate vessels for all [of them], [one may do so otherwise].

Having brought the food offering (naivedya) into a single vessel for the attendant deities and the deities of the enclosure, one should offer it to each individually. Then, having presented fragrant water to Śiva, offered a flower with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ," and visualized the collection of substances as complete—

Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) with the root mantra ending in *svadhā*, and having given sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and other ingredients for the purpose of rubbing the hands of the deity with the left and right hands,
one should contemplate the washing of the hands, the rinsing of the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa), the washing of the feet, and so forth. And all [these acts].

Having removed the *nirmālya*, one should offer the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva, together with the *nirmālya* of perfumes and flowers previously placed in the eastern direction, to Caṇḍeśa in the northeast.
Now, with which face does Sadāśiva eat? With the upper face.
For it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Edibles, foods, drinks, and so forth—licked, sucked, and of many kinds—all that is prescribed here should be offered into the upper face."
Food is of five kinds: solid (bhakṣya), soft (bhojya), drinkable (peya), lickable (lehya), and suckable (coṣya).

It should be offered with the face turned upward by means of the heart-mantra and the six-faced mantra, according to the statement "twenty twice" (i.e., forty times). Alternatively, he eats with all five faces as well; [this applies] to the five faces.
Furthermore, because the prescription for offering food (*naivedya*) is seen for each of the five faces individually in the passage, "Or again, the food offering is for the upward-facing face" (p.
85), the presentation of the food offering to the upward-facing face should be performed by visualizing that upward-facing face as having turned toward the south at the time of worship.

Because the deity faces the north while the worshipper stands facing it; Śiva faces the practitioner on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and the mobile liṅga (caraliṅga); He faces inward in the case of the water-pot and similar vessels; and on a fixed image (sthira), He faces the door—such is the orientation of the deity during the worship of the mobile liṅga.

Because it is heard [in scripture] that [the deity] faces the worshipper; and thus, in a worship performed for one's own sake, even the heart, the secret parts, and the feet of Śiva must be situated in the southern direction in order to establish His facing toward the practitioner. As for those [limbs] which belong to the worshipper...
Statements regarding the avoidance of standing facing Śiva—

such as "not in the east in front of Śambhu, nor in the north where there is a woman, nor in the west because it is one's back; therefore, one should resort to the south," and so forth— these [are the rules].
These [rites] concern a fixed liṅga (sthiraliṅga) facing the east. Regarding the worship of a mobile liṅga (caraliṅga), there is a specific statement to be observed:

"In the case of the worship of a mobile liṅga on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), Śiva faces the practitioner. Furthermore, this is in accordance with the scriptural injunction: "One should worship the Lord while standing either in the southeast (Agni) or the southwest (Nirṛti)."

If it is argued that when the worshipper stands in the south-eastern direction (āgneyī), Śiva cannot face the worshipper, this is true; however, that statement refers specifically to a fixed linga (sthiraliṅga). Because a fixed linga bestows grace upon the world universally, it faces whichever direction is desired by the worshipper in all four directions.

In whichever direction the door is located, one should face that direction; there, together with the feet moving from the heart, it should be directed upward and facing toward that door. This is because of the scriptural statement: "One should arrange [the visualization] there, facing the door with the face turned upward. In whichever direction the door may be—

And because of the statement, "One should conceive of that [face] as facing east. Alternatively, only the single upward-facing face, together with the faces of the heart, the secret place, and the feet, faces the door. However, the faces such as Tatpuruṣa and the others are situated precisely in the directions starting from the east; they are not differentiated by a distinction of doors. Of the temple...

Let the door be as one desires, according to the wood; however, it does not abandon its position in the eastern and other directions, because of the statement that "the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa [occupy] the positions of the east and so forth. Both of these two views regarding the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa are approved by the Kāmika [Tantra]. For this very reason, in that [text], regarding the worship of the western door—

Having begun with the instruction, "One should visualize the body facing upward and directed toward the door," [the text continues]: "One should contemplate the Person in the eastern or western direction;
or one should contemplate the multiform one in the south or in the north. [And] in the north or in the south as well.

The Guru should meditate upon Vāmadeva. It has been stated that one should meditate upon and install Sadyojātamukha in the west or in the eastern region. In that very same context, regarding the worship at the southern door, it is also said: "One should properly worship Aghora or Puruṣa in the south; or else Aghora or Sadyojāta."

One should worship [the face] in the west; or one should worship the Sadyojāta face, or the Vāmadeva face, in the northern direction. Or one should worship the Tatpuruṣa face, or the Vāmadeva face, in the eastern direction. All [images], whether stationary or otherwise—whether it be a *liṅga*, an image, or something else—should be worshipped facing north.

Regarding the direction: according to the statement, "In each respective [direction], the sacrificer should worship Śiva facing north," in that context of the primary worship of the Liṅga facing east, it is only the worshipper standing in the primary south-eastern direction who can truly be said to be facing north. And this does not apply to the Deity.

Since the Goddess is seated in the western direction (nairṛta) on the left side, when the worshipper is present there, the prohibition that "a woman [must not] occupy the north" would apply; however, in the *Kāmika* Tantra, in the chapter on worship at the western door, it is stated:
"Manonmanī should be installed either on the left or even on the right."

Since it is accepted that in the worship of a linga facing west, the Goddess is to be installed on the southern side— [she who is] "joined with the face of the God" and "endowed with two hands and one face"— for the worshipper situated in the south-western direction (Nairṛti),...
This is because the visualization of the Goddess is established on the right side of the Deity. Thus, in the worship of a *liṅga* that faces east in a secondary sense—
where the east is actually the south— the Deity, situated in the south-eastern direction (the secondary Agni-quarter), faces north in a secondary sense, which is actually the east.

In the worship of the *liṅga* facing east—which is secondary insofar as it is oriented toward the north—the state of facing north, which is secondary insofar as it is oriented toward the west for one situated in the southeast (the direction of Agni), is indeed consistent. Thus, the rule of being oriented toward the worshipper is not violated. This applies everywhere in the context of worship performed for one's own sake (*ātmārthapūjā*).

This is because of the injunction beginning with, "having turned toward the north and being seated upon a beautiful seat. In this regard, there is this distinction: those seeking the destruction of sins and those seeking liberation should, by relying on the orientation of the faces toward the directions, meditate upon the Aghora face as being directly in front of them, but not [the face] of the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu).

One should stand in front and not behind, even in the presence of women. For the sake of destroying the flood of sins and attaining liberation, one who is skillful should worship while standing to the right. Just as frost, wind, and cold burn away the lotus, so too does Aghora, though peaceful, cause the burning away of evil. He is indeed great.

"Just as an elephant follows its driver, so one should worship facing north according to the words of a trustworthy authority. Since this praise of Aghoramukha is seen because of his quality of removing all sins,
those who are fearful regarding rebirth take refuge in this very Rudra, considering him alone to be unborn.

"The face turned southward is for the purpose of protection," because the *Vāyusaṃhitā* shows praise for the southern face as being the bestower of liberation (*mukti*). However, for those who seek liberation preceded by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*),
[the northern face] is used according to the logic of facing the door or the logic of facing the practitioner, in relation to the *tatpuruṣa* face.
Or, relying on the perspective of being oriented toward the practitioner, the face of Tatpuruṣa should be meditated upon as facing [the practitioner];
for the Lord’s [face] is characterized by serenity, that of Puruṣa by stillness, and that of Bahurūpa by ferocity,
which serves as the cause for liberation, maintenance, and destruction— this refers to the face of Tatpuruṣa.

Because it is heard that [the deity] is the cause of stability; in every respect, the upward-facing [deity] remains indeed facing south. And thus, the orientation of the deity toward oneself, effected through invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, attains naturalness in worship for one's own sake. Otherwise—
In the case of worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*), it might somehow be justified by the mere fact that one who is facing upward abandons the state of being directed upward; however,
this is especially so in the case of worship for the sake of others, which has the purpose of benefiting the world.

It is logical that in those cases [of external worship], the worshipper’s facing [the deity] is not required, and thus a certain figurative sense of "facing" can somehow be established for one who faces the door. However, here—
in this self-oriented worship performed for the sake of favoring the practitioner upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a mobile liṅga— [such a requirement does not apply].
The view of some is that, by the force of the word "cet" (if), why was the straightforward possibility of facing the practitioner (*sādhaka*) overlooked? Others, however, say:
in worship for one's own sake, [the deity] faces upward, together with the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
And the face of that *tatpuruṣa* [form] is indeed facing eastward.
In the *Aṃśumat-tantra* and other scriptures, in the very section concerning worship for one's own sake (*ātmārtha-pūjā*), it is stated:
"One should not stand before the Lord, nor behind him, nor even near a woman; neither in the presence of a woman, nor in front of him."
Since statements such as "it should not be [performed] behind the master" have been recited,

they cannot be interpreted as referring to worship performed for the sake of others; furthermore, because the statement regarding the practitioner's orientation is recited in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*), it does not apply to the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) from that context.

Because the presence of the practitioner (sādhaka) cannot be obtained [in that case]. Nor should it be argued that, since there is no occasion for the worship of a mobile liṅga (caraliṅga) during initiation (dīkṣā), the statement regarding the presence of the practitioner in the mobile liṅga refers exclusively to the subject of daily worship;
for even during initiation, there is worship of the mobile liṅga.

Because there is an absence of defects; therefore, from that which is beyond reproach, and according to the statement "not having reached the front," Sadāśiva possesses universal authority over all— whether for obligatory, occasional, or optional rites— and is "eastward-faced, with Lakṣmī as his western face, and his body composed of eight kalās," as stated in the *Lakṣmī-Keśava-saṃvāda* regarding initiation and other rituals.
To the west of Ghaṭeśa, one should contemplate the Guru; one should always meditate upon Sadāśiva— who is Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Śānta, whose faces are eternally ancient—
in the reflection of the face, facing east, as the support for the water-pot at the beginning of initiation and other rites.

Regarding the statement "facing west," since the *Bṛhadbhārgava* and other texts prescribe facing east for Īśāna and Puruṣa in all rites— whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)— except for those specifically ordained as *dīkṣā* (initiation) and the like, these scriptural declarations [are thus established].

In the worship of Śiva—whether performed for one's own sake (ātmartha) or for others, and whether it be obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), or optional (kāmya)—the facing east is the general rule (autsargika). This is because the fixed and permanent lingas have abandoned the orientation toward the doors, whereas movable lingas and the like necessarily face the object [of worship]. This applies to the occasional rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth.
The specific statements regarding facing south and so forth constitute an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule].
Furthermore, they say this other thing: Sadāśiva, even though he is between the faces of Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa, eats with the face of Tatpuruṣa alone; thus, the western direction is the door.

Regarding the statement "the food offering (naivedya) is for the eastern face," this is because of the subtle scriptural injunction [that the faces are arranged as limbs], and because offering food to the northeastern face would be contrary to worldly custom, since that face has the form of the head.
Let it be that he eats through the Tatpuruṣa face—this is one possible position; however, there is no restrictive rule that he eats through that face alone.
Since it is understood that food is to be offered even with the face turned upward— by such previously cited discordant statements as "edibles, foods, drinks,
and so forth," and by such statements as "one should cause the offering to be presented to Mahāsena with his face turned upward"—
the offering of the oblation (*havis*) follows from the statement, "the food offering (*naivedya*) is for the five faces."

Indeed, for the five faces of Īśāna, one should offer pure rice in the Īśāna face; then, in the Tatpuruṣa face, jaggery-rice; in the southern face, kṛsara; and likewise in the northern face, mung-bean rice. In the western face, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), being composed and attentive, giving each in its own respective direction according to its own name.

It should be placed in front of Īśāna. Furthermore, because of the collection of scriptural statements establishing the various types of food offerings for each face— such as "In the absence [of the five sacrificial foods], pure rice is desired in front"—
and because of the feeding with the five faces, the authority of the Āgamas is indeed not undifferentiated.
It is logical that a specific meaning is to be practiced by one person and not by another;

therefore, it is indeed reasonable that there is an option (vikalpa) among even the three positions established by the statements of those respective scriptures. Now, when a worshipper offers the food offering (naivedya) to Śiva by means of the gesture (mudrā) of presenting the offering, what [is the effect] for Śiva?
Should that [offering] be placed in the hand, or rather directly into each respective mouth? In this case as well, there is indeed an option. Later it will be said:

"Having rendered it nectarine, having offered it with *gostanī* [milk], one should place a flower. One should give the excellent drinking water into the right hand of the one to whom the offering is made" (p. 89); thus, [it is to be given] in the right hand.

Because of the scriptural injunction regarding the offering of the *naivedya* (food offering), and because it is heard that "whatever is prescribed here should be given to the one with the upward face (*ūrdhvavaktra*)," and further that "O Mahāsena, one should cause the oblation (*āhuti*) to be offered to the one with the upward face," the offering is made to the mouth. Thus, in this case, there is an option determined according to what is appropriate.

Whatever is to be offered into the mouth of the Puruṣa, which is equal in size to the heart and other [limbs]— namely all foodstuffs such as solid foods and edibles, with the exception of liquid substances— that should all be presented in the left hand while displaying the *abhaya-mudrā*.
This applies both to that which is to be offered into the interior of the mouth and to the various kinds of liquid substances such as water.

One should imagine that all of this, like an *agnihotra* oblation, emerges from the vessels in the form of a subtle essence and arrives together with the *naivedya* mudrā up to the deity's respective mouth; thus, it should be offered directly into that very mouth. And so, in the hand—

Because the act of offering is possible through the rubbing [of the food] with the hand, there is no futility [in this action]. Since the offering is not placed directly into the deity's mouth by the worshipper's hand, there is no risk of the worshipper's hand becoming defiled by contact with the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering). Thus ends the procedure for the food offering (*naivedya*).
The offering of betel-leaf.

Then one should offer mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) and betel (*tāmbūla*). That which is given after the meal for the purpose of perfuming the mouth is called *mukhavāsa* based on the etymology "that which makes the mouth fragrant. This consists of the powder of cardamom, cloves, black pepper, nutmeg, and camphor.

It is said that it should be formed into pills ground with snow-water (*himajala*). Cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, *jātīphala*, and camphor powder—either combined with a small amount of honey and sugar or used alone—is known as the "Five Aromatics" (*pañcasaugandhika*) and is considered excellent. [Used] alone...
Alternatively, the middling [offering] consists of the powder of camphor, nutmeg, cloves, and cardamom; or, for an oblation of one *prastha*,
there are forty-six pieces of soft betel-nut divided into two portions,
along with white *vevā* leaves which, relative to the betel-nuts, are fourfold, threefold, or twofold in number.
Having gathered all these— roots and tips cut into pieces,
powdered stone, camphor and other ingredients, along with well-ripened and prepared coconut and citron fruits—
one should offer betel leaf (*tāmbūla*). Then, having offered the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*) with the root mantra, one should proceed.

Having displayed lamps arranged in one, three, five, seven, or nine rows, and having also displayed lamps placed in vessels shaped like a triple-tāla, a five-tāla, a nāga-wheel, a lotus, a man, a deer, an elephant, or the form of Indra and other gods, one should perform the *ārātrika* according to one's means.
p. 90) The Ritual for the Ārātrika Lamp-Waving Ceremony.
Its form is as follows: made from any one of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal,

measuring twenty-four finger-breadths [in length], with a width of half that, or a third of that, and having a fillet (paṭṭikā) for the height of the rim (yāma) measuring two barley-corns and a height equal to one-fifth of its own measurement, together with a pericarp (karṇikā).

Then, having placed a wick made of camphor and other substances upon lamp-stands— made either of natural materials or of rice-flour— arranged around the center of a beautiful, well-rounded vessel that is adorned externally with eight petals and provided all around with a rim and a pericarp (karṇikā), one should place them within the pericarp in the middle and all around.

Having lit either nine or five lamps—or even a single lamp—placing them upon a tripod, and having consecrated them through the rites of inspection and so forth; if there are nine, one should place the Sun in the center, Guru, Śukra, Budha, and Candra in the cardinal directions, and Bhauma, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu in the intermediate directions; if there are five, [one should place] the Sun in the center.
One should worship Fire in the directions, as well as Space, Wind, Water, and Earth; or, if there is only one lamp, one should worship Fire alone.

Alternatively, in lamps numbering nine, five, or one, one should worship the powers beginning with Vāmā, the five Brahmans, and Śiva. Having thus worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra-mantra*.
Having formed the *surabhi-mudrā* and displayed it with both hands, having lifted [the water] and whirled it three times over the head, heart, and feet of the deity,
[using vessels] made of gold or other materials, whether circular or square in shape.
Having performed the *nīrājana* (lustration) rites— using lamps placed upon lamp-stands made from either natural rice flour or flour mixed with the tips of unopened buds,

and with wicks made of camphor and other substances set within those lamps— whirling them like the *ārātrika* ceremony while consecrating them with the *nirīkṣaṇa* (inspection) and other purificatory rites, [he should place them] upon the ground.
Having performed the ritual placement with the Astra-mantra, one should extinguish [the fire]. There are three types of vessels for the *nirājana* rite:

the best is one with a width of one *prādeśa*, a thickness of two barley-corns, and a stalk eight finger-breadths long, with a bud-shaped top corresponding to that; in its center is a single seat for the lamp.

In the five enclosures (āvṛtis), there are respectively nine, fifteen, twenty-one, twenty-seven, and thirty-three lamps, totaling one hundred and six. Alternatively, according to the sequence of the enclosures, there are eight, fourteen, twenty, twenty-six, and thirty-two lamp-seats.

There are one hundred and one lamps. A bowl measuring half the size of an excellent bowl is the medium-sized bowl. Within this [central bowl] is one lamp, and in the four enclosures are eight, thirteen, eighteen, and twenty-three lamp-seats; thus, there are sixty-three lamps. A measure half that of the medium-sized bowl [is the small-sized bowl].

The smallest [mandala]. In its center, among the three enclosures, there are sixteen, ten, and fourteen lamp-seats; thus, there are thirty-one lamps. Now, [there are] the mirror, parasol, chowrie, fan, and palm-leaf fan.

Having offered [the oblation] in sequence with the mantras beginning with Īśāna, and for the sake of avoiding the defects of speech, mind, and body acquired on that day, as well as for the attainment of union with Śiva (śivasāyujya),
[he offers] a handful of flowers accompanied by dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, unbroken rice grains, and bilva leaves, with the mantra: *hāṃ hauṃ*.
"Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva. Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Vidyā-tattva. Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātma-tattva.
Thus one should offer [the oblation] three times. If one is a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), it should be done in the order beginning with the Ātma-tattva, or otherwise.

One should offer [the offering] just once with the mantra: "Obeisance to Śiva, the sovereign lord of all reality. Then, [one should visualize the deity] satisfied by the worship, turned toward oneself, being served by all the limbs of enjoyment while his hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture, and being praised by Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, Candra, Sūrya, and others outside the entrance of the sacrificial hall.

Having meditated upon Śiva— the ocean of the nectar of boundless compassion and the granter of all desires of his devotees— one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the venerable five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*) according to one's ability for the sake of ensuring the perfection of the worship.
The ritual procedure for the recitation of the five-syllable mantra.
Now, the method of the glorious five-syllabled mantra is set forth;
it should be guarded with great effort according to the path taught by the Guru.
On the southern petal of the lotus-seat of Śiva, on the right side of the form of Aghora,
[one should meditate upon her] who resembles molten gold, with full and elevated breasts,
four arms, three eyes, and a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She holds a lotus and a blue water-lily, is serene, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
she is endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
One should mentally invoke the glorious five-syllabled vidyā, seated upon a white lotus throne, with dark, curly hair at the crown of her head, through the rites of invocation and so forth.

Seated on a comfortable seat, having protected his senses and facing north, with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose and observing silence, he should perform self-protection while worshipping with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
One should visualize [the body] above and below as joined with lunar disks, which flood all the quarters of space with a mass of flowing nectar.

One should contemplate one's own body as being composed of nectar, situated within the center of a bimba-capsule and drenched by streams of nectar, through the showers of nectar belonging to the Śaktis.
This self-protection shall be such that it cannot be breached even by the gods;
having thus performed the protection of oneself, one should then practice the protection of the mantra.
One should exhale the air from the abdomen through the right channel (dakṣanāḍī) with the Astra-mantra;
then, one should fill the abdomen from the outside with air via the Iḍā channel using the Śambhu-mantra.
Having drawn the apāna upward and having restrained both prāṇa and apāna,
one should employ the wind within the suṣumnā by means of the kumbhaka and the mind.

The practitioner of mantra should apply the mantra within the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the mother of mantras, which resides in the center of the suṣumnā at the region of the heart and is united with Śiva.
The wise one, recollecting the mantra-syllables as radiant as jewels and the deity of the mantra,
should mutter the mantra while performing the practice of its coming and going.
One should recite the relationship between the signified and the signifier with the mind absorbed therein;
this is the protection of the mantra, a compendium guarded by the gods.
Having understood this, one should perform the rite of recitation with diligence;
that sequence for the rite of recitation is now set forth very clearly.

One should contemplate the supreme Śakti, who consists of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, who is of the nature of bliss, and who resides within the Suṣumnā from the navel up to the end of the twelve finger-breadths.
Having awakened that [power] by means of the vital air, starting from the *ādhāra-cakra*,
[one awakens] Brahmā, Keśava, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

Having abandoned them one by one— starting from the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā— the wise practitioner [visualizes] that [light], which resembles a streak of lightning, while reciting the portions of the *astra-mantra*.
Having uttered the mantra ending with the *nāda*, one should then recite it one hundred and eight times by means of the practice of its upward and downward movement, as it resides in the *mūlādhāra*.
Having performed the recitation in this manner— either twenty-eight or eight times, as instructed by the Guru— the practitioner of mantra shall attain union with Śiva.

Japa should be performed either internally by means of the garland of letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa', or externally by means of a rosary made of rudrākṣa beads and the like. The method of internal japa according to the Tantras is now described:
at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there is a white eight-petalled lotus and a square yantra situated above it.

A lotus is to be meditated upon. In its pericarp is space (*vyoma*), which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the collection of the fourteenth vowel and the *visarjanīya*, along with its preceding letter. On the filaments are the eight pairs of vowels; on the petals are the five letters each starting with *ka* and so forth, belonging to the square-shaped yantra.

The seed-syllable of nectar (*sudhābīja*) is in the cardinal directions, and the seventh letter is in the intermediate directions. A lotus formed in this manner from the *mātṛkā* [letters], through mere meditation, is a supreme remedy for death. Then, following the sequence of the doors, [the process is] ignited by the flame of the fire at the *mūlādhāra*, which is fanned by the upward-moving breath.

Having entered the aperture of the *suṣumnā* together with the power of *kuṇḍalinī*, and having ascended as far as the *brahmarandhra*, [one perceives] from that *mātṛkā*-lotus— touched by the rising *iḍā*— a continuous stream of nectar-drops in the form of a row of phonemes beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*.

One should contemplate that very Śakti Kuṇḍalinī, which exists pervading from the *brahmarandhra* down to the *mūlādhāra*, and which, through its state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*) with the flame of fire at the *mūlādhāra*,
has ascended via the path of the *suṣumnā*— which is manifesting light— up to the *brahmarandhra*.

One should contemplate the power of Mātṛkā as being of the nature of supreme bliss, becoming nectar through the state of aesthetic rapture (*sāmarasya*) with the stream of nectar-drops trickling from the lotus of Mātṛkā. Regarding this, they say: "Shining forth at the first departure..."
Upon our return journey, we beheld the seal of bliss moving within the path of the mind, appearing as if it were nectar itself.
In the Śakti who exists in the form of the Mātṛkā, pervading from the lotus of the *brahmarandhra* down to the *mūlādhāra* in the sequence beginning with the letter *a*,
there is one group consisting of eight letters beginning with *a*, and another consisting of eight beginning with *ḷ*.
By means of the five letters beginning with *ka*, there are seven groups (*varga*s) consisting of five syllables each.
These nine groups, in sequence, take the form of the jewels representing the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu.
This praiseworthy rosary, fashioned from gems such as rubies, lapis lazuli, topaz, diamonds,
coral, pearls, and emeralds,
is composed of the nine planets and is complete in all its colors. [Take] this rosary...

One should visualize [the deity] as having the form of the light of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), appearing like a lamp situated in the center of the heart-lotus, emerging from the power known as Prākhya. In front of that, one should visualize the letter *kṣa* as Mount Meru, emerging from a flower at the tip of a wish-fulfilling creeper made of the nine gems, which is itself produced by the root mantra.

Having arranged [the beads] in the sequence beginning with the letter *la*, one should visualize the coming and going of the root mantra upon the rosary. Through the visualization of the mantra’s ascent upon that [rosary], having placed the letters of the mantra together with the letter *la* and accompanied by the *visarga* at the head of the mantra, [one proceeds]; then, through the visualization of its descent—
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters of the mantra, beginning with *a* and ending with the nasal bindu (*m*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*).

When this is done, there are one hundred repetitions of the mantra. Following that, [one should place] the group of sixteen vowels, the five groups of consonants (*sparśa-varga*), the semi-vowel group (*anta-stha-varga*), and the eight sibilant and aspirated groups (*ūṣma-varga*).
Having sequentially arranged the mantra, one should repeat the mantra eight times;

in this way, the recitation (japa) is performed one hundred and eight times. At the time of beginning the recitation, by means of the root mantra, one should [visualize] that supreme deity as having become one in essence with the jewel, like its radiance.

Together with the root mantra, one should contemplate its constituent syllables, beginning with the letter *na*, as having yellow, black, smoke-colored, yellow, and red hues; and one should visualize Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva as being of the nature of that deity and merged in a state of aesthetic identity (*samarasa*) with it.

One should gradually abandon Brahmā and the other deities at the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), along with the letters beginning with *na*. This entire meaning has been briefly indicated in the verses written previously. Thus, for one who is unable to recite by means of the internal rosary (*akṣamālā*), [the following applies].

At the time of beginning the recitation (japa) according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should visualize the mantra as mounted upon the power of the Mātṛkā; then, having visualized the letters of the mantra and the Mātṛkā, one should recite the mantra alone while counting it with an external rosary made of rudrākṣa beads or similar materials.

Its varieties are as follows: according to the sequence of superior and so forth, they have the size of an *āmalaka*, a *badara*, or a *caṇaka* (pea), and possess from zero to three faces, or alternatively, from three to eleven faces.

[This is performed] by joining faces together with one another upon a thread made of gold, silver, or the like, or of silk cloth and so forth, which has a count of eight plus one (nine), forty-five, or twenty-seven, [the individual faces] being of a different number and unmixed [with others].
And with Meru-beads joined together by their tails and sewn,

fashioned from Rudrākṣa beads corresponding to the respective colors, and consecrated in sequence one hundred times each with the Sadyojāta and other mantras, it was made to have a Meru at its center.

Worshipped according to the sequence of Śiva-pūjā through the rites of invocation (āvāhana) and so forth; sprinkled at the time of beginning the recitation with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and the like by means of the Heart-mantra and the display of the Mālā-mudrā.

In the case of whispered recitation (*vācikajapa*), one should place the rosary—held in the right hand and concealed by a cloth—upon the middle finger, using the index finger and thumb; in the case of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśujapa*), one should place it upon the ring finger, using the middle finger and thumb; and in the case of mental recitation (*mānasajapa*)...

Placing the ring finger upon the little finger, one should count with the ring finger and the thumb. One who desires worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should move the rosary downward; one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) should move it upward. For the fault of overstepping the *meru*, the expiation is the recitation of the Aghora mantra one thousand times.

To avoid contact with those defects, the rosary should be made of large beads. Likewise, if the rosary falls at one's feet, there should be a thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra; if it falls on the ground, thirty recitations; if it falls on clothing, a hundred recitations. At the time of beginning the recitation, [one should offer] one...
Having placed the flower between the little finger and the middle finger of the right hand, one should recite the mantra.

One should recite using a rosary of rudrākṣa beads for the sake of ease in grasping them. Having placed the flower held in the right hand into the left hand, one should recite the mantra with a recitation that is neither too fast nor too slow, and with full attention.
Having offered [the flowers] and placed the *astra*, *kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras one above the other upon the palm of the left hand,

and having placed the flower held at the time of recitation upon them, he should enclose it with the *hṛdaya*, *kavaca*, and *astra* mantras, protect it with the *astra*, conceal it with the *kavaca*, and then take it up again in the right hand.

Placing [the hand] at the region of the heart, resembling the full moon, and meditating on the recitation as being centered therein, with the right knee placed upon the ground, one should say: "Hāṃ! O protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us; may success be mine through your grace while you remain within me."
"Hāṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! O Śrī Paramaśiva, I entrust this recitation (japa) to you.

With this, one should offer the recitation into the hand of Śiva, which is in the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā), using a handful of water for the guest-offering (arghya) along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata), kuśa grass, and flowers. This [offering] removes the pride regarding one's own performed recitation for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Out of fear that [the teaching] might be destroyed by acts such as public proclamation, the loss of the ritual, or contact with water, it was entrusted to the hand of Śiva for its protection. The meaning of this mantra-verse is as follows: You alone are the protector of the most secret [teachings], such as the mantras and the principles (tattvas).

Therefore, since you are the protector of all, please accept even our recitation (*japa*). While you are present during that recitation, by your grace, both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) will surely be ours. Thus, out of compassion for me, please accept it. Then: *Hāṃ*, O Lord, whatever action there may be, whether well-done or ill-done...
"O Śaṅkara, for me who am established in the state of Śiva, consume and destroy [my sins]! Hāṃ Hoṃ, svāhā to Śiva!

O Supreme Śiva, I offer unto You both my good and evil deeds. Thus, with a handful of water, one should offer all karma consisting of good and evil deeds according to the previously mentioned sequence.

One should offer [the fruits of one's actions]. In this regard, there is the *nivedanī* (offering) for the purpose of protecting the collection of good deeds—that which is intended for enjoyment and that which serves to remove obstacles to liberation—and for the purpose of exhausting the collection of evil deeds. Therefore, the application of the meaning is: "Enjoy and protect the good; exhaust and destroy the evil," for one who is free from desire for worldly enjoyment.

However, for one who seeks liberation (*kevalamumukṣu*), the prayer for protection is simply "eat what has been offered," in order to avoid obstacles to liberation; this applies to the merit performed for the sake of enjoyment,
which is incidental as a secondary fruit of the worship of Śiva.

[This refers to] that which leads to the attainment of enjoyments ranging from those of human beings up to those of Hiraṇyagarbha, yet— which, according to the method stated in the Purāṇas, "O dear one, these are indeed hells [compared] to the state of the Supreme Self"— induces hell for the seeker of liberation alone who feels revulsion toward sense objects.

It is used in the sense of "destroying" because it takes the form of a *duṣkṛta* (evil deed). Although the root *bhuj* in the sense of "protecting" is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*, and thus one would expect a *parasmaipada* form such as *abhunakṣīt*, nevertheless, in this verse which has the nature of a mantra, this is an archaic (*chāndasa*) usage, similar to the employment of *rakṣasva* in Vedic mantras.

The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is due to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85). Alternatively, the word *bhuṅkṣva* refers only to enjoyment (*bhoga*), not to protection (*pālana*). Furthermore, by the word *sakṛta*, only that merit (*sukṛta*) intended for enjoyment—which is undesirable to the worshipper seeking liberation alone—is expressed, and not that which is required for the purpose of worldly experience (*bhukti*).

The enjoyment of that [food] by King Śiva is like the enjoyment of a king, consisting of a mode of distribution under his own control; it does not mean eating it himself. This "mode of distribution under his own control" consists of its being served, in whatever manner, to the beloved kinsmen or friends of the worshipper. For one seeking liberation (mumukṣu), this is unnecessary.

It is well known from the Śruti that Śiva bestows the merit of one’s good deeds upon his kinsmen and friends; although there is also a scriptural tradition that he bestows their misdeeds upon their enemies, nevertheless,
the worshipper of Śiva regards everything as the form of the eightfold Śiva.

Thinking, "May he not hate them," it is appropriate to pray for the very destruction of one's own evil deeds—namely, their failure to produce fruit within oneself; thus, such a prayer is incorporated into the mantra. Therefore:
"Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is this entire world; Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere."

"He who is Śiva is indeed I myself. With the mantra *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*, one should offer [the oblation] with water from the hollowed palms (*culaka*) according to the previously mentioned method, thinking, "I offer the Supreme Śiva, who is my own Self, unto You. In this verse of the mantra, by the portion "so'ham" (He am I), [the identity of] oneself and Śiva is expressed.

The relationship between the body and the embodied is established. Since Śiva is the embodied one by virtue of being the controller, and since [the individual] is the body by virtue of being the controlled, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "I am He" within this body-embodied relationship, just as in the expression "the handsome king, who knows dharma. Thus it is said.

This is the exclusion of non-connection [with impurity]. As for the one who is Śiva: the word "Śiva," which denotes the supreme auspiciousness, refers by conventional usage (rūḍhi) to that which is untouched even by the threefold impurity—consisting of the āṇava, māyika, and karmic types—due to the prior absence of any connection with beginningless impurity; thus, by its very nature, it is called Śiva.

The meaning is that [the term] is well-known in such passages as "by the virtuous ones who know the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva. Alternatively, based on the etymology: from the root *śīṅ* (to sleep) with the addition of the *van* suffix belonging to the *rauṇādika* class—whereby the short vowel is substituted and the form is established—it is so called because the collection of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇajāta*) resides within it in a state of identity (*sāmarasyena*).

He is a mine of all the jewels of auspicious qualities conducive to being sought as a refuge—such as mutual non-contradiction, magnanimity, sweetness, discernment of distinctions, unsurpassedness, forbearance, and so forth.
Whatever is inauspicious does not exist in him at any time; rather, every single auspicious quality exists in him.

The meaning is that [the word] is well-known in such passages as "Since Śiva is the Supreme Self" (paramātmā). Alternatively, the word *siṃha* is derived from the verbal root *hiṃs* (to injure), while *śiva* is traditionally remembered in the sense of "desiring mastery" (*vaśakāṃti*). Through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), it is established that *kaśyapaḥ* means "one who desires Śiva," based on the rule for the formation of the word *paśyakaḥ*. Thus, [the name] is derived from the fact that he desires Śiva.

The meaning is that he is well-known from such passages as: "By virtue of his etymological derivation, he is one who desires the welfare of all beings," and "Because he constantly promotes the commencement of all undertakings for men, desiring their auspiciousness, he is therefore remembered as the God Śiva. Alternatively:

From the word *śiva*, which denotes "auspiciousness," by applying the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "one who performs that" (*tatkaroti*), followed by the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class), and with the elision of *ṇi* according to the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, the derivation *śivaṃ karoti sarveṣām* ("he makes all [beings] auspicious") results in the meaning "the benefactor of all living beings. Thus:
"All the Dānavas and the immortals (Amaras) become equal to me; I am Śiva."
The meaning is that "auspiciousness" (*śivatvam*) for all beings is well-known from such [scriptural] passages as "Therefore, O gods... and so forth.

Alternatively, [the word *śiva*] is derived from the root *śyaiñ* (to go) with the addition of the Uṇādi suffix *van*, along with the elision of the vowel *a* and the consonant *y* by means of two irregular rules (*nipāta*), resulting in the etymological analysis: "that which is attained (*ayate*)"—meaning it is reached—by those seeking enjoyment and liberation.

"He is to be worshipped. By means of him, intoxicated elephants, horses with the speed of the wind, and women with faces like the full moon [are obtained]; such is the fruit of the rite of Śiva-worship. Abandoning everything else, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness. The Supreme Lord of Gods is the supreme object of meditation; thus ends the Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad]. (p. 98)
The meaning is that this is well-known from such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as these. Alternatively, it refers to such passages as:
"Even a three-syllable name uttered by men even once, when encountered, quickly destroys their sin;
yet you, O evil one, hate that Śiva whose fame is pure and whose command is inviolable. And so forth.

The meaning is that the well-known referent of the word *śiva*, which has been taught as the remover of all evils, is [the subject]. "Śiva sacrifices everywhere" means that in all worlds, Śiva alone sacrifices and remains established as the one entitled to perform dharma; he alone consists of all living beings who are subject to karma.
The meaning is "the controller. Śiva is this entire universe;

the meaning is that he is the self of the whole insentient phenomenal world consisting of the elements and their derivatives, and its regulator. He is the enjoyer and the protector of those who have sought refuge. He is the giver to those who have sought refuge.

When obstacles such as sins arising from negligence exist, he is the purifier thereof. These adjectives are applicable to Śiva and the offering of one's own self (*svātmanivedana*) along with its constituent parts. To explain: [they apply] to the worshipper who is to be disciplined and to Śiva, who is the discipliner.

Self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*) consists precisely in the contemplation "I am yours" by one who worships Śiva through the relationship of body and embodied being, which takes the form of the relation between the controller and the controlled.
Thus, in the expression "I am that very one," the term "that" refers to Śiva, and by means of the term "I," one's state of having Him as one's own body is expressed.

By the word *eva* (only), which serves to exclude its non-connection [with other objects], its necessity—consisting in being the object of constant reflection—is stated as that which establishes it. And they say that this self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*) possesses five limbs along with their ancillaries: the resolve for favorability (*ānukūlyasaṅkalpa*).
Avoiding hostility, the conviction that "He will protect me," and likewise the choosing of Him as one's protector.
Regarding "miserliness" (*kārpaṇya*): therein,

the entire multitude of living beings constitutes the two limbs— namely, acting in accordance with all beings and avoiding what is contrary to them— which support the worshiper toward Śiva, the refuge.

The term "body" has been mentioned here. By this, it is understood that every living being who worships Śiva should behave with favorability toward the king’s body, like a servant, and avoid any conduct contrary to it.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā, in the section defining the eight forms of Śiva:

The Self is the eighth form of Śiva, the Supreme Soul; it pervades all other forms. Therefore, the universe is of the nature of Śiva. To perform service for all, to bestow grace upon all, and to grant fearlessness to all—this is the worship of Śiva.
"The wise know that if the restraint of any embodied being whatsoever is carried out, it is undoubtedly as if an offense were committed against the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva);

of this there is no doubt. However, regarding the assurance that [the Lord] will protect [us], an explanatory justification has been stated through all the qualifying attributes. First, the quality of having me as His very body (*svaśarīrakatva*) was expressed by the words "I myself" (*ahameva*).
This serves to establish confidence in self-protection. For who would not protect their own body?

[The Lord is so protected] by the absence of the impurities that cause attachment, aversion, and other such factors—which are contrary to the confidence expressed by the word "Śiva"—and by His possession of all auspicious qualities, which is essential for being worthy of taking refuge in Him.
The state of being one who desires the welfare of all beings, the state of being one who effects the welfare of all beings,

and the state of being denoted by the word "Śiva"— which signifies the auspicious one who turns back all evils that oppose welfare— all of this is established by the [scriptural] statements: "Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere" and "Śiva is this entire world."

The state of being the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratva*), characterized by the governance of the entire phenomenal world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities as expressed by the two qualifiers, is also a supporting factor for that [conclusion]. For it is possible to have confidence that the Lord of All is capable of granting the desired objects of His devotees; this is because [the root *īś*] has the sense of protecting (*pālana*).
By the two qualifiers "eater" (*bhoktā*) and "giver" (*dātā*), derived respectively from the verbal root *bhuj* (to eat) and the root *daip* (to purify) in the sense of habitual action,
his nature as a protector of devotees and his nature as one who removes all the misfortunes of those [devotees], including even great sins committed through negligence, are expressed.

That this [dependence] is the means of establishing that [protection] is quite clear. Even in the choosing of a protector (*goptṛtvavaraṇa*), it is precisely the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) that serves as the means of establishment.

For how could one who is himself by nature a protector, when prayed to with the words "become my protector," fail to protect? By the word "but" (*tu*), [the text indicates] his own state of helplessness (*kārpaṇya*), which consists in being independent of any other deity, as the means of establishing that [protection].
The distinction is that the absence of the relationship between the governed and the governor among other deities is expressed by the word [the negative particle].
Thus, after performing the recitation and self-surrender with three handfuls of water,

one should also recite the five Brahma-mantras and the six ancillary mantras (ṣaḍaṅga) in conjunction with a tenth part of the root mantra; then, having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) and three handfuls of flowers, [one should remain] before him.

Standing with palms joined in *añjali*, one should also offer a hymn of praise (*stotra*). One should praise according to the circumstances, using the hymns of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), or other hymns seen in the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, or hymns composed by former teachers; or one may use a hymn composed by oneself.
The Paurāṇikas say it is equal to the Śruti.
The ritual procedure for circumambulation.
Having praised [the deity] in this manner, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), prostrate with the eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*),

perform three circumambulations (*pradakṣiṇa*), and after prostrating five times, perform circumambulation once more. For the sake of ensuring the success of the worship, circumambulation is essential.

One should move from foot to foot with the hands free from movement; praise with speech and meditation in the heart—this four-limbed circumambulation is like a woman near childbirth who carries a jar full of oil and proceeds very slowly; in that same manner one should perform it.

Circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). That circumambulation is threefold: clockwise (*savya*), counter-clockwise (*apasavya*), and both clockwise and counter-clockwise (*savyāpasavya*). That which is performed by keeping the deity to one's right is *savya*. The opposite of that is *apasavya*. The combination of both is *savyāpasavya*.

All three types [of circumambulation] should be performed starting from the direction of Indra and ending with the direction of Indra. They may be performed moving clockwise and counter-clockwise, or starting from the location of the *somasūtra* and ending at the location of the *somasūtra*. Among these, the clockwise path is for celibate students (*brahmacārin*), the counter-clockwise path is for ascetics (*yati*), and both clockwise and counter-clockwise paths are for householders and forest-dwellers (*gṛhin* and *vānaprastha*).
One view is that the left is common; another view is that the right is for ascetics alone, while both the right and the left are for those who have been initiated.
The Ritual of Prostration.
Prostration is of four kinds: eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*), five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*), three-limbed (*tryaṅga*), and one-limbed (*ekāṅga*).

The eight-limbed prostration is of two types: the staff-like prostration (*daṇḍapraṇāma*) and the simple prostration (*kevalapraṇāma*). When performed with the two feet, the two hands, the chest, the head, and the voice, it is called the staff-like prostration.

Another alternative view is that the *daṇḍapraṇāma* (staff-like prostration) is performed with both feet, both hands, the chest, the head, speech, the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*dhi*), and the sight.
