Here, by "mind" (*manas*), it is meant that one's attention is focused on nothing else; by "intellect" (*dhi*), [it is meant that one understands the significance of the act].

The distinction is that this hymn, consisting of an investigation into the greatness of Śiva, is being analyzed. There is also another view: that it is performed with the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, the chest, the head, the mind, the speech, and the sight—or with the two feet, the two arms, the chest, and the head.

There is also the view that [an act] is performed by means of the mind, speech, and sight. A mere prostration performed while touching the ground with the head, both hands, both ears, the chin, and both arms is the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) prostration. With the head and both hands...

The *pañcāṅga* [prostration] is that which is performed by touching the ground with both knees; another view holds that it is that which is performed by placing the head, hands, and forearms upon the knees.
The *tryaṅga* [prostration] consists of joining the palms in *añjali* upon the head. [This is] exclusively...

Bowing with the head alone is the single-limbed salutation (*ekāṅga-namaskāra*). These prostrations should be employed as appropriate, depending on the requirements of place, time, strength, and other factors.
The procedure for the fire-ritual.
Having thus gratified the Supreme Lord with hymns of praise, circumambulations, and prostrations,
and having requested permission by saying, "O Master, I shall perform the fire-ritual," and having received the command from Śiva,
he should go to the fire-sanctuary while holding the general *arghya* water.

Having kindled the fire— produced from fire-drills (*araṇi*), sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*), or the like, or collected from the house of a *śrotriya*— upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit and made of either clay or sand, which has been purified by the four consecrations beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), [one should perform the rite] with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having cast out the flesh-eating portion of the fire toward the southwest (nirṛti) corner, having gazed at the fire with the root mantra,
having performed sprinkling and striking with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
and having sprinkled it with the armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should worship] with: *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ namo vahnimūrtaye*.
Having joined the consciousness of the fire with the inhaled breath (pūraka) residing in the heart-lotus by means of the withdrawal gesture (saṃhāramudrā),
and having brought it together with that [fire] to the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta) through the path of the Suṣumṇā,
one should unite it with Paramaśiva; then, exhaling (recaka) through the Piṅgalā, one should eject it with "HĀṂ HRŪṂ."
Saying "Obeisance to the Consciousness of Fire," he should cast it into the blazing fire with the *udbhava-mudrā*. Thereafter,
having worshipped the fire with the five mantras beginning with *sayojātā* and ending with *namaḥ*,
he should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* and the *śakti-mantra* ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
Having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, protected with the Astra mantra, and worshipped with the Hṛdaya mantra;

having contemplated the supreme power of the Lord (pārameśvara-vīrya); and having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara in a state of non-dual union (samarasa) situated in the northeast and southeast directions respectively—[one should proceed] by means of the channel within the womb of Vāgīśvarī.
One should visualize that seed-syllable being cast by Vāgīśvara directly into one's own mouth;
then, having offered five oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should assign the name "O Śiva-fire, you are the consumer of oblations" (*hutāśana*).

Having visualized the fire as purified by the five sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, and having worshipped the two parents with the heart-mantra and then dismissed them, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the girdle (*mekhalā*) with the water from the general *arghya* vessel while reciting the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, starting from the directions of the girdle.

Having spread ten *darbha* blades with their tips pointing eastward and northward using the *kavaca* mantra, and having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Ananta in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions of the girdle (*mekhalā*), he should inform [the deity]: "Protect the sacrificial fire-pit. [Then he visualizes] the red [deity] endowed with five faces.
Adorned with seven tongues of flame, possessing ten arms and three eyes, and embellished with all ornaments.
Clad in red garments, seated upon a lotus in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana),
and endowed with ten weapons— one should meditate on Śivāgni; above its face are three tongues, namely Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiriktā, located in the faces starting from the east.

One should meditate upon the four tongues as being radiant white, black, red, and golden. Then, having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni," and having offered five oblations of sesame seeds with "Hāṃ Hrūṃ, svāhā to Agni," [one recites]: "O Agni, you are the divine splendor, the supreme purifier."

Therefore, having informed the Fire with the words, "I shall satisfy [the deity] by placing it within the lotus-heart of your lamp," and having worshipped the Fire with all ritual offerings (upacāras) after first performing the invocation (āvāhana) of the Seat-form (āsanamūrti) and Sadāśiva into the heart-lotus of the Fire, one should contemplate the presence of the faces of Śiva within the faces of the Fire.

Having offered one hundred or half that number, or as many as possible according to one's capacity, with fuel sticks, cooked rice, clarified butter, parched grain, mustard seeds, sesame seeds, and so forth, using the root mantra ending in *svāhā*; and having offered oblations amounting to one-tenth of those for the Brahma-mantras and the ancillary mantras; and having given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the upward-facing mouth with the mantra *Hauṃ Śivāya Vauṣaṭ*; [one should proceed] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having offered a *caru* measured at three mouthfuls, having offered one oblation each for the limbs of Brahmā,

having provided water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having given sandalwood paste and betel leaf, one should worship with ashes, water for the feet (*pādya*), and the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*). In the absence of clarified butter and other such materials—

Or one may offer oblations with leaves, flowers, and so forth. Then, having gratified [the deity] with hymns of praise, circumambulations, and prostrations, and having offered the *arghya* for the turning away [of the deity], one should raise Śiva and worship Śiva while he resides within the *liṅga*.
Then, taking up the *darbha* grass used for the surrounding strewn layer (*paristaraṇa*), one should soak the tips, middles, and roots in clarified butter (*ājya*).

Taking up a single blade of *darbha* grass, one should burn the remainder starting from the tip. Having cast that single blade of *darbha* into the fire, one should apply a *tilaka* on the forehead with its ashes.
Wearing those ashes increases longevity, prosperity, and fame, and brings about victory and health. Then, of that...

Having drawn a square mandala on the southern side, one should place Rudras, the groups of Mothers, and Yakṣas in the great directions starting from the east and ending with the north outside the mandala;
and in the intermediate corners starting from the northeast, one should place the Planets, Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas in the center of the mandala.
Having worshipped the Nakṣatras, the Rāśis, and the Viśvedevas in the Īśāna, Agneya, and Nairṛta corners,

and having worshipped Kṣetrapāla between the directions of Vāyu and Varuṇa, and having offered the Arghya water, one should present the Bali offering of food mixed with water to Rudra and the others, and then offer water for sipping (ācamana).

In the worship of Rudra and the others, the mantras consisting of their respective names end with *namaḥ*; in the offering of the *bali*, they end with *svāhā*. The distinction is that for Kṣetrapāla the singular is used, while for the others the plural is used.
Then, on the square mandala in the eastern portion, [the offerings are made] to those beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu.

One should offer an oblation to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Then, on a circle of cow-dung in the courtyard outside the pavilion, one should offer separate oblations as follows: "Svāhā to the crows and others who violate the covenant! Svāhā to Agni and the others!
Svāhā to all the planetary deities (*graha*) and the deities of the site (*vāstu*). Thus, [he offers] the oblation individually.

Having given [the offerings], one should also give a single *bali* to the horse-demons (*aśva-bhūta*), the fallen (*patita*), the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and so forth. Or else, summarizing for the sake of all: "Those Rudras who perform Rudra-deeds, who dwell in fierce abodes;
and whoever are gentle, dwelling in gentle abodes; the Mothers, and those of the form of Rudra."
And those who are the lords of the hosts, as well as other obstructive spirits residing in the cardinal and intermediate directions— may they all,
with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering;
may they swiftly grant us success and protect me from all fears.

One should offer a single *bali* with the mantra. This entire *bali*-rite must be performed only by one who is authorized for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), not by everyone. Even when there is authorization for the fire-rite, if there is a deficiency in the implements for the *homa* or an inability to perform it, one should recite the *homa* mantras ten times over, according to the required number of *homa* offerings.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the knowledge of Śiva.
The Ritual for the Worship of the Knowledge of Śiva.

The Śiva-knowledges are the divine Āgamas beginning with the Kāmika. Among them, the Kāmika has three divisions and consists of one hundred million verses (*parārddha*). The Yogaja has five divisions and consists of one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣa*). The Sūkṣma is a single-tantra work consisting of one hundred thousand verses (*padma*). The Sahasra has ten divisions and consists of one hundred thousand verses (*śaṅkha*).

The *Aṃśumat* consists of twelve divisions and five hundred thousand verses; the *Suprabheda*, a single tantra, consists of thirty million verses; the *Vijaya* consists of eight divisions and thirty million verses; the *Niśvāsa* consists of eight divisions and ten million verses; and the *Svāyambhuva* consists of three divisions and one and a half million verses.
The Anala-tantra consists of thirty thousand verses; the Vīra-tantra has thirteen divisions and one hundred thousand verses;
the Raurava has six divisions and eight hundred million verses;
the Makuṭa has two divisions and one hundred thousand verses; and the Vimala has sixteen divisions and one hundred thousand verses.
*Prodgīta* has sixteen divisions and three hundred thousand verses; *Lalita* has three divisions and eight thousand verses; *Siddha* has four divisions and one and a half crores of verses;
*Santāna* has seven divisions and six thousand verses; and *Śarvokta* has five divisions.
The *Pārameśvara* consists of seven divisions and twenty thousand verses (*lakṣa*).

The *Kiraṇa* consists of nine divisions and fifty million verses (*koṭi*). The *Vātula* consists of twelve divisions and one hundred thousand verses. Thus, there are twenty-eight divine scriptures (*divyāgama*) comprising these divisions.
The number of these texts is fifty-six thousand six hundred and sixty-two, less one hundred and twenty-six thousand, plus one *parārdha*, one *śaṅkha*, and one *padma*.
Their subdivisions number two hundred and eight. All such [texts] as these—

One should have some or even just one of the divine scriptures written down in books that possess the proper characteristics— either as many as are available, or at least just the *saṃhitā* useful for one's own worship.
Regarding the books, the manuscript should be twenty-two finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.

Lakṣmībhadra: twenty-one finger-breadths long and three finger-breadths wide is the Śrīrakṣa. Twenty finger-breadths long and slightly less than three finger-breadths wide is the Candrakānta. These three constitute the highest category. Eighteen finger-breadths long...
The *nalinam* measures two and a half finger-breadths in width and seventeen finger-breadths in length;

the *śrīnivāsam* measures three finger-breadths plus three barley-corns in width; and the *śrībhadram* measures sixteen finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths plus two barley-corns in width. These three constitute the medium-sized group.
The Lakṣmīnivāsa is fifteen aṅgulas long and two aṅgulas plus one barley-corn (yava) wide; the Umābhadra is fourteen aṅgulas long and two aṅgulas wide;
[the third] is thirteen aṅgulas long and two aṅgulas minus one barley-corn wide.

Vīrabhadra: In such books, one should have the sections favorable to the patron made hollow between the fourth part and the third part of the leaves, and then bind them with cotton threads the thickness of barley grains. Of these—

For the worship of the books of Śiva-knowledge, one should construct a library for the sciences (vidyākośagṛha) in the south-western or north-western quarter of Śiva’s [temple], having made it of any one of the dimensions ranging from thirty cubits down to three cubits.

In the center of that [hall], whose walls are smeared with fragrant sandalwood and other substances, one should place the Vidyā-siṃhāsana fashioned from ivory and other materials and adorned with golden lines and so forth;
having spread silk cloth or similar material upon it, [one should place the deity] in its center.

Having placed within it a chest (*mañjūṣā*) made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, brass, iron, wood, bamboo, split bamboo, and so forth, which serves as a jewel-casket for knowledge, one should deposit the books therein. Upon them, one should recite: "Salutation to all the Śiva-knowledges."

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should praise and prostrate, saying: "I take refuge in the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), Śambhu, the bestower of all knowledge and the destroyer of all ignorance, through body, mind, and speech. In the absence of a book, [one should do so].

Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus within the square mandala, and an eighteen-petaled lotus as its enclosure, one should worship Śiva together with Vāgīśvara at the pericarp with the mantras: *hauṃ śivāya namaḥ* and *hāṃ vāgīśāya namaḥ*. Then, on the ten petals starting from the east...

Having worshipped the divine scriptures known as the Śaiva Āgamas— beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Suprabheda*— which were directly composed by Śiva without dependence on any other foundational authority, [one should place] those beginning with *Vijayā* and ending with *Vātula* upon the eighteen petals,
as they were composed by Śiva through the agency of the primordial Rudras and others.
One should worship those known as Raudra. Then, having approached the Guru seated upon his own seat, washed his feet,
and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings while perceiving him as Śiva, one should offer three handfuls of flowers,
prostrate three times with the eight limbs of the body, and rising up, place both knees upon the ground.

With palms joined in reverence, he should say, "Forgive me. Following the scriptural injunction: "Just as a bee greedy for honey goes from flower to flower within the forest, so a disciple greedy for knowledge may go from one guru to another," he approaches another guru for the sake of superior knowledge.
Nevertheless, one should worship even the former guru as before.
Then, having approached Śiva and worshipped Him with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),
and having presented the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*), one should perform a prayer while prostrating oneself on all sides.

"Whatever has been done by me through delusion, whether deficient or excessive, may all that become complete through your grace; thus having prayed, 'May this oblation reach its fulfillment,' [one should say]: 'Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night; considering me as a servant, you should forgive me.'"
"O Lord, compassionate toward devotees! I, a lowly servant of impure intellect, have caused you distress;
yet, being pleased by the power of my devotion, please forgive this," thus he should petition.
Then, according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta...

Having worshipped the auspicious Śiva in the five heads and having worshipped the limbs, beginning with the weapon-mantra and ending with the heart-mantra, in reverse order; and having prayed as before, "Be facing upwards as you desire," [he offers] the *parāṅmukha-arghya* (the oblation for the one turned away) with: *HĀṂ HAUṂ ŚIVĀYA SĀṄGĀYA PARĀṄMUKHĀRGHYAṂ SVĀHĀ*.
Having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya*, one should join the *brahma-mantras* beginning with Sadyojāta and the *aṅga-mantras* beginning with Astra—
which constitute the form of the inner enclosure— to the limbs of the Deity. One should also offer the *parāṅmukha-arghya* to the other deities belonging to those respective enclosures.

With the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, casting the flower upward with the tips of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands using the *nārāca-mudrā*, one should raise the mantras and join them to the heart-center of Śiva with the divine mudrā, reciting: *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ namaḥ śivamūrtaye*.

One should contemplate their dissolution therein. Thereafter, having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* even to the Guru’s abode, the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), the seven Gurus, Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the door-keepers, one should dismiss them with their respective mantras. Then, [one should offer it] also to the deities of the retinue.
Having offered the *arghya* with its face turned away, and having covered each [liṅga] individually with cloths along with flowers,
one should place them at the sides of the chest using the *astra-mantra*. Then, having recited the *Śiva-mantra*,
one should take the liṅga from the lotus-seat and wrap it with fine silk (*dukūla*) and other cloths.

Having placed [the deity] within the chest (peṭaka), while recollecting Bhīmarudra and requesting the command of Śiva, "Protect [him]," one should perform the closing. Then, one should perform the mixed worship (miśrapūjā).
For one who has not previously performed the worship of Caṇḍa, after the dismissal (udvāsana) of Śiva, [one should perform] all the services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
One should perform the fierce worship (caṇḍapūjā) together with [the consort].

In this manner, worship should be performed at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight; or during the periods beginning with dawn; or during two such periods beginning with dawn; or even during the time of dawn alone, for three *ghaṭikās*. This applies to times other than the transits of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, the eighth (*aṣṭamī*), the fourteenth (*caturdaśī*), and so forth.

One who desires worldly enjoyment (bubhūkṣu) should avoid performing worship at night. Even for such a person, if worship is performed during the three periods of the day, the evening worship must be completed within three *ghaṭikās* starting from sunset. However, for one who seeks liberation (mumukṣu), there is no restriction regarding time; or rather, even for one who desires enjoyment, there is none.

Regarding the restriction of time: according to the observation of the scriptures, one should perform the sacrifice for one's own sake at whatever time is possible, using as many *nāḍikās* as are available, in accordance with one's capacity.
Thus, being unable to perform the elaborate ritual services (*prapañcopacāra*), one should perform sixteen or five services.

The sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) consist of invocation, seating, water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), bathing, clothing, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*), prostration accompanied by hymns of praise, circumambulation, and dismissal. Alternatively—

The sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are: the seat, the invitation, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the bath (*snāna*), clothing, perfume, flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), sacred ash (*bhasma*), and a handful of water (*culakodaka*).
[Alternatively: the invitation, the seat, water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering, the bath, clothing, perfume, flowers, and food offerings.

The ten services (*daśopacārāḥ*). The five services consist of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*). Although the substances such as perfumes and flowers may be terrestrial—consisting of bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth—or aquatic—such as water, milk, clothing, curd, cow’s urine, and so forth—or fiery—such as gold and gems; [these constitute the five services].

The lamp, ornaments, and so forth; the wind-related [offerings]: the fly-whisk, incense, and the fan made of palm leaves; the etheric [offerings]: song, instrumental music, and the like, such as the sounds of the lute and the flute—these are declared by those who know the scriptures to be the five types of offerings. Thus end the five offerings.

These have been shown through elaboration (*prapañca*). Furthermore, for those who are incapable [of performing all], there are only five services (*upacāra*), beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*), which correspond respectively to the earthly, ethereal, aerial, fiery, and watery elements.
All these services are performed like the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Śiva.

It is well-known in the scriptures that [these rites] should be performed by means of restraining the movement of the moon and the sun in the form of exhalation and inhalation; furthermore, in certain ritual applications, a regulation of time by counting *mātrās* is also shown in the scriptures. There are twelve *mātrās* for the invocation (*āvāhana*), and [the same] for the water for the feet (*pādya*).

Five [prostrations] for the water for sipping; three for the water of honor (*arghya*); one for the fragrance (*gandha*); twelve for the incense (*dhūpa*); six for the lamp (*dīpa*); twenty-four for the food offering (*naivedya*); seven for the waving of lights (*ārātrika*); sixteen for the ceremonial waving of lamps (*nīrājana*); seven for the offering of ashes (*bhasma*); five for the parasol (*chatra*); ten for the fly-whisks (*cāmara*); and three for the fan (*vyajana*). Thus.

While the ritual services (upacāras) are being performed by means of arresting the movement of the moon and the sun, their respective mantras should be recited mentally alone. Furthermore, the mantras— consisting of the Prāsāda, the Śiva-mantra, the five Brahmans,
and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga)— should be applied according to the rules for each specific ritual service.

In that regard, for the services of invocation, water for the feet (*pādya*), clothing, unguents, ornaments, mirror, umbrella, chowrie, fan, recitation (*japa*), hymn (*stotra*), prostration (*namaskāra*), and other services not specified otherwise, the word "namaḥ" is appended to the end of the mantra.

The word *svāhā* is used for the offering of the *arghya*, bathing, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), drinking water, mouth-freshening water, the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), the sacred thread (*pavitra*), recitation (*japa*), worship, and the final dedication (*samarpaṇa*). The word *vauṣaṭ* is used for sprinkling (*mārjana*), pouring water (*secana*), flowers, and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). [The word *phaṭ* is used] for the bath of impurities (*malasnāna*), purification (*śodhana*), and the severing of bonds (*pāśacchedana*).

The word *huṃ phaṭ* is used for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), piercing (*bhedana*), and warding off obstacles (*vighnanivāraṇa*). The word *phaṭ* is used for protection (*rakṣā*). The word *svadhā* is used for sipping water (*ācamana*). One who is unable to perform even the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) according to these stated rules should worship with the "eight flowers" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) alone. [Regarding] the seat (*āsana*):

The first flower should be offered with a pure mind; one should perform the visualization of the form (mūrtidhyāna) within the heart, and then with another flower. By the offering of five flowers, one should assign the five limbs (pañcāṅga); likewise, with the eighth, Śiva [is worshipped]—thus is the "Eight Flowers" (aṣṭapuṣpikā) described.

The five limbs beginning with the head are the five Brahmans, excluding the eye, or they are the heart and so forth. These eight flowers are common to all; they bestow all accomplishments here in this world, as well as in all stages of life (āśramas), and are common to all castes (varṇas).
And one should worship [it] once a day, twice a day, or thrice a day.
In the morning, at midday, and likewise when the sun has set, one should worship with supreme devotion according to the rite of the eight flowers. [One should also worship] for those who are poor,
the helpless, children, women, and the simple-minded, as well as for those who enjoy worldly pleasures and those afflicted by disease.

For those who have dedicated their souls to meditation, who are devoted to the scriptures of Śiva, whose nature is beneficial through various supernatural powers (siddhis), and who are both attached and detached—it is said that "this [is] the Aṣṭapuṣpikā," according to the statement in the *Kālottara*. "Bhoga" is the protection of a kingdom; those who possess this are the "bhogins," and for them, it is the protection of the kingdom.

The meaning is "of those who perform [these acts]. By means of protecting the kingdom, by promoting the worship of Śiva in many Śiva-sanctuaries and in the homes of Śiva-devotees, great merit is obtained.
This refers to those who are devoted to the Śiva-scriptures (*śiva-śāstra*), being intent upon their exposition and their study.
Indeed, by explaining the Śiva scriptures and by correctly promoting the worship of Śiva in the world,
great merit is obtained; and through their study, one subsequently obtains great merit by worshipping personally for a long time in accordance with the rules.
The ritual procedure for the worship of Kapilā.
Having thus completed the worship of Śiva, one should perform the worship of Kapilā: "Salutation to Kapilā,
who embodies the five lineages (gotras) and is known by the names Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanas," and having honored her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

"O daughter of Surabhi, Mother of the World, Bestower of nectar upon the gods! Accept this morsel, O Giver of boons, and grant me my desired object. Having thus offered the morsel, you were saluted by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Atri. "O Kapilā, take away the sin and whatever evil deed has been committed by me."

Having made this prayer, one should recite: "Cows are always before me; cows are indeed behind me; cows are also in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows. A man who is self-controlled and pure should recite this mantra at the three junctions of the day. Liberated from all sins, he attains the world of Śiva.
The vision of the ālaya for the sake of others.

Then, staying near the temple of Parā, at the conclusion of the worship, one should go to the temple of Śiva and perform service there as well. The procedure for this is as follows: having gone near the temple, one should stand outside the gateway of the *gopura*, or outside the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*), or [before] the gross form of the *liṅga*.

One should perform a salutation to the temple (*vimāna*). Then, having performed salutations to the auspicious emblem (*bhadraliṅga*), the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*), the flagstaff (*dhvajastambha*), and the bull (*vṛṣabha*) as well, [one should pray]: "O Blessed One, grant permission for entry within, for the vision of Śiva, for the worship of Śiva, and for the attainment of the fruit of this [rite]."

Having prayed to the bull, saying, "O Bull, may this person prostrate at your lotus-feet be pleased with me," one should perform an eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma) to Śiva at the front of the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha).
One should not prostrate while covering the body with a garment. [One should prostrate] in front of, behind, or on the left side of Śiva.

One should not prostrate within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). One should prostrate on the left side of the *liṅga* when it faces west or faces north. Having prostrated, one should scatter a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) before the deity.
Thereafter, one should perform circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*). Circumambulation within the inner sanctum is for the worshipper alone.
Circumambulation within the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala) is for those who have been initiated alone; within the inner enclosure (antarhāra) and the other enclosures, it is for everyone.
Therein, circumambulation in the inner enclosure yields one-fold merit; in the middle enclosure, three-fold;
in the boundary (maryādā), four-fold; and in the great boundary (mahāmaryādā), five-fold.

The field is sixfold in its excellence. Thus, in a location appropriate to the strength, time, and authority [of the practitioner], one should perform twenty-one, fifteen, seven, five, or three circumambulations;
or, if there is absolutely no opportunity, one may perform a single circumambulation. Thus.

While performing circumambulation, one must not cross the *somasūtra* as conceived within the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) and the inner maṇḍala. To avoid such transgression, within the sanctum, one should proceed strictly keeping the *somasūtra* and other boundaries to one's left and right.

Then, outside that, within the mandala itself, one should proceed clockwise and counter-clockwise. It was previously stated that this should be done starting from Indra or from the *somasūtra*. At twilight, however, one should draw [the figures] starting from Vṛṣa up to Caṇḍanātha;
[specifically], the bull and the *somasūtra*, then again the bull and Caṇḍanātha on the sides of the region of the stalk (*nāla*).

One should proceed again toward Caṇḍa and likewise toward Vṛṣapṛṣṭhaka; thus, moving to the left and to the right is here called "pradakṣiṇa. The four stations of the god Vṛṣa are declared to begin and end [the circuit]; it is joined with the three stations of Caṇḍa and consists of two stations.

The *somasūtra* should be constructed according to the method described. The *somasūtra* extends from the exterior of the temple (*prāsāda*) to the region of the stalk (*nāla*), measuring either the width of the temple or half that measure.
There is a fault in overstepping it; however, there is no fault in overstepping it on the outside of the cord. Even within its interior, [there is no fault].

In a narrow space, one should cross over [the Soma-line] after concealing it with grass and so forth; for there is the scriptural injunction: "Having again concealed it with grass, wood, leaves, stones, clods of earth, and the like, one should cross over the Soma-line. In certain cases, however, there is a prohibition against the *apasavya* (leftward) manner.

It is seen [in scripture]: "Wherever there are two Soma-lines (somasūtra), there is a temple of Viṣṇu; one should not perform the circumambulation counter-clockwise (apasavya), but should indeed perform it clockwise (pradakṣiṇa). Then, having paid homage to the door-keeper and Nandikeśvara, and having entered within with their permission, [one should worship] Vighnarāja.

Having offered handfuls of flowers while striking the head [in salutation] and having prostrated, one should approach the pavilion; then, having bowed to the God of gods and joined the palms (añjali) at the head or the heart,
one should [worship] according to one's qualification with Vedic, Āgamic, Paurāṇika, worldly, Drāviḍa, and other hymns.
One should offer praise. Therein, the service for the preceptor alone consists of entering the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*);
for the other Brahmins, of entering the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*);
for the Kṣatriyas, of standing at the entrance of the half-pavilion; and for the Vaiśyas—

On the head of the bull for Śūdras; on the back of the bull for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Having drawn a square mandala with cow dung on both the head and the back of the bull, a handful of flowers should be offered right there. Thus.

One should also perform prostrations preceded by offerings of flowers to the dancing forms and others. Thus, immediately after these prostrations, one should bow to Caṇḍeśvara. In this manner, following the salutations from the pedestal (pīṭha) up to Caṇḍa, within the temple—

In order to wash away committed offenses, one should recite the root mantra of the Lord as much as possible in the presence of the Lord; then, without turning one's back upon the Lord, one may depart. Furthermore, the offenses include mounting a vehicle within the precincts of the temple of Śiva.
Walking with shoes on, crossing the shadow of a temple gate or an image, touching or stepping over ritual offerings (nirmālya),
walking through the middle of the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) of Śiva, touching a woman, looking at her with passion, and idle laughter, singing, or speaking [in such a manner].
These include prostrations with the upper garment on, circumambulations, salutations with one hand, salutations from the left side, and salutations at improper times.
Having asked for forgiveness for any such faults that may have occurred among these, which ought to be avoided, one should depart. Thus [one attains] Śiva.
Service consists of performing service through material objects ranging from village ornaments to leaves and flowers,
or through physical activities such as sweeping,
or even through mere verbal expressions that culminate in assisting the temple.
One should indeed perform this service daily; however, if one is unable to serve every day, one may serve on the eighth day and other such occasions.

By serving on the eighth day, sins committed over eight days are destroyed; by serving on a festival day (*parvan*), sins of a fortnight (*pakṣa*); by serving at the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), sins of a month; and by serving during the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*), sins acquired through the three modes of action (*trividhakaraṇa*) are destroyed.

There is the destruction even of the most grievous sins. Through service during the great festivals of the equinoxes, solstices, eclipses, and so forth, one attains the state of Śiva. Then, having returned home, one should listen to or practice the Siddhānta scriptures in small measure as occasion permits.
One should perform [the rite] while avoiding proximity to those who have been initiated alongside one who has not yet been initiated. (p.

111) "O fair-faced one, this knowledge must not be disclosed to those who are not devotees; it must be guarded with effort, just as wealth is guarded from thieves"—because of this statement. Now, at the time of midday:
One should worship with elaboration, or with contraction, or even with merely the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*).

If, due to some deficiency, one does not obtain the opportunity to worship the *liṅga* one has accepted, one may perform the mere eight flowers in brief upon a *liṅga* worshipped by another who follows the same practice. [The] *praṇava*...
The *mātṛkā*, *māyā*, *vyomavyāpī*, the six-syllabled mantra, the *prāsāda*, and the *aghora* mantra—

these seven are considered common [to all]. Having thus worshipped Śiva in any manner whatsoever, when desiring to eat at the proper time, one should set aside the best portion from all the cooked food and offer half of it to Śiva.
Having offered half [of the portion], one should perform the Vedic and Śaiva fire-oblations (homa) according to one's authority;
the Vedic is the Vaiśvadeva-homa, and the Śaiva is the Cullī-homa.
The Cullī-homa.

This is its sequence: (the word "buddhim" means) having purified the hearth by means of inspection and other rites, one unifies the fire there with the *bindu* at the locations of the navel and the heart through the *pūraka* and *kumbhaka* breath-retentions, [thus uniting] the triad of fires— the elemental, the lunar (*baindava*), and the digestive (*jāṭhara*).

Having expelled [the breath] with the *recaka* and cast it into the fire on the hearth by means of the *piṅgalā*, immediately thereafter: *namaḥ agnaye*; *namaḥ somāya*; *namaḥ sūryāya*; *namaḥ bṛhaspataye*; *namaḥ prajāpataye*;
*namaḥ sarvebhyo devebhyaḥ*; *namaḥ sarvebhyo viśvebhyaḥ*; *agnaye*.

"Salutation to Sviṣṭakṛt. Having thus worshipped Agni and the other deities, beginning with Āgneya and ending with Pūrva, in the fire, and having offered oblations with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, one should dismiss them.
Eating the remains of offerings.

Then, one should eat either that which has been offered [to the deity] or the remains thereof. Many scriptural statements regarding the fruits of consuming what is offered to Śiva are heard: "The remains of my food, the water from my feet, and the flower or petal—these grant, respectively, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa."

Prohibitory statements regarding that [offering] are also heard, such as: "One should never wear Śambhu’s *nirmālya*, nor should one eat it," and so forth. These are regulated according to whether one possesses the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva or is devoid of it. The *nirmālya* is stainless, pure, and because of its stainlessness, it is beyond reproach. (p. 112)
Therefore, the remains of offerings (nirmālya) should not be consumed by those who are impure or whose nature is inauspicious.

Some maintain that this is because of a statement in the *Śivapurāṇa*: "One who is addicted to the fickleness of the tongue, devoid of the purificatory rites of Śiva, and who eats the remains of offerings (nirmālya) to Śiva, shall go to the Raurava hell.
Furthermore, according to the *Kāmika* and other Siddhāntatantras, these rules of conduct (*samayācāra*) are prescribed specifically for those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*).

Prohibitory injunctions such as "one should not consume the *nirmālya*" and "one should not revile the food of Śiva’s devotees," as well as prescriptions for expiation such as "if one consumes *nirmālya* through negligence, one should mutter the Aghora mantra ten thousand times," are heard in the scriptures. Therefore, these [prohibitions] are to be respected and followed.
"Whatever other drinks there may be, those indeed should be given, O Śambhu; one should consume them out of the state of being a servant"—

such statements from the Purāṇas indicate that the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Śiva is to be accepted only by those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*) through the Śiva-saṃskāra prescribed in the Vedic, Paurāṇika, Pāśupata, and other traditions, and not by others.
Some say [this applies] to those initiated by the Siddhāntatantras such as the Kāmika. In the Kāmika itself:

"An impure self, being unclean due to greed, who eats what has been consumed by me—the supreme purifier—meets with destruction, just like a twice-born man who consumes [forbidden] meat. [This applies even to] those in the world who wear my liṅga..."

This is because of such statements as: "Those who are teachers, devoted to Me, and have Me as their sole refuge—they alone are worthy, and not other living beings," and from the Vātula-āgama and other scriptures: "Even a thousand fasts and a hundred *prājāpatya* penances are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of one who has attained the grace of Śiva."
Even for those who have been initiated into the Siddhāntatantras, that which is offered to Śiva is indeed praiseworthy.

As for the scriptural statements regarding the prohibition of *śivanirmālya* (the remains of offerings to Śiva) and the penances for them, they refer to [other types of] divine property, substances belonging to the deity, and food offerings (*naivedya*) that have not been offered, or those cast outside after being consumed by Caṇḍa.

There are five types of objects concerning *nirmālya*. In the *Kāmika*: "The property of the deity, the substance belonging to the deity, the offering (*naivedya*) that has been presented, the substance for Caṇḍa, and *nirmālya*—thus *nirmālya* is sixfold. The property of the deity belonging to the Lord of the village and so forth, and the substance of the deity such as cloth and the like [are the first two].

The food offering prepared for him is presented as the remains of the deity's meal; that which is given is the "Caṇḍa-substance," and the *nirmālya* is cast outside. Thus, immediately after the enumeration of the sixfold nature of the *nirmālya* and the proclamation of the fault in consuming it, the instruction on its expiation follows.
This is because the two and a half verses beginning with "The impure person, out of greed... have been cited for the purpose of granting permission to accept the *nirmālya* known as *nivedita*.
And thus, in the Siddhāntatantras, there are statements prohibiting [the consumption of] what has been offered to Śiva (*śivanivedita*). (p. 113)

Others say that these [rules] refer to those who have not received the Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*). In the *Suprabheda*: "The remains of Sadāśiva's offerings (*nirmālya*) are not food for humans; one should cast them into water for beasts and elephants, or else burn them with fire or bury them in the ground."
"A wise man should have it buried"— by this statement, the inedibility of the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Sadāśiva is established as being common to all human beings;
furthermore, since its disposal (*pratipatti*) is described as being only among [the elements] such as the earth, fire, cows, and elephants, [it follows that] the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva...

Even for those who have been initiated, [the food] is indeed not to be eaten. As for the scriptural statements that "for them, the *nirmālya* of Śiva is praiseworthy," these refer to the *nirmālya* of the *sakala* (manifest) forms. This is because, regarding all images, it is stated that "Caṇḍa shall have no authority," thereby prohibiting Caṇḍa’s jurisdiction over all *sakala* forms.

Because of the description of the authorization for all the food offerings (*naivedya*), stating that "the food offering of all the [deities] belonging to Kārttikeya shall become the meal for everyone," even that must be consumed only by those initiated into Śiva and his attendants. This is because the *Suprabheda* states, following the passage beginning with "the remains of Sadāśiva’s [offering],"...

Others, however, maintain that this is because it has been stated: "The remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) belonging to all [deities] are food for the attendants; even that would cause fault if consumed by other people. Furthermore, regarding the remains of offerings of Sadāśiva, the prohibition applies only to those offered at Śiva-liṅgas installed by humans and the like, but not to those from mobile liṅgas (*caraliṅga*) and so forth.

And because there is an absence of authority for Caṇḍa over them, [it is said]: "In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile [liṅga], a metal [liṅga], a jewel-liṅga, a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) one, and in all images, Caṇḍa does not have authority. In liṅgas that are self-manifested, Bāṇa-made, made of jewels, made of gold, or established by a Siddha, Caṇḍa shall have authority. Thus it is stated.

Some say it is because of a scriptural statement. Regarding the statement that "there is no authority for Caṇḍa over moving liṅgas and so forth," such statements concern the Vedic, Paurāṇika, Vāma, and Dakṣiṇa Tantras and the like, but they do not concern the Siddhāntas such as the Kāmika. [This applies to] those made of stable or mobile materials, as well as gems, clay, wood, and stone.

And Caṇḍa, the Restrainer, resides in an arrow made of variegated iron; according to the Siddhānta, he is not in other Tantras, neither in the Left nor in the Right. [He is present] in unmanifest and manifest lingas, in the mandala, on the sacrificial ground, in fire, in mobile and immobile forms, as well as in gems, in those variegated with jewels, and in lingas produced from scent and food.

Furthermore, because specific rules are observed in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures— such as the injunction that the worship of Caṇḍa must be performed upon a liṅga made of clay, ash, wood, or flowers—

the distinction between the rules regarding the disposal of offerings (*nirmālya*) and their prohibition is not established on the basis of whether the object is mobile (*cara*) or immobile (*sthira*). Rather, [it is established otherwise].

Some maintain that it is because [these items] are objects of a specific kind of *nirmālya*. According to the statement: "Betel, ashes, oil, scented flowers, cakes, fruits, and other substances fit for consumption are not called *nirmālya*," so say some. In the *Kāmika*: "And that which is offered to one's own chosen *liṅga* is like the *caru* offering."

There is a doubt [regarding this]. Based on the statement concerning the example of the *caru* offering—namely, "one should cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be given to brothers, sons, and sisters"—it is argued that even if a crystal or a *bāṇaliṅga* has been installed, or even if it is merely a *caru*, one should not consider the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) offered to it as ordinary *nirmālya*. This applies to children... [and so forth].

Furthermore, because it is stated that "the food of young women increases strength," which establishes its status as *anirmālya* (not leftover from worship), even food offered at mobile *liṅgas* (*caraliṅga*) and the like is indeed fit to be eaten. However, it must not be eaten by the worshipper himself, due to specific scriptural injunctions such as, "The *naivedya* [is for] brothers and sons," and so forth. This applies to all items except for betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) and similar things.
Some, however, maintain that the statement regarding "being graspable" refers specifically to the *liṅga* installed by humans and others.
Having prepared an offering for Śiva, he would say, "This remnant is offered to me," and would eat it daily with devotion; such a person is like unto me.

In the *Kāmika* it is stated that "the sacrificial food (*caru*) substance should likewise be so [prepared]," and because it is established that even the one who performs the offering may eat its remains, the food offered to Śiva is indeed fit to be eaten by the worshipper as well.
As for those statements prohibiting the eating of what has been offered: [The text continues with the prohibitions.]
Some also maintain that these [offerings] should be applied as objects presented to the Saṃhāra-Rudras and others;

for in the divine Āgamas, it is frequently heard that the prohibition of what has been offered applies specifically at the conclusion of the description of the worship of Sadāśiva’s form, following the invocation of Paramaśiva.

It is indeed proper that every kind of Śiva-nirmālya, variegated by thousands of injunctions and prohibitions, should be avoided; for it is heard that there is great fault and it is heard that there is great fruit. Regarding these two, the fruit must be abandoned, according to the saying: "The fault is indeed more powerful."

It should not be argued that a prohibition regarding eating what has not been offered is heard in the *Nacakāmika*, which states: "One should never eat leaves, flowers, fruit, water, food, water for the feet, or medicine without having first offered them to the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva. This is because [the rule applies] even to the consumption of such items when they have not been offered.

Because it is possible for that [text] to be intent upon enjoining the eating of what remains after [offering], just as there is a prohibition against eating a meal devoid of hospitality toward guests,
[as stated]: "The wise man, having given food, medicine, water, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth to Śiva, should eat the remainder thereof."

Because it is established in the same way in the Siddhāntaśekhara, others explain it thus. In this manner, nine positions have arisen upon investigating the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions regarding *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings).
[This applies] only to those who possess initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the form of the Śiva-saṃskāra.
The first position is that permission regarding the *nirmālya* of Śiva is granted to others, while its prohibition applies to them; however,

even among those who possess the Śaiva consecration (*saṃskāra*), permission for it is granted only to those who have received Vedic initiation (*vaidikadīkṣā*), such as those belonging to the *atyāśrama* stage and so forth,
but not to those who have received initiation according to the *siddhāntatantras* such as the *Kāmika*.

The second position is that [the prohibition] is based on the observation of injunctions regarding the penance for its prohibition and for consuming it. The third position is that the instruction regarding the prohibition and the penance applies only to the five kinds of *nirmālya* (remnants) other than what has been offered (*nivedita*), whereas even for them, the *nivedita* portion is indeed to be accepted.

The fourth position: Even though it has been stated [that offerings] made to the middle [of the linga] are prohibited, since there is a prohibition against what is offered to the Śivaliṅga, only that which is offered to the *sakala* (the whole) liṅga is to be accepted. It is not the case that everything offered to the Śivaliṅga is forbidden;
rather, it is specifically that which is offered to a fixed (*sthira*) liṅga installed by humans and others that is prohibited.

The fifth position is that what has been offered by means of mobile *liṅgas* and so forth should not be accepted, because there is no authority for Caṇḍa in that regard. [This view holds that] there is no definitive rule regarding the prohibitions and permissions concerning what has been offered found in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, as these apply specifically to immobile and mobile [objects], within the established path (*siddhāntamārga*) of the *Kāmika* and other tantras.

Furthermore, because Caṇḍa is present even in the worship of the chariot and other such rites, there is a restriction regarding food and the like, whereas there is permission regarding fruits, rice-cakes, betel, and so forth; this is the settled rule. This is the sixth position, based on the existence of specific statements concerning those other items.
The seventh position is that even food and other offerings presented at a *caraliṅga* and similar shrines are indeed to be accepted;

however, they must be given to one’s brothers and others, and not consumed by the officiating priest (*pūjaka*). The eighth position is that what is offered to Śiva may be consumed even by the officiating priest, provided it is done with the intention of offering it back to Śiva (*śivārpaṇabuddhi*).

The ninth position is as follows: since between a statement regarding the results [of an action] and a prohibitory statement, the prohibitory statement is more authoritative, it is proper to avoid all *śivanirmālya* (remnants offered to Śiva). This ninth position, however, is utterly untenable; for in the acceptance of *śivanirmālya*...

For this would entail the invalidity of the many words of divine scriptures, Purāṇas, and so forth, which establish great fruits; indeed, not even a single syllable among the words of the Ṛṣis can tolerate invalidity, much less so in the case of the words of Śiva.

The ringing proclamation of all the divine scriptures is that even attempting to establish the authority of those [texts] by treating them as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) leads to great transgression. Furthermore, the statement regarding "the hearing of a great fault" and so forth applies to cases where there is scope for the authority of both injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*niṣedha*) elsewhere. In such instances, between those two...
This refers to the principle that when two [injunctions] meet in a certain instance, the prohibition is more powerful.

For example, the authority of the statement praising the consumption of *āmalaka* on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) finds its scope on a *dvādaśī* that is not conjoined with Sunday; whereas the authority of the statement prohibiting it on Sunday applies when there is such a conjunction.

When Sunday is devoid of conjunction with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), there is scope for its observance; however, when there is a conjunction of Sunday and the twelfth lunar day, two prohibitory statements apply. In such a case, the prohibitory statement is more authoritative than the statements regarding the fruits [of the rite]. This establishes that the statements concerning the fruits are entirely lacking in authority.

However, those who rely on authoritative means of knowledge do not regard mere strength [of argument] as decisive; therefore, it is more appropriate to demonstrate the specific application of the scope for injunctions and prohibitions.

We shall demonstrate that [practice] by means of the path previously shown, in accordance with all scriptures and in a manner pleasing to all Śaivas. The meal for Śaivas is of three kinds: at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva, it is like the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) performed in the external sacrificial pit (*bāhyakuṇḍa*).

Immediately following that, there is one [rite] consisting of the thought: "After the fire-ritual (agnikārya) for Śiva comes my own meal. At the time of the food offering (naivedya), the act of offering consists merely of the commencement of presenting to Śiva the substances being offered by way of surrendering their form; however, the meal for oneself is for the sake of Śiva.

The second [stage] consists of the fulfillment of the offering through the contemplation that it is characterized by the surrender of one's own taste. At the very moment of the first offering, the sacrificial food (naivedya) is consumed by Śiva along with one's own relish in a subtle form— just like the sacrificial oblation (havis) in a ritual for another— thereby becoming the self-nourishment of the servant of Śiva.

The third [practice] consists of the contemplation that [the ritual] is of the nature of accepting the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) of that [offering]. Regarding this, the first [of these three] is explained in detail in the *Suprabheda*, in the chapter on the fire-ritual (*agnikārya-paṭala*):
"At the conclusion of the fire-ritual, one should perform the oblation into the fire of the vital breath (*prāṇāgni-homa*). Beside that, in the fire-chamber..."

The place for eating is now described: the supreme sacrifice to the fires of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra) should be performed even at home. Having especially made that place pure by smearing it with cow dung.
Having adorned it with flour-dust, provided with a canopy and lamps, one should take up this vessel— whether made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal, or even a plantain leaf—
and having purified it as is appropriate, one should place all [the ingredients] into the vessel.

One should worship Śiva, who resides within one’s own self. This very self is the sacrificer; the intellect is known as his wife. The hair on the head and body are the *darbha* grasses; the tongue and other organs are the sacrificial vessels. One should worship him well within the fire situated inside, upon the altar of the lotus of the heart.

Having spread *darbha* grass from the hair of the body, having uttered the *praṇava* conjoined with Śiva, and having sprinkled [the water] around, one should then sprinkle it upward with the mantra of Śiva. Having recited the Śiva-mantra over the water,
and having recited the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga*) in sequence, one should meditate upon Śiva and drink the water, saying "To Śiva."
Furthermore, with the heart-mantra, one should offer oblations to Śiva using the five Brahma-mantras beginning with the Īśāna-mantra;
taking the food slowly with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.

Having recited "That which is immortal," and so forth, one should especially not drink water; rather, one should offer five oblations with the five *prāṇa* mantras. After touching the vessel, the practitioner should eat, and having sipped water (*ācamya*), [he should proceed].

Standing facing the sun according to the prescribed rite, he should then touch his abdomen with the *Śiva-mantra* using his left hand. Recalling Śiva and the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, he should cause water to flow from his right thumb onto the big toe of his right foot.
While reciting [the mantra], this handful of water should be taken from the base of one's own feet.

"This is declared to be the perpetual Prāṇāgnihotra; this is proclaimed as the fire-rite (agnikārya). Listen now to the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). This meal must be performed with food that has not been offered [to the deity]. For that purpose, from the food intended for the worship of another, one portion should be set aside as the offering.
"One part may be offered as a *homa*;

one part is for the *bali* offering, and the remainder is for the teacher's meal"—this is shown by the words of the *Āgamas*. In a worship performed for one's own sake, having set aside half of the cooked food, one should offer half of that to Śambhu; with the other half, [one offers] into the fire.

"One should perform the oblation; its various rules are now declared," and so forth, as shown by the scriptural statements in the section on the *cullīhoma* (stove-oblation). Furthermore, the second meal is shown in the *Vātulottara*: "Having offered the form of the substance, one should also offer the relish to Śiva."
If the food offering is devoid of the dedication of both [merit and enjoyment], it shall be fruitless.

The offering of *naivedya* is said to conclude with the enjoyment of that specific grace (*prasāda*). For it is stated that if the gift of grace is lacking, even the *naivedya* is fruitless, and so forth. This [offering] must be performed with food for which the act of offering has begun but not yet been completed. At the time of the *naivedya* service, [it should be done] in front of the Deity.
The act of offering (*nivedana*) begins at that time with the placing of the food as an offering upon it; this continues until the transfer of its flavor (*ruci*).
Thus, that very food is "that whose act of offering has been begun but not yet completed. And that [act] is performed with reference to the gods, ancestors, and so forth.

The worshipper, with the same intent as when offering it, should consume that which was offered as if it were already submerged [in the fire], with the thought of offering it to Śiva; that is the third meal. Among those in the world who bear my liṅga, who are devoted to me as their teacher, and who have me alone as their refuge—it is fit for them, and not for other beings.
"O Śambhu, whatever is to be tasted, chewed, drunk, or otherwise offered—

these indeed should be consumed out of the state of being a servant. Only by those who have entered the path of servitude, who abide in the Śaiva Pāśupata [tradition], and who are seekers of liberation, should these things be drunk, eaten, and smelled."
This practice is well-known in the *Kāmikāgama* and other scriptures: the offering must be made with that which has already been presented as an oblation (*nivedita*).

At the time of the ritual service of the food offering (*naivedya-upacāra*), those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) should understand that whatever was placed before the Deity has at that very moment been consumed by Śiva along with His relish (*ruci*) in a subtle form.

It is said that what has been offered is declared as follows: just as a Śūdra who has entered into the service of a Brāhmaṇa may eat the remnants of his food for the sake of service, so too one who has entered into the service of Śiva should eat that very remnant of Śiva (śivocchiṣṭa). And thus, those general prohibitory statements regarding the remains of Śiva’s offerings (śivanirmālya) [apply only to others].

The [prohibitions] concerning mere humans who are of the nature of bound souls (*paśu*) and devoid of the realization of being Śiva’s servants have one scope; whereas those prohibitory statements concerning the initiated who possess the realization of being Śiva’s servants have as their scope the five kinds of *nirmālya* other than that which has been offered. Thus, there are two distinct rules.
This has been shown by the ancients themselves. Herein, the second arrangement—that among the six kinds of *nirmālya*, only one is fit for consumption—is well-known from the scriptures (*āgama*).
The first arrangement is clearly elaborated in the *Śivapurāṇa*; for it says therein: "My *naivedya* is unworthy [of consumption]..."
"The water from the feet is the flower and the leaf"—thus some great sages have declared according to the Lord.

To the question of Jaimini, "O Lord, they speak thus; please tell me what is the truth," [the Lord replied]: "In that regard, O Jaimini, the subject matter of the words of the God of gods concerns those who have been cursed by Vīrabhadra, who are averse to devotion to Śiva, and who [place their faith] in other gods instead of Śambhu."

"Those who are devotees but not initiated, and those who perform pure rites for Śambhu but possess equanimity toward others—for them, that fourfold grace of the Lord is unattainable. Such is the statement of Vyāsa observed. There are also other [statements] regarding those who are uninitiated and non-devotees.

Regarding the point that the *nirmālya* of Śiva is unfit [for consumption], the statements well-known in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures have been cited previously. Now, [it may be argued]: "The *nirmālya* of Śiva removes all sins, cures all diseases, bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, and is equal to bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
It is proclaimed by those who know the Śiva scriptures that this is the sole means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation;

yet it is also said that it must not be eaten nor touched by those devoid of devotion and initiation. How is this consistent? For [the scripture] is endowed with the power to remove all sins and so forth.

For this yoga must indeed become common to all, just like the performance of universal expiatory rites (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) or the chanting of Śiva’s names; how then could it be something to be avoided by some? Therefore, it is only on the grounds that "Śiva’s *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is inferior" that it might be avoided by some.

Why should it not be the case that "it was"? Haradattācārya has also stated, in the same manner, regarding both excellence and deficiency: "Whether one avoids [an action] through excellence or through deficiency, we do not know what latent impression (vāsanā) exists for whose sake."

The sages reject with equal disdain the desirable food of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice and of one who has fallen from his caste. How is it that the touch of a Caṇḍāla, a Caṇḍila, a funeral pyre, a liquor-seller, or of cows, Brahmins, fire, an initiate, or a woman, becomes forbidden through mere mental conception?

Or rather, when touched, purification is effected by reciting the stories of Śiva. They say that even for one who has been initiated, food [touched by] fire is to be avoided; however, that which has been purchased from a king is indeed fit to be eaten. A conch-shell bone is purifying, whereas the bone of humans is impure. Such being the case, here is the authoritative statement: *varjyānnam āhur api dīkṣitam agnikalpam bhojyānnameva kṛtarājaparikrayam tam | śaṅkhāsthi pāvanam apāvanam asthi nṛṇām ittham sthite vacanam atra ||* They say that even for one who has been initiated, food [touched by] fire is to be avoided; however, that which has been purchased from a king is indeed fit to be eaten. A conch-shell bone is purifying, whereas the bone of humans is impure. Such being the case, here is the authoritative statement.
