There is no room for dispute here; for even in those Purāṇas and Āgamas where a prohibition against certain things is made, it is established therein that [the Lord] possesses such qualities. Indeed, statements are heard in the Purāṇas and Āgamas: "The water from His feet and the floral remains (nirmālya) should be worn with devotion."

Through diligent effort, even sins born of mind, speech, and body do not touch him. That man who, praised as pure, eats [this] with devotion—being a Brahmin of purified soul—his sin is swiftly destroyed. Those who have taken refuge here should always wear my grace-water and flowers.

Especially by the sick and those who have been smeared with poison, whatever is offered with effort at one's own chosen *liṅga* is like *caru* (sacrificial rice); of this there is no doubt. O Nārada, one obtains the fruit of a thousand *Rājasūya* sacrifices. [There are] the great holy site of Pṛthūdaka, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā river, and the Narmadā.

O Sage, the Sarayū, the Viprā, and likewise the river Godāvarī are always present in the bathing water of Śambhu; indeed, that bathing water of Śambhu, containing all sacred fords (tīrthas), is worthy of being resorted to.

"One who practices yoga should give ten thousand [cows] to a Śrotriya who maintains the sacred fires; by bathing in the water from my feet, one obtains that same fruit," and so forth. And in the medical treatises (Vaidyaśāstra): "By consuming the water of the floral offerings (nirmālya) of the trident-bearing God of gods, one is liberated from consumption, leprosy, fever, and asthma."

"Even by sins," it is said. In the *Rāmāyaṇa* as well: "There, the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the gandharvas, and those dwelling upon the surface of the earth touched the water fallen from Your body, [considering it] pure. In the *Bhāgavata* also: "Or rather, do others besides You not know that what is called Śiva is actually inauspicious?"

"Brahmā and the other gods, with their matted hair disheveled in the cremation ground, bear upon their heads that which was cast from his feet by Śiva— namely, those flowers, ashes, and human skulls in which the Piśācas dwell. Thus, even regarding the touch of the *nirmālya* (remnants) of Śiva, who is supremely purifying...

The prohibition for some regarding the touching of the Śivaliṅga is indeed due to their lack of qualification, just like the prohibition [against certain others]. For instance, even though the Śivaliṅga was previously merely a specific worldly stone, through the consecratory rite (pratiṣṭhā-saṃskāra) [it becomes sacred].
Having become composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), its impure form—which was a transformation of *māyā*—has been cast aside;

therefore, immediately thereafter, it became untouchable for those who have not received initiation. In the same way, even the *nirmālya* (the remains of offerings), having been transformed by the multitude of purificatory rites such as inspection and so forth, likewise became [untouchable] immediately thereafter by Śiva.

Because it was fit for their own enjoyment, it was consumed by Ugra; thus, having become exceedingly pure, it became untouchable for them. With this intention, it is stated in the *Vātulottara*: "Just as there is no prior conceptualization regarding well-established Liṅgas, so too it is with the grace of Śiva."

"One should recollect the former name. Thus, such remains of the offerings to Śiva (*śivanirmālya*) are to be touched like the Śiva-liṅga and consumed with knowledge only by those devotees of Śiva whose impurities have been shaken off through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and whose bonds (*pāśa*) have been severed; for they indeed—

The devotees of Śiva, through initiation into Śiva and by means of the daily practice of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the placement of the staff and the tonsure (daṇḍamuṇḍa-kalānyāsa), have attained a non-material form like that of the Śiva-linga and the sacred offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva.

"A wise person does not despise those who bear my form, even if they be commoners, because they possess the same characteristics as Rudra, such as hands, feet, and so forth"—according to this statement from the *Vāyusaṃhitā*.
As for the question: "If [the mantra] possesses qualities such as the power to remove all sins, why is it not like a universal atonement (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)?"...

The doubt that [the merit] has not become common to all is also refuted by this, because it has been stated that others lack the qualification for even touching the extremely pure *nirmālya* of Śiva. For the Vedic hymns such as the *Aghamarṣaṇa* do not remove great sins like the killing of a Brahmin; [this power belongs only to the *nirmālya*].
Even for those outside the three *varṇas* who lack the qualification to hear the Vedas, this [work] is common;
yet, by that fact, there is no diminution of the Vedic hymn (*sūkta*), but rather its very exaltation.
It is with this very intention that the word of the Lord is found in the Purāṇas.

"One whose self is impure and who is unclean, by eating out of greed what has been eaten by me—which is supremely purifying—meets with destruction, just as a Śūdra does through the study [of the Vedas]. As for the objection: "Why is it that the *nirmālya* (remains) of Śiva, though exceedingly pure like the name of Śiva, is not common to all?"

Regarding the doubt as to how it was born, Drumila says: By the command of Śiva, even the name of Śiva—which is exceedingly pure and non-material—has become common to all. The five-syllabled Vedic mantra, which is a jewel for living beings, is likewise composed of that [name]. Thus, it is said in the Vāyusaṃhitā regarding the defiled Kali age:
In this time that is difficult to conquer and hard to transcend, when the world is shrouded by the greatest of demerit and turned away from dharma.

When the conduct of the virtuous has declined, when confusion has arisen, when all authority is in doubt or has been overturned, and when the instructions of the guru have been disregarded through the transgression of teacher and disciple—by what means, O Maheśvara, are your devotees liberated? Thus was the question of Ambikā; and this was the word of Śiva:
By taking refuge in my supreme, heart-pleasing five-syllabled Vidyā,
people born in the Kali age whose souls are purified by devotion are liberated from the defects born of mind, speech, and body—
defects that are beyond the scope of description or remembrance— and even from those who are corrupted, ungrateful, and merciless.

Even for those of wicked nature, who are bound and crooked-minded, if their souls are inclined toward me, my five-syllabled Vidyā shall carry them across the fear of saṃsāra. O Goddess, this was repeatedly promised by me alone upon the surface of the earth: even one who has fallen, if he is my devotee, shall be liberated.
"By means of this knowledge... Furthermore: "If a mortal has not fallen in any way, he may become fit for ritual action;

however, whatever rite is performed by one unfit for ritual action leads indeed to hell. Therefore, how could one who has fallen be liberated by this knowledge?"—in response to Ambikā’s question, Śiva spoke these words: "This which you have said is true."

"Even though it has been declared thus, listen, O beautiful one! Considering this a secret, I have previously concealed it. If a mortal fallen into his own karma should worship [the deity] out of delusion—without my five-syllabled mantra—he shall become a denizen of hell; of this there is no doubt. Thus [it was said].

It is also designated therein as "established by command" (*ājñāsiddha*) precisely because it has been brought about for the common benefit of all by the command of Śiva. Regarding this, it is said: "This statement consists of few syllables yet is rich in meaning; it is the essence of the Vedas, bestowing liberation; it is established by command, free from doubt, and its nature is Śiva."
Therefore, the greatness of the name of Śiva is inconceivable;
thus, it is entirely appropriate that it is common even to outcastes such as Caṇḍālas. Enough with this elaboration.
Let us return to the subject at hand.
As for the statement that the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Sadāśiva is not to be consumed by humans, that refers specifically to the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva that has been offered to Caṇḍa.

In the *Kāmika*: "Having brought the *nirmālya*, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa; because it attains a state of purity (*nirmalatā*), it is proclaimed as *nirmālya*. Having given the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) to Caṇḍa, one should then dismiss the *nirmālya* by casting it into deep water, into fire, or by offering it to cows."
Because the rule for disposal in water and so forth is prescribed immediately after the offering to Caṇḍa; as it is said in that very [text]:

"The food of Caṇḍa is inviolable and must be avoided with great effort," and "The property of the deity or the food of Caṇḍa is not to be used for the enjoyment of others. Thus, regarding the substance belonging to Caṇḍa...

This is because, by establishing that [the offering] is entirely unfit for consumption, it follows that only that specific portion requires such treatment regarding water and other substances. Now, if this were the case, it would follow that every *śivaliṅga-nirmālya*— including things to be licked, sucked, or consumed as food and drink— is indeed unfit for consumption.

Some maintain that because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra for the offering to Caṇḍa— "Betel, garlands, and ointments— all these offerings (*nirmālya*) are given to you by the command of Śiva"— it is understood that all of Śiva’s *nirmālya* must be offered to Caṇḍa. This is not so.

In the *Kāmika*: "During the worship for the sake of others, one should worship Caṇḍa in the northeast with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order. One should offer to him all the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) that have been prepared.
Thus, [it is taught] that all the *nirmālya* belongs to Caṇḍeśa.
Having stated the position that [the deity] should be transferred, some say: "The Liṅga is situated on the top;
others say it is situated on the pedestal (piṇḍikā); or, situated on the pedestal in the northeast, one should lead it outside to the chamber of Caṇḍa."

Since it has been stated that there is even a position regarding the offering of only a single portion of the perfumes, flowers, and floral garlands, by that same logic, one may infer the acceptance of a position regarding the offering of only a single portion of the consecrated food (*niveditānna*) as well. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "The garlands, perfumes, food, drink, and so forth, which have been enjoyed by Śiva, are likewise called 'consecrated' (*nivedita*)."

It is declared to be the supreme remover of all sins. Furthermore, because it is explicitly established that among the six kinds of *nirmālya*, only the *nivedita* (offered) is to be consumed—and that this status of being edible belongs specifically to the *nivedita* substance as distinct from the *caṇḍadravya* (substance for Caṇḍa)—[it follows that this applies to worship for one's own sake]. However, in the case of worship performed for one's own benefit (*ātmārthapūjā*), [the rule is different].
There is no room for such doubt; for in the *Kāmika* [Tantra] itself, immediately after the description of the worship of Śiva,

it begins by stating "one should worship Caṇḍeśvara at the end," and subsequently prohibits the worship of Caṇḍa by stating, "Caṇḍeśa is not [required] in the case of a Liṅga made of stone, metal, or clay, nor in one that is self-manifested (*svayambhū*)."

Even in the *Ajita*, regarding worship for one's own sake, it is stated: "No worship of the gatekeeper should be performed, nor the offering to Caṇḍeśa; there is no oblation with name-mantras therein, nor indeed a daily festival"—thus, because of that prohibition. However, if [one acts] according to the statement from the *Kālottara* cited previously:

Even if the worship of Caṇḍa is performed, there is no fault. In the *Aṃśumatī*, in the chapter on the worship of Caṇḍeśa, it is said: "It is considered to be threefold: Kevala, Sahaja, and Svatantra. Kevala is declared for one's own sake (ātmārtha), while one should offer [the others] into the mandala. Sahaja is to be known as that which pertains to the limbs of Yāmala."
The form of Caṇḍa is established. If it were an independent limb of the village, the worship of Caṇḍeśa would be threefold;

thus, having introduced the threefold nature of the worship of Caṇḍeśa, [it is described] in the context of the worship of Caṇḍa at the conclusion of the sacrifice performed for one's own sake (ātmārthayajana):

Having offered ointment and a gift by means of its root mantra, one should likewise cause the food offering (naivedya) and betel to be given by that very root mantra. Having thus separately described the offering of scents, flowers, and so forth, the worship of the Kevala [form] and the worship of the Sahaja [form] have been declared.

Listen: "The wise one should install Caṇḍeśa within the region of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala) and within the range of the maṇḍala, and should worship him with the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
This is because the offering of the *nirmālya* has been prescribed specifically for the worship of Yāmāṅga-Caṇḍeśvara.
And in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*, in the section on the worship of Caṇḍa: "Having offered the food offering as prescribed by the rules, together with betel."
Furthermore, because it has been stated that one should offer what has been used by Śiva as a limb of the *yāma* [rite],
and in accordance with the subtle injunction regarding worship for one's own sake which says, "One should offer the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva to Caṇḍeśa," [the offering is made] to Caṇḍeśa.

Even in the case of offering the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering), there is no fault; for, according to the method described for worship performed for the sake of others (*parārtha-pūjā*), it is possible to offer even a single portion of it. Furthermore, in the *Smṛtinibandhanas*, it is stated: "A hundredth part of the *naivedya* should be given to Viṣvaksena, as well as the water from the feet (*pādodaka*)."
And because it is established that the hundredth part offered to Caṇḍeśvara is indeed a portion of the fierce sun (Caṇḍāṃśu) itself, as stated in "and [the offering] to the Liṅga Caṇḍeśvara. Thus,
according to the Kāmika and other scriptures, the statement in the Suprabheda that "[this is] the *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva" [is justified].
The meaning is that whatever remains as the *nirmālya* (offering residue) of Śiva which has been offered to Caṇḍeśa is not to be consumed by human beings. Alternatively, this is the intended sense:
the *nirmālya* of Śiva [is forbidden] for those who, being devoid of the state of service to Śiva, are like bound souls (*paśu*).
It is simply not to be eaten by humans. Therefore,

when a great abundance of sacrificial offerings is presented— whether in worship for the sake of others or in worship for one's own sake— the temple attendants, who are unable to consume that much food, [should do so].

In the absence of those who dwell in the temple of the worshipper, or other Śiva-bhaktas who have received Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā), the remainder left over from what was given to them should be given to any human being whatsoever; however,
it should rather be given to cows and elephants.
It is intended that [the remains] should be cast into deep water, or into fire, or buried in the ground; this is the ultimate rule.

For example, in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, when the officiating priests (ṛtvij) lack the capacity to consume the remnants of the oblation (haviḥ-śeṣa), the remaining oblation offered to the priests is given to other castes who have not yet undergone initiation (anupanīta).
It should not be given away; rather, it should be given to the invited Brahmins and others, or cast into the fire—this is the intended meaning.

This statement, "If the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are unable to consume the remnants of the oblation (haviḥ-śeṣa), they should either bestow them upon the Brahmins or cast them into the sacrificial fire," is made for this purpose.
Or, for example, just as it is stated that in the absence of a Śūdra who is a slave or one who eats the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa,
those leavings should be thrown into water or buried in the ground— meaning that in the event of extreme incapacity, one should bury them in the earth or cast them into water.
With this very intention, Haradattācārya stated:

"O Lord, they remember that even though you are a Brāhmaṇa, they consider what is offered to you among the hosts of the denizens of heaven as unfit for consumption; yet, O Sovereign, even that which is the leavings of the twice-born is distinguished when it has fallen upon the ground."

"Or it should be buried in the ground or immersed in water"— the purport of this verse is not that even when a servant who eats the leftovers is present, those leftovers must be buried in the earth or immersed in water. [This refers to] the leftover food...

Worn-out garments are to be given, because there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) that remnants of food are to be given to a Śūdra who has sought refuge and desires to serve; [as it is said]: "Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, clothing, and mats, as well as the eating of remnants and the practice of a craft."

This is also because of the Smṛti texts regarding the duties of Śūdras. Likewise, regarding the statement "the food has been offered to you," even here, one who is worthy of consuming what is offered to Śiva and has surrendered to the state of being a servant of Śiva—if such a person is not available—it must not be given to just anyone; rather, it should be disposed of by means of digging it into the ground or similar methods.

The intended meaning is that this is for the purpose of establishing that [point]. Thus, by means of this verse, the Teacher has clearly demonstrated that the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) is to be avoided by those other than servants only on account of its excellence (*utkarṣataḥ*), and not on account of its inferiority (*apakarṣataḥ*).
This is further clarified by the subsequent verses beginning with "on account of excellence" (*utkarṣataḥ*) within the section defining the excellence of Śiva.

The demonstration that the excellence of his grace is not [the primary] purpose has been adopted here as a bold and unconventional method for the sake of clarification. As for those [scriptural passages] which establish that even what is offered to one’s own chosen *liṅga* must be given specifically to brothers, sons, sisters, and so forth—

These [offerings] have as their objects the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), the form [of the deity], the meal, the officiant, and the worshipper of Śiva. Therefore, it is impossible for him to consume them himself; for by the very act of his own eating—which consists of the fire-ritual and the form of Śiva—his own duty, which takes the form of an obligation (*prasaṅga*) [to offer], is also accomplished (according to another lexicon, *kḷpti* means "obligation"). However, [as for] those who are uninitiated...

That gift is prohibited; like the remnants of sacrificial oblations (*haviḥ-śeṣa*) used in rites such as the *iṣṭi*, it must be disposed of by eating it according to the rules in order to avoid the fault of neglect. Furthermore, for those who are initiated (*dīkṣita*), consuming that [gift] yields great fruit. Therefore, when there arises the expectation of "to whom should it be given?"—

These [verses] are intended for those such as women and children who, even while being under initiation within their own home, are not qualified to perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); they are to be given [the remnants]. As for what is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having stepped over the *nirmālya*, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times; by stepping over [it], [one incurs an offense]."

Regarding the rule "equal [is the penance] for touching, selling, or eating," this prescribes an expiation even for those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*) upon touching the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from leaping over it. And as for that which is stated: "Whatever has been touched by the *nirmālya*, or eaten by a person—therein, the previously mentioned [penance] is reduced by one-quarter."

Regarding the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) concerning touching, leaping over, or consuming *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) and those who have consumed it: in all such instances, the term *nirmālya* refers specifically to *nirmālya* that has been cast outside. Within that section on expiation, [the term] *devasva* (the property of the deity)...

The substance offered to the deity is the *naivedya*; the substance offered to Caṇḍa is the *nirmālya*. Since the term *nirmālya* is specifically applied when [the offering] has been cast outside, that which remains on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is not considered *nirmālya*, even though it belongs to the deity.

Furthermore, even after the dismissal of the deities (*visarjana*), because there is a description in the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*)— using the terms "the property of the deity" (*devasva*) and "the substance of the deity" (*devatādravya*)— that the purpose of the expiation ending with the external casting away is to avoid the penance for contact [with such substances], it follows that these are not *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings). Otherwise, [the following would be the case]:

If the words "nirmālya" occurring in the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) were to refer to all *nirmālya* without exception, it would follow that the specific designation of "nirmālya" by stating "cast outside" (*bahiḥkṣipta*) therein would be redundant; for [the substance] is already outside even after the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
Furthermore, it would lead to the inconsistency of describing the absence of "nirmālya" status up until the point of discarding [the flower]; for,
since there is fault in touching the ground of a deity or those touched by such [objects],
the word *nirmālya* occurs in the context of penances for touching [prohibited things].

And because it must necessarily have a specific object: that which is called "cast outside" refers to what remains after being given to the attendants who eat the great sacrificial offerings (*mahāhavis*) and so forth,
or what has been led outside for cows, elephants, and the like, or cast into water and such, or given for the purpose of an external offering (*bali*).

All of that, by the force of the scriptural injunction, becomes untouchable immediately after the offering of incense, just like the incense itself. Now, if this is so, then since the instructions regarding penance for consuming temple offerings (*nirmālya*) and the like apply only to those items discarded outside, what then of the property of the deity, the materials belonging to the deity, and the *caṇḍadravya* (materials offered to the *caṇḍa* deities)?
If it is argued that no rule for expiation is found regarding the consumption [of such things] and so forth, we say no; for in that very same [text],
rules are prescribed for the consumption, neglect, giving, selling, transgressing against, and touching of *nirmālya*,
as well as for the consumption, transgressing against, and touching of what has been touched by the *nirmālya* or by its consumer.
After the prescription for atonement,
[the text describes] one who consumes rice and other grains— whether originating from the property of a temple or from a village belonging to a deity—
by whatever means or pretext whatsoever.

Because, in the passage beginning with "one who is deluded, impure, or a thief," the penance for theft regarding the use or giving away of divine property (*devasva*), materials offered to deities (*devatā-dravya*), and offerings to Caṇḍa (*caṇḍa-dravya*) is described separately; [and] in the *Sūkṣmāgama*, regarding the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings)...

In the event of transgressing regarding the *nivedya* during the act of giving, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; for it is said that "one should cast it into the mouths of the serpents. Thus, because the term *nirmālya* is used specifically in the instruction on atonement even when referring to the taking of the *nivedya* separately from the *nirmālya*, these words denoting *nirmālya* are applied in a specialized sense.

It is understood that their scope consists solely of objects that have just been cast outside. Otherwise, if they were intended for the sixfold *nirmālya*, then since the *nivedana* (the offering) would also be included therein, the prior mention of the *nivedana* would be redundant. As for what is stated in the Kāmika itself:

If he is sprinkled with bathing water, milk, or other substances, then he should bathe—that is, wash—in two ways: above and below the navel. This same rule is prescribed even for a mobile liṅga in the sacrificial hall. Thus, at the time of Śiva’s consecration, there is the use of consecration water, milk, curd, and so forth.

Even according to worldly convention, the practice of bathing and washing by distinguishing between the upper and lower parts of the body does not apply here with the intention that the drops of water from the consecration of Śiva and so forth would render the worshipper impure;
for the excellence of the water used in the consecration of Śiva has already been elaborated upon previously. (p. 126)

However, after that, it is improper for one whose body has been sprinkled with the *nirmālya* (remnants) of Śiva to perform the anointing with perfumes and other services for Śiva which the officiant is about to perform; likewise, it is improper for a disciple whose body has been sprinkled by drops of oil from having performed the massage and bathing of his guru.

This is said with the intention that it is like applying fragrant ointments and so forth to one's guru. In this same manner, other similar statements should also be understood. Thus, while eating with the thought that it is an *agnikārya* (fire-sacrifice), one should consume the remains of what has been offered; [one should eat] with the thought of being a servant.

The rule that what has been offered should be eaten by those who eat is faultless. Thus it is also shown in the Vāyusaṃhitā: "Then one should eat pure food at one's pleasure, either what has been offered to the Lord of Gods, or the remnants thereof, for the sake of self-purification."

One who has faith should offer perfumes, garlands, and other such things, not out of greed and not what is presented to a fierce deity; in that case as well, this same rule applies. However, the wise man should not form the thought "I am Śiva" while consuming what has been offered.

One should not form the notion "I am Śrī Śiva" merely by contemplating Śiva as residing in the midst of the fire within the lotus of one's own heart—intending thereby that one is the performer of the fire-ritual for Śiva (meaning: the agent of Śiva’s command)—and thus regarding oneself as the performer of Śiva’s worship. Rather, [one should act] as follows:

The meaning is that one should cultivate the very consciousness of being a servant of Śiva. Thus, for one who eats the food offered [to the deity], even the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutayaḥ*) must be performed only with what has been offered.

"He who performs the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths (*prāṇāgnihotra*) solely through the grace of Śiva, for every morsel of food mastered [as an offering], gains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices."
"A man shall become [such]," according to the statement from the Śiva Purāṇa.
The Procedure for Eating.

Now, the procedure for the meal: Having offered oblations with the mantras prescribed in one's own Sūtra, ending with "svāhā," one should dismiss them. Thus having completed the fire-ritual, with washed feet and hands and having sipped water (ācamana), one should sit together with devotees of Śiva who follow virtuous conduct.

Avoiding those of low birth and those who have not been initiated from the same row, having reached the place for eating and sat upon a seat facing east, according to the sequence of the Ācārya, the Putraka, the Sādhaka, and the Samayika, using a square space measured by the span of a hand;
On a ground adorned with a mandala marked by four, three, two, or one line, and surrounded by lines of ash, [one should place] a vessel made of gold,
silver, copper, or iron— or perhaps made of bell-metal— which has been purified seven times with ashes and consecrated with the Aghora mantra.

In the absence of that [vessel], having placed a vessel made of blameless leaves such as those of the plantain, palāśa, lotus, mango, or madhūka tree, and having spread a layer of ghee therein, one should sprinkle with water using the Astra-mantra the pure food— which has been served, twice-drenched with ghee, and accompanied by side dishes— preceded by the three-syllable Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.

Having consecrated [the food] seven times with the mantra "To Mṛtyuñjaya, Vauṣaṭ," and having performed the sprinkling and other rites according to the respective colors, one should offer [a portion] of food measuring half a mouthful with the formula: "To Nāga, Kūrma, Krakra,
Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya— the subordinate vital airs— Svāhā."
One should offer [the water] upon a mandala smeared with cow dung on one's own right side.

Then, having offered a handful of water to the Nāgas and others using the little finger of the left hand as a ladle, one should consume the water intended for the washing of the *māṣa* beans— water consecrated by Śiva— which is the nectar (*amṛta*), while reciting the *amṛta-mantra*.

One should perform five oblations of breath. By that, one should contemplate the satisfaction of the vital airs—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—which have been invoked in sequence as their respective sources; and likewise the satisfaction of the ancestors dwelling in the depths of Pātāla and the gods. Then...

Having taken some leftover food and offered it on the ground with the words "Svāhā to the inhabitants of hell," and after performing the *uttarāpośana* (the final sipping of water), one should pour out the remainder of that water using the little finger,
and then perform the rites beginning with the wiping of the hands and ending with the pure *ācamana*.

For the purpose of purifying the fault of having consumed [forbidden food], one should sprinkle the Kālāgnirudra located at the tip of the big toe of the right foot with water from the thumb of the right hand. However, regarding the specific procedure for those who eat what has not been offered, it has already been shown previously by way of the example from the *Suprabheda*.

For those who eat what has been offered (*nivedita*) as well as those who eat what has not been offered (*anivedita*), whatever else— such as medicine, betel, water, or other food, or fragrant flowers and other objects of enjoyment— is presented at any time other than the mealtime,
all of that must be eaten only after mentally offering it to the Deity. [The leaf...]

"One should not eat flowers, fruits, water, food, drink, or medicine without first offering them to the Blessed One while remaining composed," according to the *Kāmika-āgama*. "Whatever object is present before one for enjoyment, having offered each of those to the Deity, one should thereafter appropriate it for oneself."

And because of the words of Vātula: "The wise man, having offered food, medicine, water, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth to Śiva, should eat the remainder of that. This injunction regarding the consumption of the remains of what has been offered—such as medicine and the like—is [as follows]:

For one who eats without first making an announcement for the sake of a specific purpose, the food taken during the middle of the meal must be restricted by the consumption of medicinal herbs and the like. However, in other cases, those who are servants of Śiva (śivadāsa) may take only the remnants of what has been offered to Śiva (śivocchiṣṭa).
Furthermore, whatever worldly or Vedic rite a devotee desires to perform with a view toward some particular fruit—
All of that must be performed with the realization that it is of the nature of the worship of Śiva.

Even the pleasure produced by those various actions, since Śiva is its enjoyer, should be enjoyed with the realization: "Having offered it to Śiva, I am now enjoying the pleasure within this worldly existence as it is experienced by Him. Thus, even without...
The objects known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which present themselves through one's own effort,
should be experienced by one's own senses only after first offering them to Śiva and with the understanding that they are His leavings (ucchiṣṭa).
Likewise, the pleasure arising from the experience of each of those objects should also be enjoyed only with the understanding that it is His leavings.

Whatever action is prescribed that arises before one, the wise person should perform each of those with a mind dedicated to Mahādeva. Whatever pleasure has arisen from the senses, having offered it to Śiva, one should enjoy it as a grace.

For it is said that [the goal] is attained through the gateway of the senses; therefore, one who desires that [goal] must always remain vigilant. One should be constantly attentive during unions and separations—whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse.
For it is heard in the *Bṛhatkālottara*: "But he whose mind is dedicated to Śiva is indeed devoted, and not otherwise.
Thus, for one who performs action preceded by the dedication of that action, and experiences objects preceded by the dedication of those objects—

And for a devoted practitioner who, while enjoying happiness preceded by the offering of the happiness produced thereby, remains vigilant, even if he occasionally performs prohibited actions due to negligence at the end of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births, he does not experience the objects of those prohibitions.

Even for one who enjoys prohibited pleasures, no taint of sin occurs; rather, by contemplating that "everything is the propitiation of Śiva," everything indeed becomes solely for the pleasure of Śiva.
In that regard, [one may engage] in activities such as watching dances for one's own enjoyment, or sporting in palaces, gardens, and ponds.
When undertaking various actions, at the time of each respective action,
there are those [results] to be accomplished through the operations of the organs of action— speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—
and those to be accomplished by their respective objects produced by the organs of cognition: the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose.
And for the purpose of bestowing various pleasures,

[He meditates] upon Īśāna and the others, who are respectively present as presiding deities over His own five cognitive organs beginning with the ear and the five organs of action beginning with speech.
Having integrated the ears, speech, and other faculties with their respective counterparts such as the [supreme] ear,

and having contemplated those very pleasures— accomplished through the functions of each respective sense— as being experienced by Śiva, the presiding deity of the forms [of the deities] beginning with Aiśāna; those very pleasures...
One should consume these three with the thought that they are the remnants of Śiva.

At the times of enjoying those various objects, you ought to do so with mindfulness, offering them as the effortless presentation of sensual pleasure. This may be done either in the morning or at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva.

Thinking, "Until the end of the observance (*samaya*), I offer to the Auspicious One all objects of sense consisting of fragrance, together with the experiences thereof and the pleasures produced by them, which have been cultivated with effort and devotion," one should offer them simultaneously. In this way, the simultaneous offering of objects may be performed in the heart and other [centers].
Either by identifying with one's own ears and other senses [the Sāṃbaśiva] meditated upon in locations such as the heart,
or [the Sadāśiva] meditated upon in locations such as the heart, sequentially within the ears and other senses situated in the faces beginning with Īśāna.

In the case of the combined [mantras], the rite should be performed for Īśāna and the others in relation to the ears and other sense organs. In every instance of offering, the mantra of Śiva ending with *namaḥ* is the mantra; its meaning should be contemplated as "this is for Śiva, *namaḥ*.
And that meaning is obtained through the letter *ma*, which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), being in the genitive case.

Thus, all of this is a supreme secret. In this manner, every day at dawn, one should perform the meditation on Śiva preceded by bathing as far as possible, the wearing of sacred ash (vibhūti) and rudrākṣa beads,
and the performance of the sandhyā rites— either three times, twice, or once [daily].
Worshipping Śiva with forty, sixteen, ten, or five modes of service, or even with merely eight flowers, studying the scriptures of Śiva at appropriate times, and listening to discourses on Śiva;

At the time of eating, accepting the remnants of what was offered to Śiva with the thought that it is the performance of the fire-rite for Śiva— or with the thought of being a servant of Śiva— accepting what has been offered to Śiva; and knowing other objects of enjoyment, such as betel, water, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, to have been surrendered to Śiva.

Having contemplated that the collection of actions intended to be performed consists of pleasures in the form of their fruits which are to be enjoyed by Śiva, and performing them with the intention of worshipping Śiva, one disregards personal effort regarding even those sense-objects that have spontaneously arisen, whether they occur at the times of their respective appearances or all at once.
Offering all pleasures to Śiva and experiencing them solely with the thought that they are the remnants of Śiva’s meal,
even at times of reflecting on external worldly affairs, he remains engaged in the constant contemplation of the infinite names of Śiva.
Making fruitful the internal path by wandering through the coming and going [of breath],
he beheld at the appointed times the line of bliss (*ānandalekhā*), which is of unsurpassed radiance and possesses an unreal form;
[he beheld] the Supreme Deity of five syllables, whose lotus feet are sought after by all the Upaniṣads.

The sovereign of all deities, an ocean of boundless compassion, the bearer of the burden of protecting those who have taken refuge, sporting together with Ambikā within the hollow of the lotus of his own heart,
the very embodiment of a mass of bliss.

Constantly beholding the Supreme Śiva within with his inner vision, he dwelt happily together with his beloved kinsmen; and in the noble heart and abode of the Lord of Cinna, the sovereign of Velūr, [he saw] that [bliss] which had been increasing for a long time.
Thus, by the command of the Lord, [the author] has fully explained this procedure for the worship of Paśupati, which is to be joyfully celebrated by the immortals.
Possessing the innate brilliance of the *Ṣaḍrājayoga*, with divine splendor arising from the essence of the *Anāhata*, the *Ājñā*, and other powers;
he is exceedingly steadfast and skilled in the subtle arts of the ritual sequence of invocation.
The illustrious Bommabhūpatilaka shall be a worshiper of Śiva.
May Jvarakaṇṭheśa compose this moonlight of his own worship,
which shall endure until the end of the kalpa, like the moonlight in the celestial realm.
Hariḥ oṃ.
May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the Gurus!
I worship the lotus feet of Mṛtyuñjaya, the Lord of Fever and the Throat,
by taking refuge in which the Moon always shines under the guise of his nails.
The Śivārcanācandrikā is completed.
